title: The laptop stand I'd been looking for
text:
I give this Aidata laptop sand five stars. I bought it the day after I saw someone using one, and have used it for about a month, and it is everything I've been looking for. The two major problems with using a laptop on a table, for me anyway, have been getting the screen high enough that I don't get a 'crick' in my neck from bending my neck down to see the screen, and getting the keyboard at enough of an upwards angle as to minimize any repetitive stress injury. No laptop stand can fix either of those perfectly, since so long as the screen and keyboard are conjoined, the closer down you get the keyboard to your hands, the lower the screen goes, and the higher up you get the screen to your eyes, the higher the keyboard goes. But this stand, with its six different positions, always makes things better, and specifically lets you choose which of the two problems to focus on--to get the screen up really high, or to get the best keyboard angle possible given the table you are using.
I use it with a MacPro 13", and again, it's the best I've found. (I have one other I like, but it has only one position, a relatively low position that is good for the keyboard, but not as helpful with the screen.) It's reasonably light, it packs easily into its small convenient neoprene case, it takes up almost no room in your backpack or briefcase, it's attractive in use, it's easy to unfold for use and refold for transport, and I like the turntable, which stays put unless you quite deliberately turn it, but which can indeed be turned if you want to show your screen to someone else.
Yes, it feels pricey, but I've been looking for a good stand for a long time and was happy to pay for this piece of gear since it is just what I wanted and will serve me for a long time to come.

title: Probably a good travel lens, mine was just cranky...
text:
I was looking for a good travel lens that would cover all spectrums of shooting, and this lens might work for some (obviously it has based on the ratings), but it’s performance -for me- does not replace the convenience of not having to switch lenses. But more importantly for me, I had what I can only determine was a defective unit, and along with that I had to return it.
The defect: from day one, the lens was temperamental with my D5600 – sometimes locking up the camera (required the lens to be re-mounted), but mostly would intermittently display “Lens Not Attached”, and on rate occasions it would stop the camera completely with the LCD displaying the message that I needed to set the lens aperture manually (a false message). Many times this happened when I was trying to shoot an important moment. At times, I could wiggle the lens and get it to intermittently cause the problem. Having just purchased this, I wasn’t in the mood to try to trouble shoot a new lens when all other lenses were working fine and have never had this problem.
The lens: I think the performance is close to the price-value, but there are some things that I didn’t like. First, the zoom – the ratio of twist-to-zoom isn’t good; I feel that it could be more aggressive where less twist is required to move through the zoom range. I found myself having to zoom, reposition hand, zoom to get from center capture to intended zoom and shoot. As well, the effort to twist is both tight, and also inconsistent (there were “hitches” in the twist which kind of make it hard to stabilize when zooming quickly). Second, the images are pretty soft around the edges, and the images themselves aren’t very sharp. I believe this is because the lens needs to be configured with the Tap-in - like it seems most Tamron’s are needing to be that are now Tap-in compatible (is Tamron a little sloppy in setting their lenses tack-sharp because now the user can?). So I imagine the lens can be configured to be much better, just given the other problems I had, I wasn’t interested in messing with it. And third, while Tamron’s VC is generally really good, I found that it wasn’t very good on this lens past 200mm. Switching from mode 1 to mode 3 seemed to help a bit.
If it wasn’t for the annoying defect, I’d give this 4 stars because I think you get a lot for the money and it probably will work for most people especially if they take the time to dial in the lens with the Tap-in (which everyone should).

title: My Best Speaker and Headphones
text: This Motorola Sphere combo Bluetooth speaker and headphones is the fifth or maybe the sixth Bluetooth speaker I’ve gotten over the last year or so and the only one that also comes with a set of headphones. My goal is to get a different one for every space in my home. As of this writing this Motorola product is rapidly becoming my favorite one. The speaker itself is outstanding. It generates a warm, powerful sound with a rich base that can fill a large space with ease. This has become my preferred speaker during social gatherings at home. It can fill my great-room comfortably without cranking it up too loud or resulting in sound distortion. The headphones that come with it are likewise becoming the favorite of my several pair, though I use them selectively. These headphones nearly totally block out outside sound allowing me to enjoy music or an audiobook without distraction, but as I live in a dense city environment, I prefer not to have my awareness of my surroundings compromised by the near-complete blockage of outside sounds I experience when using them on the street. I find the design a bit peculiar, though. Motorola labelled this product a ‘sphere’ but as one can tell from photos the speaker on which the headphones rest, it’s really shaped more like a person’s head with the headphones secured on what would be the ears of this head. Now, this works well-enough in my modernist decor and its grey-black-brushed nickel and steel furnishings, but seeing what is obviously designed as an abstraction of a disembodied human head sitting in my living room does take a bit of getting used too. But that’s a matter of tasted. The product itself is by far the best of the several speakers and headphones I’ve acquired of late.

title: A great access point
text:
I've been using these Access Points in offices for the past 2+ years. The setup is very, very easy once you've installed the Unifi software. Better than the ease of installation is that these devices are steady and stable. I can't think of one client call where they went offline. Even during planned reboots, they are solid and work well.

My one gripe with them is the Unifi software's dependence on Java and why I can't give it a full 5 stars. I won't get on my high horse about Java, but the Unifi software acts erratically depending on the version of Java on your computer. When you run into an issue with it, things can get ugly. You may see the software run fine, but it can't find any access points on the network, the access point may not adopt, you could see issues loading a previous config, etc. I'd blame it on the computer I have but these issues span multiple devices so it isn't just my machine. When in doubt, blame it on the user (me)...

Even with that gripe, I do love these access points. An added bonus is that they don't need a static address, so introducing them to an existing network is seamless with no need to identify an available IP address outside of the DHCP pool. That alone has saved me a lot of time. If you're pondering APs, this one is a winner.

title: It worked great, so great that I got two more for ...
text:
I used these devices to install an NVR based home security camera system by Ctronics with four 1080P resolution cameras, and eventually added 4 more cameras. I bought a WiFi camera system, fully expecting to go wireless, but since we were already a very heavy WiFi user, with Netflix, Amazon Fire, Hulu, PCs, laptops, tablets, cell phones, etc., I found that I didn't have the bandwidth I needed. Putting four security cameras on my WiFi didn't give me the instant access and smooth motion video that I was wanting for all 4 of my cameras recording full time 24/7 at 1080P resolution. I knew WiFi wasn't going to work for me when I installed my third camera outside on my detached garage and I kept waiting and waiting before I could see the stuttering streaming video from that camera.

To the rescue came the Netgear Powerline PLP1200 Plus (PLP) adaptors to let me use my house wiring for my ethernet network instead of WiFi or trying to drill holes and string wiring around my house. One issue I have with Amazon on these, is that you get two plug-in units with the PLP model only - I don't think the advertising of these devices make it clear enough how many units you get in a box because it uses the same picture of two units whether you get one (PL) or two (PLP) units. I bought the PLP model so that I got two plug-in units. This is important when you first use these since one is dedicated to your switch or router on your network. Once you have a unit connected to your network, you only need one 1200 plug-in unit for each device you want plugged into your network.

I put one on my router, and then one on the camera attached to my garage. It worked great, so great that I got two more for the two other cameras I had installed. Eventually I got another two more, for a total of 6 units for 5 cameras and the router. This is a great solution (though not exactly a cheap one) that seems to work almost like magic. It sure solved my problem and I'm glad that I gave it a try.

title: These Things Are GREAT!
text:
I built some small shelves with regular shelving brackets for my audio monitors. They were functional, barely. Since they were fixed shelves, I had no flexibility. Then I found these clamping monitor speaker mounting brackets. They are awesome.

The WALI speaker brackets are supporting a pair of KRK Rokit 5s. These monitors weight about 10 lbs. apiece. I have the brackets fastened to studs in the wall using two screws (supplied), each. The brackets say they'll support up to 55 lbs. I don't doubt they can, but I personally wouldn't put anything more than 30 lbs on them, and for that I'd probably want to use more of the mounting holes with more screws. The brackets have six holes in total: 2 are used if mounting to wood studs, 4 are used for brick or other more brittle/frail support structure. I suppose you could use all six at once, if your wall is constructed so that'd make sense.

As the description says, the brackets tilt & swivel. It's basically like a ball & socket configuration, with the base of the speaker support as the socket, the mounting bolt & supplied plastic washer as the socket. They're very stable, & don't tilt left or right, just front to back, and swivel side to side, allowing you to aim the speakers right at your head.

I was concerned that the clamping mechanism wouldn't hold the speakers securely enough while tilted. My worries were unjustified. The clamps are tightened by a bolt mounted into the arm. Tightening them means turning a screwdriver, drawing the arm into the housing and firmly (but gently) grasping the speaker. The 7.5' of tilt is no problem. It's both enough of a tilt for my situation, but not so much that the center-of-gravity is over the front edge of the support. The supports are padded & don't seem to be capable of marring my KRKS. If one is still concerned the speakers might wiggle out of the clamp's grip during extended, bass-intensive sessions, the clamps can also be screwed into the speakers themselves. This would make a mark and make a hole in the speaker cabinet, but it would be secure.

The WALI support comes with hardware: screw to screw into the wall, bolts, washers, nuts, etc. Even a little wrench to tighten the nut that secures the "ball" to the "socket."

Considering how much money I'd spent on wood, brackets, paint, and TIME to make my prior mounting, these supports are a bargain. I am very happy I found them!

title: This is ALUMINUM wire.
text:
Don't waste your money on this. It is copper clad ALUMINUM. This is NOT copper wire.
If you heat the conductor with a torch, the copper burns off with a green flame, leaving silver aluminum wire, which soon starts to melt and drips silver. You can even tell by the weight of the spool if you've ever lifted a 250' spool of copper #8. Also, the jacket has a very low flash point and can be easily ignited with a cigarette lighter.
This is VERY cheap quality cable.

Finally used a small vise grip to lock the holding tab open and slid the screwdrivers into the sides to pop it out. They had sen t me two videos illustrating how to remove. The first one's tab had bulges at the bottom. Since they didn't want it back, I used a Craftsman rototool to relive the base of the tab. This did not help one bit. I put my iPad in the replacement and had exactly the same problem. They had said not to be afraid to use physical force when pushing on the tab. I have very good hand strength, every one remarks on my handshake, but I can't push the tab back far enough using both thumbs. You have to have the mechanical advantage of a vise grip, and even then you have to pry the iPad out. In spite of all this, I find it basically useful and have ordered the 12x and wide angle lenses. The wide angle is actually a wide/macro combo. I have emailed IOgrapher with all my concerns. They gave me a 15% discount on the lens order, which paid the shipping. I asked them to have their design team contact me, and I asked if there was a local rep or experienced user near me. I also told them that Burtenshaw Electronics here in Idaho Falls would be able to find the reason for the difficulty but that it would cost me twenty bucks. This was today so I haven't heard back as yet. I want this thing to work. It makes the iPad easy to hold with one hand even when not using it for its intended purpose, You can plug in the charger without problems. I have an idea for an accessory that I can have my oldest son make for me in his business shop, and I might suggest it to them for al %. title: Overpriced. Underwhelming.
text:
As a voracious reader, I love my kindle. When my paperwhite got destroyed I figured an upgrade to the Oasis was the smart move. But it's hard to justify it's heavy price tag with the small improvements you get. In the following review I'll start with what I like about the Oasis and then follow it up by it's shortcomings.

The design of the Kindle Oasis is superb. I really enjoy the physical buttons to turn pages or jump back. You can easily hold it in either hand and read comfortably. The buttons are much more pleasing than tapping the screen (which you can also do). The buttons seem to make it that much easier to read one handed, which is critical when I'm riding the subway to work.

The leather cover is great too. I love opening my kindle and just diving right into reading. I opted for the Kindle without advertisements and I would recommend that. I know it's a small inconvenience but when you're trying to make the most of small down times to read it can make all the difference to just open the kindle and instantly begin reading. The cover is elegant looking and seems to be taking the wear and tear of daily life well. It's marred by many imperfections by now that just adds to it's beauty.

The cover also doubles as an "extra battery" that charges the Kindle Oasis when it's attached. This is mostly a gimmick, though. It allows Amazon, on the one hand, to tell you how light the Kindle Oasis is without the cover while ignoring the fact that without the cover the battery life is terribly short. Yes you can read the Kindle Oasis for quite a while without the cover, but generally speaking you'll need that cover on most of the time to keep the Kindle Oasis charged up. As easy as it is to remove the magnetic cover I find it easier to just leave it on. And with the cover on the Kindle Oasis is not discernibly lighter than the Paperwhite.

To add to the gimmicky nature of the cover, there is no way to charge the cover by itself. It must be attached to the Kindle and the kindle plugged in in order to charge. This might not seem like a big deal, but like any external battery the usefulness of them is that you typically charge them while you use the main device. It would be much more helpful if you could charge the cover by itself because then you could actually read the super-light Kindle Oasis sans cover and charge it's external battery.

The biggest let down of the Kindle Oasis has to be battery life. Amazon claims weeks of battery life, but here's the nice little caveat they leave out: In order to get anything close to the battery life they advertise you need to have the Kindle on airplane mode. In my own experience having the Kindle on my home wifi network and reading daily I get maybe a week to ten days of use before needing to charge it. Putting it in airplane mode renders many of the greatest functions of your Kindle obsolete. One of the things I love is the ability to highlight some person's name or a famous spot in a book and quickly read the wikipedia page to familiarize myself with the information. The battery life is pretty lackluster if you want to actually use your kindle to its full capabilities.

Overall, it's a very nice Kindle and one I enjoy reading on a daily basis. However, for the steep price tag it really comes up short in terms of battery life and the gimmicky way Amazon implemented the external battery/cover. Most readers will be better off with the Paperwhite which is, for all intents and purposes, just as good as the Oasis in almost every regard.

title: Dell has an amazing idea in the Inspiron 3000 Series 2 in 1
text:
Dell has an amazing idea in the Inspiron 3000 Series 2 in 1.

It's a small, lightweight, compact tablet/laptop that is very compact and easy to use.

That said, there are a number of downsides to this device.

#1 - The first and worst feature is the power button. Some knucklehead designer/engineer thought it'd be a great idea to put the power button on the front side of the device, right where you place your hand to re-position the device when you set it down or pick it up. Unintended power ons and offs repeatedly happen and when the laptop is sitting in your backpack, right side up or down - the power button get's pressed and drains your battery with you realizing it. Dumb....

#2 - The silver case looks like a slick aluminum strong protective shell, but it's plastic and brittle.... After owning it for 2 weeks it got deeply scratched on the front cover while putting it into my padded backpack and pulling it out of my padded backpack. Also, the SD card slot, has a thin strip of plastic on the bottom of the case that broker after 3 weeks - again, while in my heavily padded backpack on a trip. Seriously Dell? That's some cheap manufacturing.

#3 - The base device that I bought can be forgiven for arriving with a celeron processor. Hey - a celeron these days is equal to a Pentium from a few years ago... But Dell really lamed out by not installing a full 8 GB of memory (which it's capable of handling) and not installing a 500GB Solid State Drive into this device. It came with 4 gb of RAM and a 250 GB SATA drive...... I removed both of those and replaced them with 8 gb of Ram and an SSD (which took quite a while to recognize and install with the new bios in these.)

#4 The power cable that comes with it fits in so-so.... seems to want to fall out a lot.

On the plus side - It's a small, compact device with a great touch screen, good batter life and is very lightweight and inexpensive. If Dell fixed the power button and the cheap, plastic case - those 2 items alone would go along way in making this 2 in 1 tablet/laptop and amazing device.

title: A Tiny Bluetooth Earbud with Good Range & Wireless Charging
text:
This little bluetooth earbud is pretty much everything I want. It is very light, very small, has exceptional battery life, is easy to charge, can connect with multiple devices at once, switching between them on the fly, and doesn't hurt your ear because it is held in only by the rubber bud.

PROS:
Extremely Small
Good Bluetooth Range
Loud
Long Battery Life (4+ Hours Easily)
Wireless Charging (sort of)
Two USB Chargers
Connects with Multiple Devices

CONS:
Sub-par Sound Quality
Can Fall Out of Ear

Honestly, there is little more that I would want from this earbud. Does it fall out of your ear sometimes like others have been complaining? Yes, if you are walking or running, you'll probably have to push it back in with some frequency. That doesn't mean it comes flying out unexpectedly, it just shakes loose, just like most other earbuds, and that's why some designs have rubber attachments that wrap around your ears. However, I didn't buy that model, I bought this one, and having to push the bud back in from time-to-time is far less annoying than having to strap on a crazy hearing-aid style wrap-around, personally. Also, since it comes with three different sized rubber earbuds, it is moderately customizable to your ear.

The "wireless charging" is awesome. How it works is the little USB chargers have two prongs in the center of an indentation that has a magnet behind it. The earbud sticks to the magnet and slides onto the prongs. If you practiced, you probably could throw it at the charger and have it start charging. I really can't stress how simple it is to attach, it's mildly magical. The magnet latches on and about a second later, the blue LED on the earbud turns and you know it is charging.

Pairing it with a bluetooth device is simple: When the earbud is off, hold down the button for about 5 seconds. At about second 3 you'll hear a slightly accented voice say "Device On" and then at second 5 it says "Device Ready to Pair" (I may be paraphrasing here). At that point you need to tell your bluetooth source (be it your phone, or your laptop, GPS, car, whatever) to start searching for a bluetooth device, and it should find a GoNovate G8 and then pair up after about 5 seconds or so. Then the voice will say "Device Connected" and you may even see the G8's power bar on your bluetooth source's screen. I can confirm it does this with the iPhone 5s, but does not with the MacBook Pro, for whatever reason.

You can have the G8 paired with multiple devices and run them simultaneously. HOWEVER: It will play audio from only ONE at a time. So you could be listening to music played by your computer, that would be interrupted when your phone gets a call, for example. Not as cool as playing both at the same time, but still useful.

Basic operation of the G8 is pretty simple: Hold down the little button for 3 seconds to turn it, listening for the voice prompt. You can pause or play music by clicking the button briefly. You can answer calls by clicking the button, or deny them by holding the button for 2 seconds. Plus, like starting it, you shut it down by holding down the button for 3 seconds. That's it. Just 1 button with different hold times, and everything is identified using voice prompts.

MY ONLY NEGATIVES:
Firstly: The sound quality isn't great on this thing. I would describe it as a bit "muddy", with a lot of different tones bleeding into each other. High notes are reasonably crisp, but voices and anything pushing into the bass ranges tend to lose distinction. Personally, I use the G8 to listen to podcasts, which don't require great sound quality. Everything is easy to hear and understand, but you aren't going to want to listen to complicated orchestral pieces on it. The G8 is designed for convenience and portability, and at $18, it is really cheap. It's not exactly a surprise that it can't match my over-the-ear, Sony Studio Monitor Headphones. What is crazy about modern technology isn't that the G8 isn't as far away from those Sony's as the price would indicate. It's no masterpiece for sound quality, but it is sufficient, and that's a long, long ways away from cheap headphones of twenty-years ago, or even ten, or possible even five-years ago.

Secondly: The original shipment arrived with a Flexible USB charger, and a non-adjustable Car USB charger. The Car USB charger worked perfectly, the Flexible USB Charger didn't fit the G8. So I contacted the seller and the immediately shipped me a second Car USB charger, which also works perfectly. I don't know if this is the case for all of the Flexible USB Chargers, but I must commend the seller (in this case: Ken from GoNovate) for rapidly responding and correcting the issue by providing a second Car USB charger for free. Now I have two chargers, as advertised, and they both charge the earbud perfectly.

CONCLUSION:
It is cheap. Its battery lasts a long time. It is very easy to use and setup. It doesn't hurt your ear. Charging it is very easy. It is cheap. The sound quality is good enough to not be annoying. It can be used by multiple devices. Plus: It is really quite cheap.

title: Does what it's supposed to with no problems.
text:
I use this to recover files from glitched hard drives that won't boot to Windows.

Plug and play. You plug it into your USB port, connect the power supply, and then plug your drive into it. Windows sees the drive and you can copy/paste files using File Explorer. I use this device to recover files from drives which are glitched and are unable to boot to Windows. As long as the drive has a readable file structure then this device basically just turns it into an external drive. I've only used it with SATA drives but see no reason why it wouldn't work with IDE drives too.

I've never used the one touch backup button so can't comment on that except that I think to use it you have to install the software that comes on the CD with the converter. The software isn't needed just to copy and paste files, though.

This converter also serves as a diagnostic tool. If a drive is really messed up then it either won't be detected or else it will appear with a drive letter (F:, G:, etc) but no information about the size or how much room is available on the drive, or a partition may be missing. In this case I know that I'll have to install the hard drive into my desktop and run a deep scan software to try to recover the files. So connecting the drive externally to this converter is a quick first step... if it can read the drive then I don't have to actually install the drive inside a machine and do it the hard way.

title: Eliminates NAGGING! Love it.
text: Purchased this in time for summer. We have 3 daughters... 10, 13 and 15. They each have multiple IOS devices. I've found it impossible to keep up with their screen time/usage. They are expected to turn in their devices to the kitchen for charging by 9 p.m. or they lose their phones for the next day. During the school year, their day is automatically regulated with school. Those are 7 hours that I know they aren't doing a lot on their devices. . However, with summer coming, the last thing I wanted was a struggle with them sitting around the house on social media sites or YouTube all day long. Along with that, the one thing I hate more than anything is nagging. Circle definitely helps with that. Everything is automatic, and now we can (hopefully) eliminate the 9 p.m. "kitchen" turn in since Circle shuts all activity down when it's time for bed. I don't feel the need to chase everyone's device down. They know how much total screen time they get and they have to manage it. I'm also in the process of allocating their Verizon data so that they don't switch to data usage and run up our wireless bill. So far, it's been hardest for our 15 year old. She's actually pretty responsible and feels like this is something for kids. So, we are allowing her to help us set her limits... lots of communication, lots of negotiation and trying to get to the point where our kids know how to SELF REGULATE, which is ideally where I want to end up. Screens are how young people learn and stay in touch. It's not all bad, but some of the apps out their are highly addictive, so we just keep talking to our girls about the value of face to face conversations with friends, spending time with other hobbies, sports, activities... Circle handles the times when they refuse to listen to us! (We've only had it hooked up for a couple days, so hopefully nothing terrible happens. Also, we have a Netgear Extender and it works just fine with it.)

title: Very nice little camera, capable of excellent image quality, but poor battery life.
text:
A very nice little camera. Small, lightweight but feature-packed, it's an impressive package. The APC image format is equal to most consumer DSLR cameras, and it shoots RAW files, so this is a serious camera. Image quality up to 2500 ISO is excellent, and above that the inevitable noise is not too objectionable, reminding me somewhat of fast negative film grain rather than digital noise. The standard 16~55mm lens is very good for a kit lens, and gives somewhat wider coverage (equivalent to a 24mm lens on full-frame cameras) than usually found on these types of lenses. Distortion at the wider angles is serious, but if you shoot RAW it's easily corrected during processing.

The camera handles well and the controls are not too confusing, although being placed so close together they can lead to accidental and unwanted changes if you're not careful. The digital viewfinder is just OK, color is poor but it enables careful framing at least, the biggest problem is that it shows the review image that is more normally inspected on the rear screen, which needs to be cleared before continuing to shoot. The biggest problem with this camera, and the only reason I did not give it 5 stars, is that battery life is terrible, at least with the original equipment Sony batteries. The stated specifications in the manual are totally unrealistic, the camera just sucks its batteries dry even when on standby. A minimum of two fully charges batteries is a must for a day's shooting, and I would recommend traveling with three.

Adapters are readily available for a variety of older SLR lenses. I used one for Pentax K-mount with a 135mm lens, and got surprisingly good results.

I have not tried the video mode, but I hear it's very good.

Edit, after 20 months' use: Still very pleased with this camera on the whole. The connection from the camera to the rear screen is starting to falter when the screen is pulled out at an angle, the image will just disappear. Not a huge problem for me, but annoying. Otherwise quality and reliability has been fine. That kit lens is amazingly good.

title: Perfect for use in Church environment and automatically connect together and then remember those connections too - awesome.
text: I bought the receiver/transmitter kit first to try it at our church by broadcasting 70 feet line of site and they worked perfectly.  Then, I bought two more receivers and transmitted to a projector over the altar and to a TV in the foyer behind a brick wall with sound proof sheathing and initially had pixilation, but after adjusting the position of the transmitter and the receiver antenna's, all three (2 TV's and a Projector) were streaming away in full 1080P resolution.  The TV's are 70 ft line of site & 85 ft behind brick wall away and the Projector is about 30 ft line of site.  I called Tech Support at J-Tech and confirmed they could not guarantee transmissions to 3 receivers, but I would say if you have unobstructed signal to all three they will do it.  If there is an obstruction, try transmitter location and antenna positioning (the kit came with an external extender antenna base for added flexibility and improved signaling around obstacles), it solved my problem rather quickly.  I'm so excited to finalize the installation & implement this solution in our church's environment and not have to run unsightly cables long distances through the sanctuary, plus, HDMI is limited to about 50ft and other cabling standards require converters anyway.  Radio transmission and reception is the way to go for a clean, professional looking install of communication based equipment.  My only wish would be for J-Tech to offer a transmitter that would broadcast to more than 2 or 3 receivers.  I've got a need to broadcast to 2 more TV's and trying to avoid HDMI splitters and long cables.  Bottom line, strong, well built devices in metal chassis (remember to mount with vent slots open to bottom and top so air can flow up through the devices) and they connect automatically every time.

title: Amazing filters.
text:
I bought these for my Mavic pro and used them for 2 months now. They come in a nice box that fit perfectly in the front pocket of the DJI Mavic bag. They are easy to put on/off given that you are careful and use the right way. Keep the gimbal clamp (to prevent applying too much pressure on the system) on and push the filter all the way against the lens. Make sure that your finger are not in contact with the lens as you do this or you risk staining the lens with your fingerprints and reducing the image quality. If the filter is not completely against the lens it will interfere with the gimbal calibration at start up and provide a motor overload error message. Also, if not properly installed it may affect the focus and the quality of the image.
I mainly use the ND16 (sunny days) and CPL (landscapes with amazing colors). The image and video quality are exceptional. My only suggestion to this set would be to eliminate the UV filter (I don't it's useful) and add an ND32 or ND64. Additionally a microfiber lens cloth would be a nice addition to the set (you are going to touch those lenses soon or later.

title: Works well, not super user friendly, and is a little overpriced
text: Bought this for use with a Vera controller in a family member's house.  The advantage is the ten chime settings that allow you to use as a door chime.  Part of what was desired was a chime like traditional wired alarms so that there would be an audible alert when a door in the house is opened.  For some reason this is the only product that i could find that does this.  The tones are pretty weak in terms of appeal to me.  There are two out of the ten that work for a chime, although one of those is really just a doorbell sound.  I configured it for the single beep when a door is opened.  It is pretty reliable as far as i can tell.  The delay is very slight... about the time the door is opened 30 - 45 degrees the chime beeps. That's perfectly acceptable for me. There are three volume settings but i have yet to see how to adjust those without LUA code.  For Vera there is a plug-in that makes selecting the tones easy via the GUI rather than having to write that stupid LUA code to call the function.  Dome's website has how-tos on triggering the chimes via LUA code, but i didn't have any luck getting one of those to run.  The plug-in is pretty stupid in my opinion as it doesn't seem to provide any useful feedback to let you know the chime is actually configured.  It makes a second dome siren in your devices, so look for that.  The second one created will have buttons to select tone chimes by clicking a button instead of writing a LUA function.  It would be really nice if Dome made these a) without the useless LED, b) with better options for chime tones that don't require an expert to program them into the device c) for less than $50, and d) make an outdoor version.  The price seems ludicrous for just being a "beeper".  The build quality seems good so i would definitely say it's not a cheap-o z-wave device.

title: Designed well but still disappointing
text:
*UPDATED REVIEW*
Update: Stars (3/5)
A few months have passed and the battery life has gotten waaaay better. I don't know if it's an adjustment I made or if the machines just needed to power cycle a couple of times, but now I'm measuring these in months instead of a week or two. That really was my principal complaint and I'm a lot closer to it being addressed. I'll put it this way, now it's long enough between charges that I've had to start writing down when I charge them so I can keep track! I've gotten it past a month now. Who knows, maybe I will hit 3 months on one charge later this year. It's certainly looking like it's possible now.

I'd also like to mention that since I've gotten this device it has helped me solve a few mysteries about what's going on outside my window. For example, I learned that squirrels daintily eat cat food one piece at a time!

Original Review: 2/5
I'm really disappointed with this camera. It's actually designed really well. I love that they made the cameras battery-operated so you can easily mount them outside. As an apartment dweller this is appealing to me. The setup of it was pretty good. The configuration of it isn't bad. It isn't uploading my videos to the cloud. Heck, when the motion detection goes off it sends a thumbnail to my Apple Watch. This is what I want!!!

Except... no. Remember the battery-operated bit? They claim in the documentation that it should last approx 3 months. I haven't gotten these cameras to last longer than a week. I get that motion detection eats up battery, but the field of view of the camera is *very* wide and the motion detection sensitivity settings are nowhere near fine-grained enough to filter out things like people walking around across the street or the tress waving. I don't see how I could even get in the neighborhood of their boast.

Oh and one other thing about the battery. When I first got it installed ONE of the cameras, its battery died, and my phone had a bunch of notifications alerting me that it needed to be charged. (That's a 7 hour process, btw.) Great! Except the OTHER camera did not alert me. I found that out when a kid was hit by a car in front of my apartment. I went to go see if I had video that'd be useful and the camera had been dead for at least a day. (The child is okay.) Now maybe MAYBE I just missed the notification, right? Welp, I charged the camera, set it up, waited a week.. same thing happened again, no notification of battery failure. Not only is this a critical feature, but it also means that these cameras are only useful 6 days a week, the 7th day for charging. No.

One other serious issue I have with this system is that I motion detection does not work very well unless the camera is outdoors, I got soooo many false positives when I had the camera in the inside behind a window. If you're a home-owner this probably isnt' a huge hurdle but as an apartment dweller it's a crappy limitation.

What is keeping me from giving this just one star is it is a useful device. For example, the next time I go on vacation and I'm going to be away from my apartment for a couple of weeks, I can tell you from personal experience this setup would be EXCELLENT for warning me if someone has entered my apartment. Seriously, if I purchased it for that particular task I'd give it 4 stars. But for outdoor monitoring, the battery life is a deal-breaker.

I do want to stress one more time... this product really does hit all the right design-marks. Seriously, I've used other cameras that don't think to do things like using a heavy-magnetic mount so you can easily take it down without it being loosey goosey and flapping around in the wind. It's just really disappointing to see something as well thought out as this was has such a crippling oversight.

title: Easy to Bypass and Slows Internet Speed
text:
All the reviews that Ive seen concerning the Disney Circle have been from parents who have been flattered by its performance. However, the device has some major flaws that I would like to point out. My parents got the Circle about 2 months ago and it has been riddled with issues. First of all, it uses ARP Cache Poisoning to carry out a man in the middle attack on your LAN. In lay terms, that basically means it tells all the devices on your network that it is the router and thus intercepts all internet traffic. This has some serious side effects however. First of all, it will slow down your internet connection. It made our latency on our WiFi incredibly slow which made gaming and watching live streams almost impossible without extreme lag. Also, besides making your internet slower, It causes some huge weaknesses with the filter itself. Im a teenager and although I do know a lot about computers, I wouldn't say I'm super technologically advanced. I was able to successfully bypass the filter within 5 minutes and I know multiple ways to do it. Since it uses ARP poisoning all you have to do to bypass it is create a static ARP entry with your router from your device and it will completely bypass the filter. You could also use an anonymous browser such as Tor and it would have no ability to filter it.
Overall, I think the device lowers your internet quality and if your kids know anything about computers, which they probably do, or just how to Google, than it won't be able to filter them.

title: Great audio, Horrible App, Limiting design
text:
This was my first sonos product. I have been looking at them for a while and the opportunity FINALLY came up to buy this.

I bought two play 1 speakers and set them up in my living room as a pair.

First impressions: The audio quality is awesome (10 out of 10). They can get very loud and music sounds awesome on them.

The biggest issues I had are:

- The app is horrible for any setup other than a basic setup. I had a tough time setting them up to my enterprise wifi network and I had a very hard time setting them up via a wired ethernet. I spent an hour trying and gave up. I setup an old wifi router and used that to setup the speakers.
- No line in. The fact that this isn't future proof is a fatal design flaw. Spending $400 on speakers that require a propriety app to run is outrageous for me.

I know there are major fans for the company or this model, but what happens if the company goes bust? Or you decide that you want a new phone or tablet that isn't supported by them? What about if you sign up for an audio service that they don't support? The only hope we have is hackers that created airsonos software (Airplay for Sonos written in NodeJS).

I tend to view audio equipment as an investment for a long time. In this case, it feels like these speakers are designed to be used for a short time.

If SONOS redesigns this with a line-in, I would probably change the review to 5 stars. With a line-in, I can use airplay, which would be a major feature.

I will next test the Play 5 speaker. I'm certain the setup will be just as challenging, but if it allows simple line-in playback, it may be a nice compromise.

title: Good for the money -- not quite perfect.
text:
Works well mostly, but has a few issues I don't like.

Pros:
+ Very sleek design that looks good with all my other "tech" equipment on my desk.
+ 7-ports with USB 3 provides the fastest USB transfer speeds currently available. I am easily maxing out the transfer rates on my old USB 2 external hard drive.
+ Indicator lights are easy to see but not so bright that they blind you.
+ Although obviously a very plasticy piece of equipment it feels like it is well built and doesn't feel cheap in hand.

Cons:
- I have two dongles, both made by Microsoft that just absolutely refuse to fit in this USB hub. I've used the dongles (for the Microsoft Sculpt Ergonomic Keyboard) for almost a year in *many* different ports and never had an issue. With that note, all other dongles, cords, and dummy plugs have fit the hub perfectly.
- This USB port has a power button. Furthermore, if you unplug or turn off your power strip, when you provide power to the hub again you must turn it on manually. This is, to be fair, a minor inconvenience but it's the only hub I've ever had with a power button and it's just kind of odd.
- The USB cable that goes to your computer is in the back of the hub but the power adapter cord is on the left. So, you have cords coming out of three different sides. This makes it impossible to butt it up against a wall to provide more desk space.
- This is probably my biggest complaint: Even though it says it provides more than 2amps of power, my tablet does not like to be charged with this hub at all. It's an old Samsung Galaxy and when I try to charge via this hub I get a little error symbol in the tablet's charging icon. Smaller, less juice-hungry devices like my phone and even a portable hard drive have all worked fine.

Conclusion:
So, it probably sounds like I'm saying this hub isn't a good piece of equipment. That's actually not the case. It's just that for such a simple device, it's difficult to really make a USB hub stand out. For the most part, you plug them into your computer and then plug things into them. USB is mature enough that "it just works." Having said that -- actually, because of that -- I find myself becoming very particular about the details of these things. And honestly, for the price, I've not come across a USB hub that I like better than this one.
Parting thought: if you can live with the things I consider cons above, it's a good product for the price.

title: Quality product, but check your Infinity amp connectors first.
text:
So apparently there are TWO differently 2002-2004 Dodge Ram 1500 with Infinity sound system wiring harnesses. One is this product and the other is 70-6510 which actually contains 3 connectors. It stated that if you don't have the telephone icon or steering wheel controls then the 70-6512 "is for you". I ordered this one before taking apart my dash to get at the Infinity amplifier which had 2 harnesses connected to it which already had me alarmed. I went ahead and connected everything anyway and nothing worked. other than the head unit was powered up. Another reviewer mentioned that if your Infinity amp has two connectors you need the 70-6510 which I have since ordered and will hopefully work as it looks to have two connectors that connect to the amp connectors and then another one to connect at the head location for a total of three which makes sense. I guess my issues is the product description mislead me as obviously there are vehicles out there without steering wheel controls or a phone icon that the 70-6512 won't work for. I'm out the cost of the harness as I didn't get to the project before the return period was up. The wires and connectors themselves look like quality products and if the 70-6510 works for me then I know it should last for years.

UPDATE: So I ordered the 70-6510 and it did not work (won't even connect!). So this harness, the 70-6512, was the correct harness, the problem is, for me at least, it's not pinned correctly! I pull out all of the pins and then used a wiring diagram and re-pin it to match and now everything is working. I've attached the wiring diagram I found that was at least correct for my 2002 Dodge Ram 1500 SLT Quad Cab. Of the two harnesses coming into the infinity amp, the smaller connector is the inputs and the larger one has the constant power for the amp and the wires going out to the speakers. So the harness is still worth it for me in that I didn't need to cut my wiring harness and butt connect all the leads but what a pain this whole experience was!

title: I like to think of myself as being very handy in ...
text:
Mixed reviews on here, so I was hoping to be one of the lucky ones.

The unit came well packed, with not a dint on the box. I unpacked it and set it up,. It is quite a substantial unit, but it has the look and feel of something that's been made in someone's garage ... in a hurry. Never mind, its what the unit does - right? I made up the fluid, and put a record on it.

I turn on the motor to rotate the record and hear a 'grumbling bearing' sound, which - to me - indicates 'cheap', but I continue. I lower the cleaning arm onto the album, and ... the cleaning arm touches only the run off track, not the rest of the album. Assuming the album (from the 70s) was bowed, I replaced it with an 180 gram album. Nope - same thing - which means that the cleaning arm wasn't parallel to the vinyl.

After trying to sort that out - without success - by raising and lowering the peg on the center bearing, I accidentally put the back of my hand on the suction area while the vacuum is switched on. I then notice there is NO suction.

I like to think of myself as being very handy in repairing things, but I had already spent the best part of two hours on something that had cost me $499. Should I really be having to fix something that costs so much and is designed to do only one thing? I think not! So it was back in the box for return and good riddance.

To me there is either very poor quality control or the thing is just very poorly made and cannot travel even when well packed. Congratulations to those reviewers who bought a peach, but I'm afraid I was amongst those who bought a lemon.

Buyer be very much aware!

title: I have always preferred IPS panels for their inherently better color reproduction as well as better viewing angles
text:
I bought this model to use first as a computer monitor and secondly as a TV. I have always preferred IPS panels for their inherently better color reproduction as well as better viewing angles. The trade off is the lower contrast ratio compared to a VA (Vertical Alignment) panel. If you are looking for a true dark room theater quality experience, this is not the TV for you. But in terms of vivid, vibrant colors and being able to view this TV off center without losing color or contrast, this is a very, very good TV. The 4K upscaling works well especially if you have a HD 1080p source. And the Magic Remote with the Web Os 2.0 Smart Platform works extremely well. As long as you can hook up by wi-fi or direct connection to the internet you can get all the streaming services like Amazon Prime, Netflix, Hulu and a host of others with this TV. The Web Os 2.0 works very well and includes an on screen user guide. You can even surf the web with the included web browser.

This TV also works very well as a large 4K computer monitor. I have tested it myself and it does function 4K@60Hz with chroma 4:4:4. To do this you have to hook up to HDMI port 1 or 2. There is no included HDMI cable, but I used the Amazon Basics high speed cable which worked perfectly. Then press the Settings button on the remote > the three vertical dots circle > Picture > HDMI ULTRA deep color > turn ON. You have to restart the TV at this point. Next go to Device Connections > HDMI 1 or 2, whichever one you are connected to, > edit > then scroll down to PC and click it on. Now go into your computer graphics card control panel and set the resolution 3840x2160 and refresh rate at 60 Hz. You are good to go now. The main drawback as a computer monitor is that it has relatively high input lag. If you are a demanding or hard core gamer, especially FPS, this will not work well for you. Turn off TruMotion which does increase input lag, but then as a casual gamer I find the input lag perfectly acceptable for me. The size takes a little getting used to but it is a big wow factor. The IPS panel is a big plus also.

As a combined monitor and tv this is an excellent platform.

title: A Great Android Tablet, With Lots of Expansion/Functional Options.  The Wi-Fi Only Function Can Be Limiting.
text:
The Samsung Galaxy S3 tablet is larger format version of my (non-Samsung) Android smart phone, but without the SIM card. This good and bad, but manageable.

From my pre-purchase research, I had three tablets within budget range. The Sony Xperia Z4, Google Pixel C and the Samsung Galaxy S3. My preference was for fully functional stylist, maximum SD card memory expansion, and good product reviews. I wasn’t looking for another PC/Window work station. I have a Dell barely portable laptop that does that function very well.

The Pixel C has no memory expansion. I was near to buying the Z4, until I found it doesn’t have system compatible stylist. With that, I made the purchase of the Galaxy S3.

In addition to the S3, I also purchased a 256GB SD card, a folio cover, the Samsung keyboard cover, a Bluetooth travel mouse, and a SanDisk 256GB WiFi/USB flash drive. The S3 is way skinny, with single Micro USB Type-C port and audio jack. All peripherals have to be Wi-Fi/Bluetooth. And yes, I did want 500GB of storage available to the S3.

The S3 replaces an old Lenovo ThinkPad tablet that died. I knew just how handy a stylist can be from using the ThinkPad stylist. The S3 is much more capable than the ThinkPad, and there are handy functions on the S3 that are not available on, or quicker to use from, my Dell barely portable.

Make no mistake S3 is an Android tablet. The first thing the initial set up did, after I entered my Google account log-in, was to install every active application that I have installed on my smart phone. My smart phone and S3 have very similar looking screens now.

There are Android and design limits that I’m still getting used to. The Bluetooth Microsoft Mouse has limited function. The left button and scroll are the same as in a Windows system. The right button and side scroll are set to button functions on Samsung smart phones. S3’s ‘Back’ button and ‘window’ button are on either side of the way-cool finger print button, and NOT on the screen. I keep trying to run the mouse cursor to both buttons, and… D’OHH!! That’s what the stylist or fingers are for.

The S3 is sold as a Wi-Fi tablet. That is one of the main differences between the S3 and my smart phone with its network SIM card. This Wi-Fi only function can be limiting. My smart phone does have Wi-Fi Hot-Spot function, so as long as my S3 and phone are in proximity, the S3 has a Wi-Fi network. Yes, Samsung sells tablets with SIM card capability. The S3 would provide better independent operation with a SIM card option. A SIM card back-fit would be nice, but appears unlikely.

I am happy with my purchase of the S3. It’s an Android tablet, not a Windows PC pretending to be a tablet. I purchased it to be quick, portable, for fun and sometimes games. My Dell barely portable laptop is there for workstation duty.

title: Worth the upgrade from PW3
text:
What’s in the box:

Kindle Paperwhite
Charging Cable

Screen/Light:

The first thing you’ll notice is a smooth, flush screen that not only looks amazing, but is also very responsive. Text is crispy and clear in all lighting settings and while using inverted black & white text. The screen is very prone to fingerprints, but luckily they are not noticeable while reading. I don’t notice any difference in lighting from the previous Paperwhite. There is no adaptive light or night mode.

Look & feel:

The 10th Gen Paperwhite is noticeable lighter and a bit smaller than its predecessor. The back is a matte finish which makes it feel comfortable to hold; however, it’s a fingerprint magnet.

Waterproof:

We finally have a waterproof Paperwhite! Ran it under water with zero issues.

Firmware:

My Paperwhite shipped with Kindle Firmware Version 5.10.1.1. I received an OTA Firmware update to 5.10.1.2. This is a great update that added some noticeable, helpful features to the Paperwhite (Note: This update is also available for the previous Paperwhite)

1) Create personal “Themes” which saves the page layout, font and font size.
2) Return library books from your Kindle by long pressing in the cover and selecting return
3) Remaining battery percentage is shown next to the battery symbol.
4) Toolbar labels

Audible:

The ability to access my Audible library and the Audible store is a huge plus. You can quickly switch between the Kindle version to Audible by clicking the headphone icon in the button corner. This will automatically turn on Bluetooth & bring you to the Audible book. If you decide you want to go back to reading simply click on the book icon. Note: Bluetooth will remain on until manually turn it off. While listening to an Audible book you can adjust the volume/speed, jump fwd/backward 30 secs, add bookmarks and view/go to chapters. One thing missing that I’d love is a sleep timer. Immersion reading would also be a nice feature.

New Accessibility Features for Paperwhite include:

VoiceView which will read your Kindle book to you using (You will need to connect to a Bluetooth speaker)
Invert black and white. I love this feature when reading in complete darkness. So much easier on my eyes.

Battery:

I was a bit concerned the battery performance would be on par with the entry level Kindle that also has Audible & Voice View. I’m happy to say the battery performance on the 10th gen Paperwhite is much better. I’ve read Kindle books for about 12 hours w/light at 50%, listened to Audible for approx 3 hours, played around with settings for maybe 30 minutes, connected to WiFi 24/7 and an OTA update was completed. My battery is currently at 42%.

I opted for the 8GB with Special Offers as 8GB will be plenty for my use as keep my Kindle/Audible content in the cloud and only download the books I’m currently reading or listening to. The special offers don’t interfere with reading and I’ve actually found new authors to love with the recommendations.

So far I’m loving my Waterproof Paperwhite. It’s everything I’ve wanted in an E-reader at an affordable price. If you’re debating if you need to upgrade your Paperwhite go for it. You won’t regret it.

text:
With this tripod, you get what you pay for. I agree with many of the other reviewers here on the pros and cons of this little device:

Pros:
- Very cheap for a usable tripod
- The built-in level is a great feature!
- Has a good aesthetic appearance to it
- When broken down, it's very small, about 14-inches long
- Comes with travel bag, tripod mount, wipe cloth, lots of accessories
- Easy to adjust and customize size and angles

Cons:
- Made with cheap materials: plastic and extremely thin aluminum
- When fully extended, it's very flimsy and almost worthless because of how much it will sway

Recommendation:
At this price point, BUY. At the smallest height, it is very sturdy. In the middle height setting, it's still sturdy enough for good usage. At the third and longest height, it's legs start to bend and it's nearly useless........but it's $12!!!! If you want something professional that will hold up in a snowstorm, then buy a professional-grade tripod. Professional tripods are easily upwards of $100. This does the job for amateurs. Another option to keep sturdiness: don't extend the tripod past the 2nd legs and instead use an extension pole on the top for more height

title: The fluid head on mine did not survive changing environmental conditions well (it begun to leak)
text:
So here's the scoop. I was shopping for a good travel tripod when I saw this lightning deal on cyber monday. this thing had all the features I was looking for on the itesm i already had on my wish list (and more). I thought, "wow, this is the one i've been waiting for". The carbon fiber legs are great... it's really stable; especially when weighted down. and the quick release has a nice safety pin to keep the camera from falling down. I didnt have any issues like some of the more common ones like making the legs so loose they fall off. I know how friction tigteners work and I know better than to keep unscrewing it until it comes apart. It's not as good as clamps because with clamps you can visually see when it's tight; you have to feel these each time you set it up. But overall it was a great product, but for one thing...

The big deal breaker for me was the fluid head (i'm likly going to return it because of this.)

The fluid head works great under controlled environmental conditions (like indoors), but it does not survive changes well. I just got back from a trip out west (western united states - Grand canyon and surrounding desert and canyoon areas [excellent vistas and spectacular photo opportunities]) and it worked great at first, but the daily changes in altitude, temperature, barametric pressure, etc... were just too much for it. it started to leak fluid on the third day. it still kind of worked afterwards, but never as good as when it was new. it wasnt smooth anymore and kind of felt like a friction swivel there after. I know how fluid heads work and I made sure to keep the horizontal axis loose while traveling so as to give it some room to expand, but I think the issue is that its a fixed fluid pressure inside the head and you cant adjust it directly. With other fluid heads you would be able to release pressure and allow for expansion, but not with this one. The fliud motion was a big selling point for me. I can get another tripod with the clamps for a bit less than this and get a better fluid head for it separrately. I really need a travel tripod to survive a diverse range of travel. I have many other trips planned this comming year in much more rapidly changing conditions. the trip west was a test for this to see if it could meet my needs. I really like all the features this thing came with but in the end I'll settle for less features and more robustness on the basics.

title: Very poor range if connected from inside house to outside.
text:
Glad I saved the box and cable so I could return it. Does it work? Yes. Does the solar charger work in bright sunlight? Yes. Will it charge fully in the shade? No. Does it have a 50' range? NO! Does the unit provide accurate sound? No. It is over-bright and lacks bass (understandable from a 4" speaker).

I purchased this speaker in hopes of placing it on a fence post near my bedroom window to play soothing, natural, ambient sounds at night to help mask the electric motor noise from the neighbor's pivot irrigation system. (We live way out in the country. It is VERY quiet here at night but the neighbors let this very noisy irrigation system move all night long—every 30 seconds or so the electric motors come on driving me batty!) The post is maybe 15 feet from my bedroom window. Add another 4 feet to my dresser where my laptop was residing for a total of under 20 feet of distance. The range of this speaker is so poor that the only way I could play any sound through it was by placing it directly under my window on a stand. So we are talking about maybe 5 feet of distance. Problem is, right at that location the speaker only gets direct sunlight for an hour or two a day—not enough to keep it fully charged for 8 hours of overnight use. In my shady spot it could not fully recharge after my initial charge from a wall charger. In addition, if I so much as walked in between my laptop and the speaker, and especially if I stood in front of my laptop, it would cause major drop outs, creating a stutter effect.

I did not have major hopes for high-quality audio from this unit to begin with but it pretty much failed on ALL accounts in my real world situation. If I could have placed it in direct sunlight it on that post as I had intended it would probably would have been charged enough each day to play all night. But because of the short Bluetooth range, this was not possible. Maybe if you have a smart phone or tablet out in your yard or on your patio and the speaker can get plenty of sunlight and it has a direct line from the broadcast device with no obstacles you might be happy with this unit. But do not expect 50 feet of range if there is ANYTHING in between the broadcast device and this speaker!

BTW, if you do not know how to set up a Bluetooth device GOOD LUCK! I know computers quite well and have paired many Bluetooth devices. It still took quite a few attempts at getting this thing hooked up. And if I moved it I had to pair it up all over again. What a hassle! So it is NOT plug and play. So unless there is a compelling need for a wireless Bluetooth speaker in your life, I'd suggest that you purchase a wired one. That will simplify your life and give you far better range than this Solaris rock speaker.

title: Quality Superzoom Point And Shoot
text:
The Coolpix B500 is a nice point and shoot camera that shares the limitations of its class. On the positive side, it looks serious (at least in black) and boasts a solid feel, generous zoom range and generally effective autofocus and exposure capabilities. However, excepting ISO choices and exposure compensation in certain modes, there is not a lot the user can do to directly control the image making process.

If not stated clearly enough already, be aware: aperture and shutter speed cannot be set nor prioritized on this camera. And, notwithstanding a few modes of autofocus, any actual manual focus control is nonexistent.

Thus, the "point and shoot" designation is appropriate, notwithstanding an impressive zoom and striking appearance. Taken for what it truly is, the B500 is a fine automatic camera and a fun one. Great images can be produced, along with misfires, blurs, and opportunities lost while the camera is deciding what to do. It may be best suited to subjects unlikely to move around much while being photographed. (Although multiple bursts can be had in sports mode.)

Positives that should be considered are this model's image stabilization capability with long zooms, its use of easily available AA batteries and a hinged LCD screen which allows the camera to be held high or low to make the shot.
Negatives, even for a PNS, include a slight tendency to overexposure (easily corrected), lack of a viewfinder and
presets that offer hue, contrast and other choices best left to post production, not estimation via the LCD.

I can't comment on the effectiveness of the Bluetooth and Wi-F- features and will eschew experimentation. This is not because I am technically obtuse and it is clear that such connectivity has become standard. From my point of view, however, it will be easier to take and share quick snaps using just my phone and I don't see the need use it to view images in the field or edit them later on.

The street price of the B500 hovers at around $250.00 and that seems reasonable given the splendid quality of the images it successfully captures. For folks on a budget or looking to add great zoom to point and shoot basics, it is well worth consideration.

title: Can do better for maximum clarity and detail, but highly recommended if your priority is a smooth sound that never fatigues
text:
These are the ones I ended up keeping after auditioning them and a half dozen other similar speakers for a couple of weeks. Elacs were right in the middle price wise, but all budget speakers close enough in price that I'd have kept whichever I liked the best. These were them, for good and bad.

The bad, first imo they were the among the cheapest looking and constructed speakers of them all, with the one exception being their binding posts- those are the nicest I've ever seen. The finish and shape of the caps are super nice, turn with the least amount of wobble. The black vinyl doesn't look or wear well I can tell already; and if you keep the grills off, the reversed pegs are pretty unsightly sticking out on the baffle (thinking about trying to pull and replace with flush magnets), grills on or off, you have that ELAC font, if that doesn't bother you aesthetically. They do have a kind of charm that grows on you though, the more I listened to them especially, the prettier they got. And I like that there is not a spec of polish/gloss/chrome to be seen. Everything flat black or brushed/dull metallic. I like that, and as a practical matter the flat woofer dustcaps and hard metallic tweeter mesh grill (nothing to tempt toddler speaker "button" pressing).

Most importantly of course is the sound. This is going to be most divisive depending on your preferences. Everyone else who listened to all these speakers with me here, a/b'ing in turn in the same two rooms, with the same two receivers, everyone else put these near the bottom of the list in either setup. It's clearly because, and I admit that I can hear it too, when you switch from these to even sony cores for a fraction of the price, you get substantially more clarity and detail at the high end with anything else. Almost every other speaker was like this, like shining a brighter light on the high end in comparison to the B6's. And some, like the KEF's in highs and mids, and JBL studios especially was more detailed across the entire range, clearer mids, highs, tighter, deeper, punchier bass, really "better" at everything.

So although it might sound like these are the abject losers given my comparisons so far, but here's the catch- when I started listening to any of these speakers for more than a few minutes at a time, instead of a/b'ing each one over and over, one after another with different segments of audio, analyzing to hear which lets you hear more with. The Elac B6 was the only speaker I could sit down and listen indefinitely to, even at a higher volume, without getting even a hint of fatigue with. The rest, the greater the clarity and detail, the shorter I could listen before getting not pain (except with klipsch, those were outright painful), but just increasing discomfort, tingling ears, pressure in the head/sinus/throat I never experienced with the elacs. At any volume. And full disclosure, no one else got similar discomfort listening to anything else here, only me, and everyone else preferred the speakers with greater clarity, no similar fatigue with those with anyone else. The frequency response curves would back this up. The others are relatively flat, while the ELac's roll off sharply in the highs in comparison. So ultimately I guess that's what I prefer, characterized as a rolled off/dark/veiled etc. sound. So if that's also you, you can't go wrong with the b6. They are like a supercharged Pioneer BS. As a guitar tone guy, a huge test to me was that nothing else I tried sounded as warm, smooth, round, sweet as these with solo jazz box guitar stuff, how I want it to sound. That's a thin slice of music that doesn't overcome their weaknesses, but just a note.

I like them, and am keeping them for good or bad, or how small a minority that puts me in. I know they are missing a level of clarity, detail, and separation I could have with others, but will never know otherwise if I'm not switching back and forth to the alternatives I'm sending back. They all provided an impressively wide enveloping soundstage, threw that out, along with all got loud enough, all had enough bass, the 6.5" models did blend with a sub a little better vs. 5" and 4" speakers, but all that is a wash, when listener fatigue is the deal breaker- and The elac b6 just provide too sweet, too smooth a sound for me to let go.

Cymbals and horns will never hurt you through these speakers. If that's ever been a problem, you owe it to your ears to try these. If you don't know wtf I'm talking about, you might find these muddy.

title: Refurb units seem to perform quite well, right out of the box
text:
UPDATE: left ear cuff is tearing at the base. It's not affecting sound performance at all, but it does suggest the headphone will unravel over time. Still a good deal.

well, got these as $50 or so refurb's from Amazon Warehouse.

Came wrapped in bubble wrap, no gift box, and scant documentation.

It's OK, I know how to go to Jabra's web site, where I could easily access the user manual and in 5 min I understood the controls and paired with my Samsung Note 3.

Sound quality is quite decent. I am talking $50 here... for $50, this headset is a steal compared to the Solo2 Beats I was close to buying.
Background hiss during paused music is negligible. I am somewhat of an audiophile, having spent far too much money on audio eqpt.
I have bought B&W headphones (while hating B&W loudspeakers), and Harmon Kardon headphones, both of those were good, albeit much more expensive. I'd say, for $50, get these, they'll be quite good enough for low fatigue (due to no harsh distortion harmonics, etc...) listening.
Bass seems at the right level, if potentially a smidge understated.
Mids and Treble seem just fine.
I do not detect any audible quality difference between Harmon Kardon wired and these Jabra Move Wireless.

Phone quality seems quite acceptable. I asked the other party could they hear me well, they said yes, why..?
So clearly the mic is as good as the phone unit or my car hands-free.
Though it is weird to talk on the phone using over the ear cups, since you can't hear your voice well.

Comfort level was good, with decent tension, they aren't going to fall off easily. They are quite light weight.

I have no idea yet on battery life, but charging seems to be quick. They claim full charge in 2 hours.

This unit can pair with up to 8 host devices, which is nice.
- Apple Macbook Pro, paired easy, excellent sound
- Android Note 3, paired easy, excellent sound
- Win 10 running on Macbook Pro laptop, paired easy, terrible sound, lot of bit errors. Something quite wrong on the Windows side.
Overall, I'd say get 'em. I hold one star back just for now in case something bad happens.
But what the hell, if they break in six months, it was only $50 !

title: Exactly what I've been looking for!
text:
This review is for the Blue 19L version (different style from the others in this listing).

Summary: Excellent bag with unique characteristics, good looking, and a perfect space balance without being bulky.

I was looking for a camera backpack that had enough room for my camera/lenses/accessories, could hold a tripod, and had a compartment for other necessities for a day trip or hike. This bag has all of that, and does it in a size that is about the same as a normal backpack. Lots of pockets you can use in whatever way you want, well constructed, and it looks good.

I can fit my Canon Rebel SL1 with a lens attached, and 2 additional lenses, (macro, wide angle, and zoom) and there is still room for lens caps, several filters, and more - and this is all in the camera compartment. The top compartment has a lot of room for either your personal gear, or more camera gear. I can easily fit my ipad in the front compartment, and my 13'MacBook would fit in the laptop compartment inside if I wanted to carry it too. Straps on the bottom secure a tripod well. Honestly, you can fit so much stuff in this bag that weight would become an issue long before space would. But again, it's not an oversized bag, so don't be scared.

I am a relatively new photographer and have been looking for a bag with the right balance of holding my gear. It always seems like most bags have either way too much space dedicated to just camera gear with nothing partitioned off for other stuff, or there just isn't enough space in general. This bag is the perfect balance.

Only complaint if I had to name something - the compartments on the waste strap are pretty big, and that might be useful if you have something to put in them, but if not, there almost overkill. This is not a flaw though. If I decide they're not useful, them, I'll just remove them.

title: Good Power Supply, a bit loud.
text:
This PSU, compared to the cheap piece of junk it replaced is very good. It seems to be built with quality parts. I have 3 different EVGA Power Supplies of different qualities. This is the lowest of the 3. My 600W 80+ bronze that I use in my main gaming PC is whisper quiet. It is quite heavy, with many heat sinks inside and, 2 years in, has never given me a problem. My 600W 80+ rated I have in a retro box is by far the loudest component in the system, but it isn't obnoxious. It also is heavy with many heatsinks inside the PSU. It also gives my no problems.

This PSU is for my wife's PC. It runs a stock FX 6300 Heatsink and Fan, A cheap 80mm Antec exhaust Fan, A dual Fan R9 280X. This PSU is by far the loudest component. It just drones on at a constant Fan speed whether idling or gaming. It works though and is quite heavy with many heat sinks. I bought this knowing that it wasn't EVGA's top of the line. It was worth the $25 I paid for it. Would I buy this if I was concerned about making a high end silent gaming PC? No. Would I buy it for a cheap office/gaming PC where every dollar counts? Yes! It's built well with some obvious cost cutting done to meet a price point. EVGA will also give you an addition 2 yrs. warranty with registration which is a nice bonus and shows that they stand behind there product.

title: Convenient with better soundstage - I only wished it came with built in bass boost !
text:
I received it last night. I use it with Alpen 2 e17k for DAC.
From PC - DAC, initially it sounded very flat and had the impression of no bass for my HD598 headphone. I use bass boost on my e17k and realized you cannot use equalizer on e17k when used as DAC. There is an easy solution - just enable Windows equalizer, or in my case, I installed free equalizer and voila ! Bass is back and all is good.
When using with my PS4, I use other Fiio DAC (optical to RCA) and again realized there is no equalizer function on PS4.
But I tried Amazon video and the sound is very good, very clear, and wider soundstage, even though lack of bass. I think I prefer it when just watching movie, but for music on PS4, I wished there is a bit more bass. I haven't tried games yet though.

Overall, it is good - I like the convenience of the volume dial and the output level switch - i was getting tired of fiddling with small E17K every time I switch source or headphone. I was a bit surprised of the size - it was bigger than I expected, but still acceptable on my small desk.

I recommend it !
