title: First Impression - Artemis Spectrum G933 vs. G930
text:
Disclaimer: I'm not an audiophile, just a random gamer! Picked up my G933 today to replace the G930 I've owned for just shy of 3 years. (Ear cups were starting to peel and disconnects more frequent, so I figured it was about time.)

Appearance/Feel
Right out of the box, I already loved the design. Even if most of it is plastic, this headset looks sturdy. The microphone looked a bit weird, but being foldable and retractable has its benefits.
The buttons are all on the left side. One improvement (in my opinion) was the power button - it's now a slide button! Not sure if anyone else experienced this issue, but I found myself having to push the power button on my old G930's really long and hard for it to register. Got a bit frustrating at times if I didn't push it at just the right way. The buttons felt crisp to the touch, although it does require a little more pressure to push down compared to the G930's keys. The volume scroll was responsive as expected. Makes a light sound indicating you've increased or decreased volume, which may or may not get annoying.
And of course, let's not forget the LED lights. To be 100% honest - as awesome as they are, I can't see them anyways, so I'll likely have them off as they'd drain batteries a bit. That said.. when I first powered on the headset, and the lights started pulsing.. was a nice sight to behold, so I'll leave it at that. If you are a streamer, or have friends over, or want to pretend you're a pro player, you can have fun customizing the lighting.
The ear cups are different from the G930's, using a soft mesh material that's more breathable. More on comfort later.

Sound Quality
There is an immediately noticeable difference in sounds (in favor of the G933). There are several configs but I ended up using the DTSx, Super Stereo Front. Just sounded right to my ears, however it definitely took a little bit of time to adjust to the differences. Was switching back and forth between profiles, G933, and G933 for a while to try to hear the differences and find which I preferred.
Not an audiophile here, and never had higher-end headphones, but I'd think the quality is pretty good, to my untrained ears. Mid-ranges, which I mostly listen to, seem spot on. Bass is present but not overbearing. Have been listening to some music, and also played a few rounds of League of Legends. At first everything (especially LoL) sounded a bit weird due to the surround sound difference with DTS, but I grew accustomed to it shortly. I'm definitely going to be using these as my all-purpose headset even outside of gaming.
Microphone - I used this on Skype with my buddies while playing League. I didn't tell them I got a new headset, and they didn't make any comments about any differences in quality. While not the most scientific way, I'd think that the mic is comparable to the G930s, maybe slightly better? Will test with some recordings in future maybe.

Comfort
Comfort is something that's very important to me, as I'll be using these A LOT. On that note, the clamp on the G933 is a bit tighter compared to my G930. Not sure if this will change after wearing it for a bit longer. As of now, it's just sliiighty less comfy than G930 because of this tightness.
Ear cups themselves seem better on the G933. The meshy/cloth is more breathable compared to the G930's faux leather. I don't anticipate this having the peeling issue, so that's a bonus, along with the fact that it's removable and washable.
So far, 4 hours in and no comfort or sliding issues resulting from them. Very snug fit! I also wear glasses, so these receive an above passing grade from me! Everyone's head is different though, so.. take this with a grain of salt.

Wireless Connectivity
As other G930 owners will tell you, at some point they've had annoying disconnect issues, where the headset drops, waits a few seconds and reconnects. These few seconds lost can be very impactful in a gaming setting, or just super annoying while watching stuff, since you'll have to pause or rewind.
I am happy to report that after 4 hours straight, I've had NO disconnects yet. I'm sitting ~2 feet from the dongle. The dongle is right next to the USB I use for my G602 wireless gaming mouse. My smartphone is within 2 feet, and our wireless router within 3 feet. I've been able to move from my bedroom to all parts of my apartment with no issues. Leaving the apartment though will cause it to disconnect.
I'm hoping that the connectivity stays strong, since this was one of my major complaints with the G930's. Seemingly at random, it would be perfect one day, good for hours at a time on others, or disconnect literally 4 times a minute on bad days.

Battery Life
After taking it out of the box, I begun using it immediately without charging. LGS told me it was at 3 bars when I first took it out - it's at 2 now after 4 straight hours with the Logo-lighting on. I may edit this later on, but I think the battery life is going to be great. My G930's weren't too bad either, but after nearly 3 years, it's maximum charge had definitely suffered a bit. According to the specs, the G933 is supposed to last up to 12 hours without lighting. So far, it's on track for that, and is pretty sweet for a wireless set. (Record goes to my travel bluetooth headset, the MEE Air-Fi Matrix2, which lasted over 21 hours.)
Bonus points - the battery is fairly easily replaceable!

Software/Misc
Some people seem to be having troubles or issues with this. I can say that with my G930, it was a struggle to get the "right" version/drivers. For this set, I've downloaded the latest version off Logitech's website, and it's been working without problems. For reference, I'm running Windows 7 Ultimate - 64bit.
Plenty of features on the software itself for lighting, G-keys, gaming profiles, equalizer, etc. No complaints from me.
I have not tried to audio mixing feature, (not sure if I will be,) but sounds like a neat feature others could find more use in. I do like that we are able to use the G933 on more devices than just PCs and laptops though, which was a limitation of the G930.
I was kind of disappointed that this did not come with a charging/USB-dock like the G930. The new dongle is also a bit fatter, so it won't fit in the G930 dock.

Conclusion
If you're looking for a gaming headset and aren't a hardcore audiophile, I think the G933 Artemis Spectrum is a nice one to go with. Sound quality is pretty good, it's fairly comfortable, and doesn't suffer from disconnecting issue of its predecessor. Comes with plenty of features and customization. However.. beware the price! At $199.99, these headsets are quite costly. My opinion? Worth!

title: Perfect fit for the Superlux HD668B, but two sets of hands will make you not go insane
text:
Ok, first off do these fit on the [[ASIN:B003JOETX8 Superlux HD668B Dynamic Semi-Open Headphones]], yes they absolutely do. Save yourself a gigantic hassle though and put them on with 2 SETS of fingers. My wife assisted me in putting these on and it literally made what would have been an infuriating 20 minute chore into less than 2 minutes total. The first thing is, stretch the pleather wrapping out lightly with your fingers, it seems to be pretty sturdy so don't be afraid to get a bit of stretching in. Then, fold it in reverse so that it's folded back around the outside of the ear foam. If you are holding the earpad, pull the pleather stuff over the top portion of the can, have your second set of fingers then press down on the pleather that you manage to wrap so it doesn't go anywhere. Then slide your fingers around the foam, causing the inside out pleather to begin flipping right side out around the ear cans. Once it's on, to get it snug you can use both thumbs to push upward on the pleather which causes it to slide ever so slightly, getting it even more securely onto the can. I hope I described this, it's difficult to do without like, drawing a diagram.

With that out of the way, this increased the comfort of the HD668B headphones incredibly. I can't even really describe it, but one of my biggest issues was that the stock pads were a bit thin, so over time my big ears began rubbing against the drivers in the cans, causing the cartilage of my ears to get annoyed and inflamed. These are about TWICE as deep, not only do they create an additional noise dampening effect on everything outside of the earphone, but it also allows guys with big ears like mine to sit perfectly inside and not hit the dang drivers. These things were seriously worth every penny and turn the HD668B's into what feels like $250 headphones.

title: It's sort of brilliant. (both for what it "is" and what it is "not")
text:
The Pebble Time Steel is my first smartwatch and I was expecting to be blown away. I wasn't. So, I borrowed a Huawei Watch to see what I might be missing out on. Android Wear attempts to crowd the full blown Android experience into a wearable device. And that's how it felt to me . . . crowded. Although I could quickly see the "cool factor" I had missed with the Time Steel, overall I found myself wondering why anyone would pay so much money just to nibble on bite sized morsels of Google fluff. It seems like an expensive gimmick to me. Even more so, I couldn't imagine wearing such a gaudy chunk of battery hungry tech-bling in public with a straight face. I don't need a hockey-puck shaped version of my phone's screen strapped to my hand. Really, I don't.
So, I decided to reevaluate my expectations and give the Pebble Time Steel another try. After playing around with the settings for a few days and actually wearing it to work, I have to say I "get it" now. Pebble watches are designed to supplement the Android experience without attempting to recreate it. It's a brilliantly simple digital wristwatch that works "with" Android, integrating itself in meaningful ways. There's nothing more going on here and absolutely nothing less. This is the evolution of a wristwatch, instead of the miniaturization of a smartphone. The display on the Time Steel never turns off and is very easy to read in sunlight. As a matter of fact, it's gorgeous in sunlight. Charging happens quite fast and then lasts for days and days. Instead of just having one more way to be preoccupied with my phone, I am surprisingly reaching for it a little less each day. I see why others love their Pebble watches and feel like I received plenty of value for the price I paid.

text:
Pros:
1) It's cheap
2) Tracks sleep relatively accurately

4) Band is very adjustable, so fits my wrist relatively well even though it's tiny. However, I wish they came in different sizes (i.e. small) as my wrist is so small that unless I wear it behind my watch it's loose even at it max adjustment.

I use a USB charger my desk lamp has built in for easy access but it can be annoying if all your plugs are behind things.

Overall, for the price, functionality, and the fact that I don't care about heart rate, I believe this is a good deal and would recommend the UP2. However, I hope my Pros & Cons provided you with the info to make your own decision.

title: One of the best value for your buck BT speakers available!
text:
Despite my first impressions, this is a fantastic speaker.

I was made aware of this speaker by Oluv, of Oluv's Gadgets aka ClavinetJunkie on YouTube. He is a true audiophile.

Oluv typically reviews bluetooth speakers that are much more expensive than this one. He spends his own money and typically reviews speakers that cost several hundred dollars, in contrast to this one which cost me $90.

When I first listened to this speaker, it was in a large room, and I was basically testing it against the distance I usually use for much larger speakers like the Aiwa Exos9, etc. At first I was disappointed. Later on, I moved the speaker into my kitchen while I was cooking dinner, and the speaker really came into it's own. The bass response is remarkable and the sound staging (for a speaker of this size) was quite impressive.

Two caveats: It is not tremendously loud in comparison to many BT speakers, even at full volume. Also, as detailed in Oluv's video it is best to pull the front grill off and remove the fabric liner inside for the best sound. Otherwise the bass will contribute to rattling. With the fabric liner removed it has not been an issue for me thus far. The front grill does not immediately appear to be easily removable, I thought mine wouldn't come off. Just push your fingertips into the recess around the grill and methodically pry. It will come off.

Due to the fairly impressive bass response of this speaker, it definitely has the potential to vibrate itself right off of whatever elevated surface you might have it on. So keep that in mind if you don't want it to take a several foot tumble onto the floor.

This speaker is apparently a copy/clone of the Sony SRSX77 which costs nearly $300. The difference being that this speaker supposedly has superior tuning to the Sony unit. (I haven't tested the Sony speaker, so this is merely hearsay)

Next to the $20 Monster Hotshot, this might be the very best value for your buck bluetooth speaker currently available. If you want to put some smiles on your loved ones faces, buy a few of these to give as Christmas gifts this year.

title: "I like this, " or
text:
My husband has reason to be jealous, because if I wasn't already married, I'd be proposing to this case. I'm not the most experienced person out there, just a hobbyist, and I've built probably ten systems over the years in five or six different cases. There were a few things in each that I might think, "I like this," or, "This is a pain in the butt," but nothing really stood out as extraordinary either way (except for an Antec case that wouldn't work with my particular mobo for some odd reason). But this case. This case is amazing. I now regret every $50 case I ever bought. If I could go back in time, I would kill Hitler and buy better computer cases.

From the moment you open the box, you can see that Fractal Design has taken great care with their products. The case is well-encased in foam, wider than I remember from other cases I've bought, the better to keep the sides from getting bashed in during shipping. Under the foam, the case is further protected by a cloth bag. The hardware is nicely organized in a bunch of little ziploc bags, put within other bags, then inside a box that fits snugly inside one of the 3.5" drives so it doesn't bang around during shipping or otherwise lose pieces.

The cable management is a dream. The front panel cables are already nicely organized within the side ties and just need to be slid through one of the grommets to hook up to the motherboard. The fan controller and hookups for the optional top fans are also neatly tied up, out of the way, and ready to be used if one chooses. The holes for the standoffs are labeled with imprints in the metal of the case with a handy key nearby. I sadly didn't see this until I had almost all of them installed, but it's another nice little detail that just adds to the overall feel of excellence. They also included a tool to tighten the standoffs. In previous builds, I'd always done it by hand (and some have eventually loosened and gotten lost over time. That won't happen with these!).

I used a modular Corsair 600W power supply. The one problem I ran into was that the ten pin power connector for the motherboard was just a bit too large to fit through the grommet over the motherboard. Next time I open it up, I'll try popping the grommet out as suggested by one of the other reviews. That and the cable to the video card (which, with them being in the middle of everything, would be hard to route stuff to from behind) are the only things I didn't get routed behind the motherboard.

My SSD must be a non-standard size, because it was just a tiny bit too wide to fit into the neat housing on the back of the motherboard. It fit perfectly into one of the 3.5" drive slots, though, and didn't even need the adapter it came with that I used in my old case. I used the included rubber doohickeys with my HDD and I'm shocked at what a difference it makes. The drive was almost silent, even when I turned on the computer as a test with both sides still open. I've only got the two hard drives, so I popped out the center housing. It came out easily, but is surprisingly solid and heavy. My burner was just as easy to install. There's a clever cover over the two bays on the front that pops out if you pull on a small handle.

I feel silly to be so giddy over a case, but it really is a gorgeous piece of design and engineering. Things just work. The construction is high quality, the finish seems like it'll be hard to damage, and I didn't find myself getting scraped on any odd sharp edges. I think I'm going to need to add another fan (the reason I moved into a new case at all), so we'll see if Fractal Design's "ModuVent" plates are as easy to deal with as they claim. I wouldn't have expected to find something this awesome at all, and especially not when I decided to be picky and hold out for a white case. I expect I'm going to be using this thing for decades unless there's some major form factor change.

text:
This screen has been great. It is a great size for a giant living room, or small venue, great size for small crowds. Watching movies plopped down in the center feels downright kingly. I was concerned from a few of the other reviews, but no problems here with ripples or waviness, I can tell it is not perfectly flat with a light off to the side, but it is not noticeable at all watching a movie, because the projector's light is coming from the front. My projector is even off the the side a bit, and no noticeable weirdness with the image, and that kind of thing bugs me, like watching movies in backyards on wrinkly sheets. I'm really glad I didn't spend a fortune on tab stretched screen, or have to trot out a giant awkward fixed screen. I thought about getting a specialty grey screen, but after testing the projector on some grey and white surfaces, I'm glad I got the standard white, because it looks better in the dark (the grey probably would look better if you need to leave lights on). I think the spill from ambient light might be a little better if I painted the ceiling, and walls black, but it looks great as is. Impressive.

The pulling and locking mechanism is solid. I had to make a hook on a stick to pull the handle down, which hangs straight down and is easy to grab. I used U-bolts from the hardware store to mount it. I had to bend the bolts inward, in a vice (threading nuts on the u-bolt, to protect the threads during the squeezing of the U shape), to get it to fit in the bracket on the screen.

The shipping was quite inexpensive for such a large object to be delivered by an independent freight company.

title: RIOTORO® CR1080 Small Gaming Case for ATX motherboard
text:
I see one review here that I believe could be very inaccurate. First off, this case is made of all steel with a plastic front. It is not aluminum. It is clearly stated on their site it's steel, and a magnet will stick to every metal part of this case proving it. It is a very solid and well built case. I love how the side panels line up show car perfect, which I rarely see in any case. The PCI cutouts on the case fold back and break off as they should in the areas where you need a slot. Mine have lined up perfectly. I have fitted a EVGA GTX 960 in it which means that my Titan X would fit. Obviously, my Classified 980 won't fit because it is monstrous at 5+ inches wide. You can't knock a case if you don't read its specifications and then buy all the wrong parts for it. This case was a pleasure to build in and if you build in as many cases as I do, you can clearly see the extensive engineering that went into it. I especially like the swing out HDD tray in the back and that you can put a Full Size ATX motherboard and DVD/BlueRay player in the front of it. These newer, smaller cases on the market make great air-cooling cases that are easy to build. This case fit a full size EVGA 850 power supply without a hitch and has a incredible amount of room for cable management. I also mounted a Noctua NH-C14 with the standard bottom fan and was able to put a 13mm thin CRYORIG XT140 on top for a push/pull setup that looks and works even better. That will max out the side window clearance of the case and still give the fan all that cut out area to function perfectly.
I would highly recommend this case and I think even a beginner could build this case as long as they take their time. In my situation I had to use an additional standoff for the motherboard which was supplied in the parts pack. Other than that, I expect to build this case again. I was uncertain if I liked the front appearance and I'm still not sure, but I can easily alter that with some mesh material. I hoped this review helped some of you.
Added two photos...One with and one without window. The build is on the left side. CPU is a Devels Canyon 4790k. Changed front fans to Noctua Industrials..changed bottom CPU Cooler fan to a 140 Thermalright high rpm Orange. Now sitting at 27 degrees C at idle with 10% load. Two 80mm NF-R8 redux-1800 PWM fans were added for exhaust. Didn't bios the fans yet but these are crazy good starting Temps with the fans running at normal speed. Cables are still sloppy but you get the idea.

title: Works reasonably well considering natural limitations of 100% wireless
text:
I'm reviewing the HomeHawk system with a single front door camera and hub. This did not include the second camera.

INITIAL SETUP

Out of the box there isn't much out of the ordinary. Just some basic instructions that will help you mount the system and direct you to the app to get things setup. Starting with the hub, I connected it to the switch in my On-Q closet, which is powered by Google WiFi Mesh. The app immediately found the hub and configured it with my network settings. There was an update waiting, so I let that install.

The camera battery was almost dead out of the box, but it paired up automatically with the hub and showed up in the app. I found connectivity to be unreliable, so I let it charge up for 7 hours as suggested. After that, connection was solid. To get things going with default settings, that's really all you need to do. More on specific options later.

PHYSICAL INSTALL

The hub itself doesn't really need install. Just a place where it can be hard wired to your network, which will usually be with the modem and/or wireless access point's switch. The Front Door camera has a plastic bracket and screws. These screws are only for siding install. Anything else and you will need provide your own, as I did. They recommend 7' 3" from the ground for optimal performance. You also want to put it somewhere there won't be constant motion. Some trees moving in the distance weren't a problem. But if people frequently walk or drive by often, expect many alerts.

After ensuring it had a good wireless signal I used my own wood screws and easily mounted above the main door to the house. Then the camera itself snaps right into place. This will make for future retrieval much easier, as you'll need to do that every few months to keep the battery topped off. More on that later.

SETTINGS

First I should note that I did provide a 32GB MicroSD card I had laying around. This is highly recommended so the hub can keep recordings local for later viewing. All settings are done via the app itself. This is where you can switch between some preset "modes" or set your own. Basically this consists of telling the camera when you want to be alerted, how, when, etc.

You can set it to have a vocal alert when it detects motion. Which by the way, is really how the camera is designed to be used. Constant recording will absolutely drain the battery faster. You can also customize night viewing mode, if you'd rather use the built-in LED light for color recording. Viewing distance is limited to ~4ft. Or use night-vision in B&W, you're up to 9ft. I recommend this.

It's compatible with Alexa and Google Home. Although What you can do with it is quite limited. Such as telling it to stream to your smart enabled TV. I never got that to work with Google. Will play with it more. Otherwise not entirely sure it's super helpful.

AUDIO & VIDEO QUALITY

The camera is only 720p. As long as you don't zoom in, the built-in software enhancements results in better-than-expected image; for a 720p camera. Once again, just don't zoom in. This is probably the biggest con for the system, along with price. If you capture somebody in the right lighting, you can probably identify their face within 6ft or so.

However, it does a poor job with contrasting background. In my case, I have a porch with a slightly enclosed entry way. So in day-light, there can be a lot of background light behind the individual. That usually washes out there face until they get really close. At which point they probably aren't look up. Unless the big white camera system catches their eye.

There is a built-in two-way microphone which automatically captures audio during motion activation and allows you to speak with whomever is at the camera. Quality is fairly low, but you can could have a brief conversation if there isn't a bunch of background noises.

REAL WORLD USE, BATTERY, & ALERTS

As noted, we have this camera mounted in the front entry way. Trees and frequent traffic is far enough away so it never sets off the alerts. As soon as somebody gets to the front steps, which are about 8-10ft from the camera, that will usually trigger motion recording. I say "usually" because about 10% of the time, I've had folks manage to sneak by without an alert or recording.

When it does capture them, you get an alert on your phone. There about a 4-5 second delay, which interestingly, happens the same time the get to the door bell. You can then view the short motion activated clip of the individual walking up to the door. Great for seeing who is at the door or package deliver notifications. Or theft. Assuming lighting isn't terrible and you can see them.

So after over a week, the battery still shows 3 green bars. They claim up to 3 months. Naturally this will absolutely depending on activity. Stay tuned for an update when I get to my first charge. I usually get maybe 6-7 alerts a week due to visitors and packages. We'll see how that does.

Also note that when you open the app, it does show Live recording. If you have led enabled, that turns on at night. So you may just want to switch to night vision as noted above. And probably avoid looking at it all the time to spare the battery.

CONCLUSION

Overall I think if you find the right use case, this is a descent camera system. Such as a scenario where you cannot or are unable to have a hard wired system. This is truly 100% wireless. Rechargeable battery and Wi-Fi. However, this is very expensive. I wouldn't even want to imagine the cost if you maxed out at 16 wireless cameras. A couple cameras, while on sale, I can see that happening.

If you own your home, can hard wire, and/or need a lot of cameras I would highly suggest you look into the cost of wired system. You'll get considerably better video quality and no need to watch battery life. Even with the expense of paying an installer, it could make more sense at the price the Panasonic system is going for.

With that said, I'll give this a solid 4 stars for those that really do need this type of system. I've found it to be a very complimentary security solution to our GSM monitored system.

title: Don't get anything else
text:
Long story short: This is a superior keyboard cover.

With the new keyboards, you basically need a keyboard cover to prevent any small particles from getting underneath the keys and making them inoperable. I purchased a similar cover to this manufactured by CaseBuy that was a more of a thin plastic. While it worked well enough, it had almost a powder that would constantly get onto the screen after closing it, and it would warp with heat and occasionally would come off when typing quickly.

This cover is a nice silicone material, with the matte side facing up and being the side you type on and a glossy side underneath that comes in contact with the keys. This cover is very well made - it perfectly fits and more or less sticks in place. I did notice after several days of usage that there are some slight marks on the screen, similar to the plastic style cover I had. I assume this is because the thickness of the cover is just enough to touch the screen on the edges of the keys. To be clear, these are not scratches or anything, just residual dirt/grime from hands typing.

I got the clear one and it looks nice - my only complaint is once you've typed with it a fair amount, at least with the clear one, you'll notice the cover starts to actually stick to each key leaving an odd coloration effect (see picture). I wanted the clear one so I could still see the backlit keyboard, so if you don't want the negligible stick-looking effect, that may be something you need to consider.

title: Thoughtful design and needed security--

The zipper pulls have handles whose ends fit into these indentations. One fits those pull ends, closes the hinged cover, and thereby has a means to lock closed the bag. With a Kensington lock and cable, one can not only secure the bag's contents but also secure the entire bag in place. It's an admirable design for a useful bag. Highly recommended--I am most pleased with this item.

title: As good as it gets for under $1000
text:
After 20 years of enjoying my Sennheiser HD580's I decided as swan song for my aging ears (59) to get my last pair of cans and make it count. I ordered the 700's and the Hifiman 400I at the same time. The 700's arrived first. I played them from my iPhone 6 through Spotify (320Kbps) via my Fiio MontBlanc headphone amp. Right out of the box the sound was stunning. Open, dynamic deep bass and incredible separation of instruments and their location. After 30 minutes of back and forth the old 580's were packed up to be donated. No comparison, neither in sound nor in comfort. For readers unfamiliar with the 580's, they were the predecessor of the 600's, both sounding very close with the same form factor and comfort. The 700's fit comfortably around my ears, while the 580's sat partly on top of my ear. I can wear the 700's for hours!
After 100 hours of play the 700's truly came to their full capability. I have not heard any better.
Then the Hifiman 400I arrived. Right out of the box they sounded like my old 580's, more closed in, darker than the 700's with far less instrument separation. They were heavier than the 700's and also sit partly on the ear making them warmer to wear. I know they weren't broken in but since the 700's sounded so much better right out of the box, I didn't want to confuse myself anymore and packed up and returned them.
Now I have received a Tubemagic A1 amplifier with matched Raytheon tubes ($250), connected to a ridiculously cheap (but great sounding) Muse USB DAC. Plugged in my Mac, I have all my music available through iTunes and Spotify. This combination sounds as good or better as my 10K plus tube system that I left behind 10 years ago. Built around the 700's I get incredible sound for less than a tenth of the cost.
Some quick notes. The 700's need a headphone amplifier, otherwise the money spent is wasted when directly plugged into phone, pc or receiver. The quality of a recording is immediately obvious when listened to; bad recordings sound bad on the 700's. The 700's are very light for their size, adding greatly to their comfort. They are open design to provide the best sound stage, as a result they leak sound and can be heard by people in the room. They don't fold and are not good for airplane travel.
If you can afford them, buy them. You will not regret it.

title: Dell Optiplex Power Supply Upgrade? You NEED this!
text:
This 24pin to 8 pin ATX adapter REALLY is a MUST HAVE if you are changing the power supply from the Dell OEM to a generic ATX power supply on a Dell Optiplex 9020 Mini Tower. This will allow you to install a standard size ATX 500-750 Watt power supply into the original Dell Optiplex 9020 chassis utilizing the same screw holes and lower mounting tab. A power supply of 750W is overkill for this application because there is only one slot for a graphics card on the Dell Optiplex motherboard. This means you can get away with 500-600 Watt standard ATX size power supply with ease
.
It is assumed that you will be adding a graphics card that requires additional power from the power supply rails which the OEM Dell power supply DOES NOT provide.

Once this adapter is connected to the power supply 24 pin and motherboard 8 pin receivers everything powers up as normal. There is no need for extra settings or BIOS prep. It just plain works as is.

text: I used the P1000X5 in a 2000 Trans/Am WS6 convertible to replace the 8 channel monsoon amp. The car has four 2 ohm woofers which sound like they have a midrange speaker and also 4 tweeters Used the high pass on all that and put some bass blockers on the tweeters for now. Customer had a box with 2 12's but it sounded horrible. I had a new dual 4 ohm voice coil Bazooka 12 laying around so I put that in to get it going so the sub channel is seeing a two ohm load as well. Customer is VERY happy. The car hit a peak 120 DB with the clip light occasionally blinking only on the sub output. The front and rear channels are turned down and make the factory speakers sound great. Even with the top down the car still has a lot of bass. The amp does get warm but I don't think it would shut down unless you were playing the unit very loud for a long time. It never got extremely hot however even though I was running it at high volume for awhile checking it out. In the real world clean sound above 85 db is very loud and this amp will pull that off with ease with ZERO strain or effort. For extra free cooling, raising the amp bottom an inch from the mounting surface makes them run cooler. I did that with an old school Zeus series 7 that does run hot. Anyway, everyone was very impressed with the sound..Will be putting a Rockford P3 12 in the Bazooka Tube as soon as he blows the Bazooka 12.. Both the P2 and 3 sound ALOT better than the Bazooka 12 and with the P3 you don't have to worry about people blowing the woofer. I have a Trans/Am coupe and will be putting one of these in it soon. The old Zeus series 7 dims the lights WAY too much..can't play it very low at all at night with out people flashing lights back at me. The Zeus is only running on JL 10 W6 DV.. The rockford 1000 does not use anywhere near the amperage.ZERO engine noise with the Pioneer head unit and center point grounding.

The experience of rubbing ones wrists against the very slightly protruding edge of the case quickly encourages one to maintain a more proper typing form, so no critiques there! I appreciate the pronounced feet on the bottom of the case so that there is a slightly larger space for enhanced airflow under the laptop.

The case will naturally add a small but noticeable heft to your laptop.

** Update **

I've not had the case for a year. Shortly after writing the 1 week review, the rubber feet loosened and soon all fell off. I wrote to Kuzy and they sent me a new set of rubber feet, which I applied and (being slightly OCD) fanatically protected as I moved my laptop, set it down, inserted it into my backpack, etc. The replacement feet lasted over six months and are now gone again, which just bugs me.

With what I would characterize as normal and constant use, after one year the rubber feet are gone and the sides have cracked and can catch on all sorts of things. There are also cracks in the corners and around the tabs that hold the cover to the computer.

In short, it's about what should be expected for a $25 shell in comparison to more durable and more expensive shells.

title: Good...can be great with software updates.
text:
I was a bit nervous, I'm a power user and wanted a prosumer grade device that could handle a solid amount of network traffic.

The OnHub is pretty idiot proof. It has a much friendlier interface than I'm used to seeing (coming from DD-WRT). There are two things that brought this from a 5 star rating, both of which should be easily fixable via a firmware update. I would have love to have seen support for WPA Enterprise (bonus points for a built-in Radius server). I would also love the ability to automatically update Google's (or anybody's) DNS servers dynamically when my ISP changes my WAN IP. Seriously, give me a terminal, curl, and a cron tab and I'll be a happy guy, Google.

Something else that I haven't seen reviewed yet is that the OnHub supports bridged mode. If you're like me and have a rackmount firewall already servicing your network and would like to keep it that way, you can have this device hanging off of a switch and it will become a dumb switch, passing DNS and DHCP requests upstream.

All in all, I'm pretty happy. This thing has replaced my aging router and range extender.

title: Great for the traveler but cord is too short.
text:
I have a pair of Bose QC25's at home and wanted something more portable for the train ride to work. While searching around for noise isolating in ear monitors, I checked into these QC20's as something better than the standard headphone set. What really sold me on these headphones was the ability of having the ability to turn on ambient noise and smaller profile of the earbuds. When I use the QC25's I feel like they are failry small for the size but still take up room in my backpack. With the QC20's they are much smaller, can fit in my cargo pants pocket.

The fitment I would say is much better than I expected with other Bose earbuds. When comparing the other series, these larger eartips fit my ears near perfect. While they do not block out sound like an inserted earbud, it's a great balance between comfort and sound. The fitment is also a plus as I'm finding the majority of non-over the ear cable routed earbuds will not stay in my ears.

Since the fitment works so well, these earbuds don't have any pressure to stay in my ears like other headsets. So there's less playing with the fitment and more time spent on work or just simple listening. Sounds silly but these little things are really annoying especially when you're traveling and have your hands full.

For the sound the headset sounds great given that it's primary function is noise canceling. While these do not sound like a nice set of open back headphones, they are enough to enjoy music while on the plane/train/bus ride. The only thing I can say is that when you power the active noise canceling feature, it doesn't sound so great but that's well known in the Bose world.

For the main feature, the active noise canceling is a big win. If you haven't experienced this, it's pretty amazing and sounds that drone on (think of the A/C sound in your car) can be easily muted. It's even enough to make you suddenly notice that the A/C in your office does make a lot of noise when you take these off. :)

But what I really like is that with the QC20's the feeling of the noise canceling is slightly less powerful than on the QC25's. For me personally the QC25's give me slight headaches and pressure in my ears from the very powerful noise canceling feature. I still can't wear the QC20's for hours on end but it's much more comfortable than the QC25's. I suspect this is the amount of ambient noise leakage into the earbuds, vs the over the ear headphones of the QC25's.

Something that was really surprising how well it worked was the ambient aware mode. Basically you click a button on your remote, and this turns on the mic so you can hear the ambient sounds without taking off the earphones. Sounds silly but it works surprisingly well. You can hear the people around you, listen to announcements over the intercom, order your coffee without readjusting your earbuds.

So some of the issues I found with these headphones is that the battery pack is IMHO too close to the end plug. When I would keep my phone in my pocket, it was difficult to have them both in the pocket and with the cable being slightly short, resulted in the battery pack dangling out of my pocket. If Bose added a few more inches to the cable, this might give you the option to store the phone in your pocket but keep the battery pack in another location, or even clip this to your jacket.

Overall, I think these are the best noise canceling option for earbuds out there. They are pricey but if you spend hours on the train, it's worth the comfort.

title: Avoid this product for laptop use if your machine has an thin bezel and the webcam is mounted "under the screen"
text:
A quick summary of my specific issue for prospective laptop usage...
If you have a laptop where the webcam IS NOT mounted into a plastic bezel, IS mounted under the screen (setup for many higher end machines) and the lid/screen closes flat with little to no gap against the keyboard... I do NOT recommend this product (at all)

Although I didn't have issues with the adhesive like many others, if you search "cracked" in the reviews you'll find a few of us are having an issue with the product damaging laptop screens.

Since it's a very small part and I have fat(ish) fingers, I installed the cover with tweezers to make it so I could see where it was going to stick. Looked good once it got set (aka better than tape or a post-it) and was very easy to "slide" with my thumb while holding the screen with one hand. That was in the morning before I walked out the door to go to a client's office. In 1hr of sitting in a padded pocket of my bag, in a laptop sleeve, this little device created enough pressure on the screen to crack the digitizer layer of my touch screen from top to bottom. It wasn't packed tightly and there was no bouncing or jostling which would have put any extra focus on my laptop during this time.

In my case, it looks like this issue stems from my laptop not having the webcam located in the plastic bezel around the screen, rather the camera lens is "embedded" under the screen (it's a higher end ultrabooks with an edge-2-edge screen). Depending on how the laptop closes, the minor "bump" created by the webcam cover (which is hard plastic) put enough stress on the edge of the screen (because it's over the top of the camera lens) where there is little flexibility/forgiveness in the material, causing the screen to "crack" from top to bottom. In my case, it just cracked the digitizer so the laptop is usable, but touch and stylus function is dead. If there were matching "feet" to go at the edges of the screen on both sides making it so the lid shut evenly all the way across, this probably would not have happened, but it did, so out for repair the laptop goes.

Based on all of the positive feedback, it doesn't sound like this happens to many laptops or phones, so it sounds like it's specific to the type of screen + webcam setup you have.

The power appears to be fairly clean even on unstable grids, although there might be something said to running a power supply of some sort after this converter if you need really clean A/C waves.  During power surges the fuse will blow so have a few spares on hand, but I consider a blown fuse preferable to a blown devise.  I always use a strip of red tape over the 220 outlet to ensure I don't accidentally plug something into the higher voltage side of the box.  Electrical grid spikes will cause this voltage converter to make popping and sometimes even banging sounds.  Those sounds don't seem to translate to surges at the outlet though.

title: I was nervous that it would be gimmicky just like when I had a smartwatch
text:
So I finally caved and got myself a speaker I could talk to. I'm a diehard Google fan and it was hard for me to decide between this and Google Home, but my curiosity in Amazon world of branded technology had me ultimately sold. I was nervous that it would be gimmicky just like when I had a smartwatch, something that I just never found all that useful or intriguing than just pulling out my phone.

Let me start off by saying that white was an excellent color choice. Sleek, modern, and with enough appeal to stand out in an attractive way. Setup was simple and I was ready to go in just a few minutes after unboxing. So I hit Alexa with all the things I had been begging to see her do. She played many of the songs I asked her to play (I've yet to upgrade to Prime Unlimited), and will shuffle many of the artists I ask her to. This is my primary use for my Echo, as it is located in my kitchen and while I work I'll ask her to play whatever music I'm in the mood for and away I go. If i'm indecisive, I ask her to play something and she makes a reasonably educated guess.

I ask about the weather. I ask about my daily news briefing. If I hear a song I've never heard before, I ask her to add it to my library. I ask her to play my local NPR station. I ask her to play my hometown radio. I ask for the latest TED talk. Whenever I'm in my home, my Echo is in use and always coming in handy. The other day, I needed cooking measurements and knew Alexa was there for it. I was happy to discover that this expensive little tool was actually not a gimmick and something that really has become something I use everyday.

My roommates made fun of me initially, shouting nonsense at my Echo and purposefully making fun of the fact that I was talking to my technology. You'd be surprised to find that now I wake up every morning to hear them upstairs asking Alexa about the weather, see what's going on in the news, and play them music. I guess it wasn't so bad after all.

I will be soon moving my Echo to my room and buying an Echo Show to go in my kitchen. I'll be getting Dots for my entire apartment and I will be fully embracing the fun Im having!

title: A waste of money due to uncontrolled microphonic interference
text: A waste of money. I have admired and owned many models of Sennheiser cans and my last earbuds before this were the CX-300s, which had flaws but fell into the "get what you paid for" category. For this pair I decided to step up and pay extra for a pair of CX-400IIs.  The results were extremely disappointing. While the sound quality is just fine, you have to sit perfectly still and not let ANYTHING touch the cables.  The microphic noise (that "stethoscope" sound you hear when you jostle the cable of a pair of cheap ear buds) is just completely out of control on these... way worse than on my CX-300s. Microphonic interference is caused by the quality of material used to cover the cables. Thickness and material selection are both factors that impact the degree to which mechanical vibrations can be transmitted up the cable and amplified by the ear bud speakers.  But for the CX-400II Sennheiser has apparently opted for the worst of all possible combinations in designing and making these cables. The consequence is just horrendous. Yes I know that if I loop the cable over my earlobes, my earlobe can have the effect of dampening the vibrations slightly. But if I have a small ear lobe and wear glasses, so it is not like I have a lot of room to be wrapping headphone cables around by earlobe every time I listen to music (people with well endowed ears may experience different results).  I do notice that the microphic effect gets progressively worse as vibrations occur further up the cable. Vibrations occurring on the cable between the plug and the volume control get dampened by the volume control itself and only a mild nuisance.Between the volume control and the left-ear/right-ear Y splitter the effect becomes much worse. But it only becomes absolutely unacceptable and intolerable on the individual cables from the Y-split to the ear bud itself. In any event, I intend to continue my search for a better pair of ear buds to replace my CX-300s. I will not be settling for the CX-400II.

title: Lasted about a year before replacing.
text:
I purchased this case back in June of 2017, and liked the texture/rubberized feel, that the thickness didn't add a ton of bulk, and was inexpensive.

It installed relatively easily, it simply snaps on, but I noticed a couple things:
1. Not all of the edges were "clean"... there was sharp ridges of plastic from the molding processes. I lived with it.
2. There were certain spots that simply didn't fit, there was extra space that you could press around the bottom of the case, and over time, the corners started to droop.

A couple other things I noticed as I used it:
1. The case definitely caused the computer to get warmer than without. The head dissipation was supposed to be handled by a series of vents/slits along the bottom of the case.
2. I baby my MBP (docked most of the day with external keyboard and mouse), work in an office setting, etc. and after about 6 months of regular use, I noticed some small cracks around the back corners, around the hinge areas. Over time, I noticed that the back of the top and bottom cases were touching or rubbing when opening the MBP. Those small cracks turned into larger ones, which I think contributed to fitment issues and having room to flex later on. I would also randomly hear a small pop sound, like plastic popping off the edge of the bottom part of the MBP when the computer was just sitting, open at my desk.

I finally decided I needed to replace it (with another brand) when there are chunks missing around the edges of both the top and bottom cases.

title: It solved my problem. Let's hope it stays that way.
text:
I saw some reviews complaining that this amp (at least the Made in Mexico one) failed after a few months. My original amp was USA-assembled and failed after at least 8 years. I knew it failed because there was no sound coming from the turn signals, no seat belt or door chime, and no sound from the stereo/speakers. I ordered this part for my 2007 GMC Acadia and got it installed by a local car audio place for about $100 in labor (call ahead of time and make sure the business allows for customer bought parts, and warranties its labor). Completely reasonable since they took me in a timely manner and got it done, whereas the dealer wanted $700-800 for the part+labor. Anyway, the part I got was made in Mexico, so although it works perfectly now, I will update this review if it fails in the near future. But right now, I am happy-- it works great.

That said, if there are no sounds coming from your GMC, it is probably the amp. This part solved the problem. DEFINITELY get someone who knows what they're doing to install it for you. The amp in my GMC Acadia is wayyy up under the steering column; it is really not possible to access it without ripping everything apart. It is best to leave it to someone with experience.

Also, I don't know why the amp failed... maybe it was just old, but I did notice the plugs that connect the car to your passenger doors were filled with water. The car audio guy I went to said that these plugs are designed to take in some water, and it most likely did NOT short my amp. But still, I was very surprised to see water dripping out of my car's door plugs. Next time it rains, double check this! Better safe than sorry.

title: Some Good, Some Bad
text:
PROS:
It does seem to play a huge array of file types -- and unlike other players, they play automatically, so you don't have to drill down through layers of menus on a tv screen to "tell" it that the file is, say, mp3. It just plays.

It has a relatively benign Privacy Policy, especially compared to Sony or Samsung, and even includes an opt-out for tracking, though you have to look hard to find it.

Although like most players these days, it has no information displayed on it's blank, black front, it does have a "status" button that will show you time and progress information on the TV screen.

CONS:
Worst designed remote ever! Small buttons, crowded together and hard to read, especially in the dark, insure lots of mistaken pushes. And the large, prominently displayed buttons for TV control (which on other players would allow you to control your TV and player with just the player remote) ONLY work with a Panasonic TV. Unless you have one, the biggest, topmost buttons on your remote are just a waste of space.

Only 6 apps, and no way to add more. It does have Netflix and Amazon, which are enough for me, but you might care.

The player advertises the ability to play content off of a connected Hard Disk, directly reading the HD file system, which could be kinda cool. But the USB port is unpowered, so you need a HD with it's own power cord. Mine is USB powered, so I can't use it. Disappointing.

Finally, for a player that touts the ability to play so many different types of audio files -- it has NO AUDIO JACKS. The only sound OUT is through the HDMI port. I actually had to buy a new receiver to plug this thing in. Maybe they are all this way, now, but it certainly sucks.

EDIT: Oops, it died 2 weeks after purchase and I returned it!

title: Only charges at 52W -- not enough to even fast-charge my phone
text:
The description claims that this connector allows up to 60 W pass-through charging. Mine only allows 52 W, which isn't enough to power a 15" Macbook Pro or even fast-charge my cell phone!

This is how I'm measuring charge wattage on my Macbook Pro:
* Click on the Apple logo on the menu bar in the upper left.
* Click "About This Mac," then "System Report."
* Under Hardware, go to the Power page.
* Scroll down to find the AC charger information, which gives the charge status and current wattage. Click command-R if you need to refresh the info.

If I plug the Apple charger directly to my laptop and follow those steps, it reports 87 W, which is what the Apple charger is rated. If I plug a 65 W USB-C charger directly to my laptop, it reports 65 W. So far so good.

If I plug either charger into the USB-C port of this connector, and then plug the connector into my laptop, the charger information reports 52 W.

That's not enough, and it's not what the product description claims. I'm particularly disappointed because this is Amazon's own brand, which I'd hoped would work according to spec. I guess not. I'll be returning mine.

For the record, the USB-A port seems to work fine.

title: A solid radio for Android Auto and Apple Carplay but needs some bug fixes
text:
A solid radio for Android Auto and Apple Carplay but needs some bug fixes. I purchased 2 of these for my wife and my Hondas in December of 2016. I am an "Android Guy" and She's an "iPhone Woman". I wanted radios in both of our cars that could upgrade the factory Honda radios beyond what was offered at the time of manufacture- Bluetooth and streaming content. I added Sirius Radio modules to both and the bypass wiring to both.
Both work very well for Android Auto and for Carplay although I do have a few gripes in general.
1) The Radio screen has a black background. If I'm listening to Satellite radio and the artist or song title are tag-able the text is white. If they aren't tag-able the text is gray, so you have gray text on black background. At night it's hard to read that text.
2) The Radio Presets that I assign do not highlight the current preset I am listening to, so I don't know what is the number of the preset that is currently playing
3) I wish there was a way for the Android Auto or Carplay experience could "break through" to the native app screens and vise-versa. For example If I have a navigation route active in Android Auto but I am listening to Satellite Radio and the Satellite Radio screen is displayed there should be a banner on my radio screen with my next turn info along with the audible guidance. If I am in Android Auto Navigation screen I would like to see Artist & Song Title for the song that is currently playing on Satellite Radio. Both of these are mutually exclusive.
4) When I recently upgraded my Android phone from one with a Micro USB port to a USB-C port the USB dash outlet that I had installed that was working perfectly fine for Micro USB was giving me errors when I plugged in the USB-C cable that came with my phone. This has been fixed by buying one of the USB-C cables that Pioneer has approved on their website. I ordered the one at the top of the Pioneer troubleshooting page and it fixed my connectivity issue
5) More and more phones are coming to market with "Quick Charge" Technology and big batteries. Unfortunately this radio is not compatible with QC technology and the Android Auto app can use more power than the charger can provide, so I have gotten net-negative charging in some cases (my battery level is lower at the end of the drive than the start of the drive even though it's been plugged in the whole time).
In conclusion. I really wish that Pioneer would more aggressively support bug fixes on this radio. This radio is designed to support bug fixes and hopefully feature upgrades so I hope it's not going to be entirely obsolete in a few years.

title: Best bang for the buck mini PC available
text:
I would give this six stars if possible. I haven't owned a device made by HP in some time (more than 10 years), so it's nice to see relevant, current, useful and capable products in their lineup again (that aren't printers). I purchased this to be my HTPC (Home Theater PC) and as an installer, I've seen, built and repaired just about every possible version of HTPC. This was completely painless and required very little in the way of upgrades to be a very capable core device for my home entertainment setup.

Understand that this is no gaming powerhouse, it's a minimalistic design and packaged accordingly. It has a Celeron processor and 2GB of RAM, which does not make for a smooth or fast Windows 8 experience. So two upgrades are required to make this a truly functional, fast Windows PC.

First, upgrade the RAM to 8GB. I found 2 X 4GB DDR3 laptop memory (1600 MHz) here on Amazon for $55. The system will accept up to 16GB, but the processor speed will mitigate the usefulness of that much memory, so 8GB was a good (inexpensive) compromise.

Second, the installed wireless card is terrible. Sitting less than 10 feet from my router, there were throughput issues when streaming video content (and signal levels were mediocre at best). I followed a recommendation and installed an Intel AC7260 card and all of the throughput issues disappeared. I also no longer have trouble connecting a Bluetooth device while WiFi is enabled. The new AC7260 card is also capable of WiDi (wireless display), which was not possible with the original card. I found the wireless card here on Amazon for $35.

While it is possible to upgrade the 32GB SSD hard drive, I chose not to. After completing the Windows 8 setup and uninstalling the bloatware (of which there was very little), there was over 18GB of user space. Plenty enough for the programs, apps and downloads I'll need. I also chose to use a 2TB external hard drive for storage, which allows me to take my media when I travel. If you choose to upgrade the hard drive, bear in mind that the Stream Mini has no SATA connection for a standard 2.5" drive (although it has the same mounting tray as the Pavilion Mini)... so a more creative solution will be required for a standard drive (along with copying the recovery partition to the new drive).

I know that the Intel NUC and Zotac fans will scoff at this review, but that's OK. I spent less than $280 for a fully capable, smooth, fast PC with a 64 bit OS... that is a win all day. I have been using Kodi (formerly known as XBMC) for my media front end and it has performed flawlessly on this PC. Along with browsing and some light gaming, I can't find any flaws. There are four USB 3.0 ports, a full size HDMI port, ethernet port as well as a display port (yep multi display capability built in), so there are plenty of options for connectivity and fast data transfer.

title: Seems just about worth the price, even with all the downfalls. Update after 90 Days: AVOID
text:
This is a decent boom-box. I work as a courier and use this for work. The antenna is flimsy at best -expect it to break within the first week of use. The stereo is not bottom-heavy and tips easily. If the antenna is up when it tips over, it will bend. I also had the antenna come apart from regular (very limited) use. As I was pulling up on the top of it to extend it, the mast split at a joint. There are two small brass shims that hold the segments together and they give out very quickly. So if your antenna doesn't break off completely, it will fall apart at the joints. Reception is not good. It is good enough, but if you are charging the battery with a 12v DC adapter/120v AC, the radio becomes unusable. The user interface is not the best either. As others have mentioned, the volume resets when you turn the unit off. The presets are also not very user friendly. Even with the instructions right in front of me, it took me a while to figure it out -very clunky. For all of its downfalls, this is still a pretty good radio for what I use it for. I can stream music with bluetooth while charging my phone on the USB port, all while running off of 12v power in a truck. The battery power also comes in handy when there is no power source.
Update: 90 days after purchase, I started having issues with the volume. It became erratic for a while and then was just very quiet. With volume turned all the way up on both devices (bluetooth), it is loud enough for a small indoor room. Amazon was awesome and returned it even though it was 90days past purchase date. I can no longer recommend. Be prepared for headaches!

<original review below>

First as a monitor to alexa supported day/night IP cameras from various manufacturer offerings on amazon to amazon's own cloud cam, "SOMETHING" limits the stream to around 20 minutes and then spot goes back to the home screen. I would think it has to do with the spot vs app stopping or dropping connection since ALL devices tried so far have the same limitation (as stated, including amazon's own cloud cam). The only way to go beyond a 20 minute segment is to do echo spot/show to echo spot/show drop in call and act as a baby cam. Problem with that is that the spot/show has no night vision capabilities so you get audio only. So the annoying thing with all this is that you get a fancy little screen echo dot that markets use of baby monitoring but is so vague about what that actually means. Apparently it means monitoring your baby only in ample lighting if using a drop in call and limited to 20 minutes if using a 3rd party camera. Seems like marketing and development arent in sync with each other. Using the spot as a baby cam would require hardware changes like night vision capabilities as currently in the amazon cloud cam or other IP cameras. title: Found My Perfect Keyboard
text: I was beginning to get some tingling, numbness, and soreness in my left wrist despite using a different, and also quite expensive ergonomic split keyboard also made by Kinesis. I noticed it while working at home for a call center. I also use a Dvorak keyboard layout that was not compatible with one of the companies software I was working for by just adding the layout to the keyboard input. For those reasons, I finally bit the bullet and bought this keyboard. I'm so glad I did! It is awesome in every way. It's plug and play, and the Dvorak programming works in all cases. My wrists feel great, and it makes typing really enjoyable. The position of the wrists and the intuitive layout made the transition to the new keyboard pretty seamless. It didn't slow my typing down for long. The hardest thing was learning not to keep hitting the left backspace key when I wanted to hit the spacebar. Keyboards are a very personal thing, so this one may not be your thing, but they do have a money-back guarantee so you can try it. I love it! I did remap a couple of keys that worked better for my typing purposes, and it was very easy. The instructions were clear and you don't have to be a programmer to follow them. There are many functions available that I may never use, but if I ever do need them, I'm glad they are there. The only negative I can say is the price is so very high. The keys are kind of loud as well, but that is specific to the keys, not the product itself, and I don't mind. Some of my favorite things are how easy it is to switch from Dvorak to Qwerty, turn on the keypad, and change the layout from Mac, to Windows or PC. I have zero regrets!

title: It's junk designed by lobsters. Good luck when you actually need it
text:
The bad reviews are justified. Awful.

I have several technical certifications, and I teach networking. I can't believe anyone figures out how to use this mess.

None of the screens have buttons that make sense. The home screen doesn't let you do anything. The help is useless.

I bought this 18 months ago when I was working at Microsoft's Silicon Valley Campus. This MyCloud seemed useful, but I never got it working, not once. I'd stick it away unused. Yesterday I thought, I paid a fortune for a thing that sits under the bed, so I set it all up again. Incredibly frustrating. The WD web site has tons of cool marketing hype, telling you how great this machine is. Very little helpful info. Once you get it installed, and up date it, there is nothing. None of the screens seem to do anything. First you wander around, thinking there must be a setup button. No. Then you search carefully to bottom. There are only five tabs. None make sense. It's like lobsters designed it.

WD decided to invent their own new interface, and didn't tell anyone how it works. The settings tab has almost nothing on it, literally! Certainly nothing useful to get it running. They tell you that you are eligible for a Pro account, but once you get it, there is literally nothing that tells you how to set it up or use it. Not in the confirmation email, not in the software, nowhere. It takes work to find the search field in the help menu, duh. Then you ask for setup help, and nothing. No user testing, obviously.

I have configured hundreds of networking, backup and security appliances. I have never seen hardware and software so poorly written and badly designed.

In the end, I did get it working, maybe. I get the sickening feeling that, when I really do need this backup device, I will find out something didn't work, because it was not setup properly. I deeply regret this buying this expensive mistake.

title: A Competetive Product
text: I purchased the 50" version of this model at the local big box retail location the day that my 10 year old 37" JVC suddenly quit producing a picture. The $429.00 they charged is a good deal for a name brand TV of this size with these specs. I had certain space and wiring considerations that drove my purchasing this set. The TV stand that I have matches the rest of my living room furniture and is only 36" wide. The pedestal of this set is 35". I also wanted 3 HDMI ports, 2 of which are already used, a component input and an analog audio output were also requirements. This also has 3 USB inputs, a RJ-45 jack for a LAN connection and an Optical audio output. Most of these connections are on the side of the TV requiring the cables to be bent in a tight radius so that they don't stick out. I did buy some 270 degree adaptors.  The analog audio out is a 3.5 mm jack, not the expected RCA jacks. There is also no cable management system in the rear of the unit. My old JVC had a couple of hooks behind the pedestal that kept the wires out of sight. This TV does come with a couple handles screwed into the back of the set that SONY recommends removing once the TV is in place. I left them in place to hold some of the wires. The book says this has built in Wi-Fi, but it will not handle a video signal. I did hook this up to the LAN network. I was able to update the software, however I was not interested in allowing SONY to track my viewing habits so I can not tell you how the TV performs with true 4K content from the internet, but the picture quality is very good from my LG BP-330 Blue-Ray player at 1080p. The component input that is connected to my AverMedia C283s produces a picture that is on par with my FIOS signal.  I also use a pair of really cheap rabbit ears for OTA signals. The tuner is slightly better than my old JVC's. If you need good OTA performance, buy this TV. I also have FIOS running through a Silicon Dust tuner into a HTPC with Windows Media Center configured as a DVR / set top box. Intel Haswell processors produce the worst 4K output known to man. I had to manually reset the computer back to 1080p output. As to the actual quality of the picture, it does look a little washed out, even with the factory default contrast setting on 100%. Also, the viewing angle is not the best. The picture starts to get soft only a few degrees off center. The speakers are rear facing and while the frequency response is good by TV standards, the rear placement may not be the best solution. Also, the factory default has the surround sound turned on. It was one of the first things that I had to reset. There are numerous other audio enhancements that seem to be marginally effective. But, the dynamic range compensator is excellent at equalizing the audio level of commercials. I did notice that the audio and video were out of sinc, but rebooting the TV after the software update seems to have corrected that issue. So far I am happy with the purchase; fortunately I can live with the limitations that this set has.

title: A good backpack for a great price!
text:
Some backstory on why I ordered this backpack: I wanted something to replace my Herschel Supply Co. Classic backpack. Herschel’s bag had been uncomfortable, along with having no space for half my books for class. In terms of water resistance, the bag had leaked water into the contents of the bag from the rain. I live in Oregon, so I definitely needed something water resistant. I figured for the new year, I’d order something new. I was perusing Amazon’s lightning deals and saw the Kaukko Canvas Leather Backpack for $35. I figured the backpack would be worth a shot at that price, since I’ve never heard of Kaukko. I’ve owned the bag for the last month, but I figured I’d do a review on it now.

The canvas backpack had arrived in the mail a few days after purchasing through Amazon. The bag came in a plastic wrap, and came with a little booklet. The bag has 3 external pockets: one pocket in the front, and a pocket on each side of the pack. I use my front pocket to hold my pens, pencils, calculators, and pencil sharpener. I use the side pockets to store my external drive and flash drive. There isn’t a lot of room left in each pocket afterwards. But that is everything I need for my classes, so I’m perfectly content.

Moving onto the main focus of the backpack: the main compartment. The main compartment is closed off with a drawstring. With my old Herschel backpack, I had to yank the sucker apart in order to grab a pen that fell to the bottom of the bag. With the drawstring, the bag’s opening can expand enough to allow easy access to everything inside. Within the main compartment, there is a laptop sleeve and 2 small pockets. I’m not sure what to use with the two pockets, maybe to hold pens? They wouldn’t even fit, so they seem a bit useless in my case.

The Amazon description says the laptop sleeve can hold up to a 15” laptop. I have a 15.6” laptop that can fit in the sleeve, but it is a tight fit. Something to note is that I own an Ultrabook, so it has a thinner profile than the average laptop. So if your laptop is any thicker than the pictured laptop, then you’ll be out of luck with storing it in the sleeve. But the main compartment on the bag is perfectly suitable for holding your laptop.

The straps on the bag use magnetic clasps to secure the bag shut. Some people find the clasps to be tacky, but they make accessing any of the pockets or the main storage fast. I had a little trouble getting the clasps to align correctly when closing the lid originally, but I got used to using them rather quickly. One annoying thing about the clasps is that the side pockets clasps pop off every once in a while. I honestly need to just adjust the clasps so they sit better.

The materials used on the bag are decent. The canvas material has a nice look to it, although the leather used for the straps is a bit cheap looking. But I paid 35 dollars for the bag, so the cheap looking leather is a given. The lining on the inside of the backpack is durable, taking abuse from my books, notepads, and laptop charger. I’ve only had it for a month though, so I’ll see if any tearing or rips appear later on.

The padding in the shoulders and the back are good. There is thick padding in the shoulders, with some thin padding in the back area. The shoulders don't cause any pain and the laptop doesn't bend against my back like the Herschel backpack. I can walk around my campus for hours and I have yet to experience back pain like I did with my Herschel backpack. The shoulder straps are easy to adjust, so I had no issues getting the backpack properly fitted depending on the situation.

In terms of water resistance, this backpack has held up very well. With the drawstring and clasps, I have yet to experience any soggy papers or a drenched laptop. It has yet to experience any deterioration from the heavy rain we experience here in Oregon, nor any damage from turbulence on my scooter. Like I mentioned earlier, I’ve only had the backpack for a month. So it may start showing weather effects at a later on. But compared to other backpacks I’ve owned, this bag is a champ.

Overall, I’d recommend this backpack. The backpack is comfortable, spacious, and can survive the Oregon weather. It has a couple of quirks, but this is a great backpack for 35-40 dollars.

title: Really Does Work Better with Weak Signals than a Regular USB Wi-Fi Adapter
text:
I'm not sure if I'd really call this "high gain", but thanks to its antenna and USB extension cord, it does a better job of pulling in wi-fi signals than your typical "nano" or compact USB wi-fi adapter. The box contains the adapter, which looks like an oversize USB flash drive; screw-on antenna, a USB extension cord that's maybe 2 feet long, and a mini CD containing the drivers.

One minuscule quibble: Like most USB wi-fi adapters, this one comes with a cap intended to protect the USB plug when the adapter is not in use. And, like most USB wi-fi adapters, it has no means for stowing or otherwise retaining that cap when the adapter IS in use. My guess is that most people eventually lose the cap. This is of no real consequence except, perhaps, aesthetics.

The best improvement in wi-fi performance is achieved by using the provided extension cord to position the adapter above and away from your computer, where it can get the best possible signal. Of course, there's no reason why you couldn't buy your own USB extension cord and use that to improve the signal with a more conventional USB wi-fi adapter. But the antenna, which actually contains metal parts configured in a way that really does boost the gain, still gives the TL-WN722N an edge over a nano adapter with an extension cord.

As with most USB wi-fi adapters, this one comes with unneeded wi-fi management software. (Most wi-fi management software has been superfluous since Windows XP Service Pack 3 gave Windows robust, built-in wi-fi management.) Unlike with some other adapters, there is no way to install just the drivers you need while omitting the management software that you don't need. But after it's installed, you can set Windows as the wi-fi manager.
