title: Transfer speeds vary - not as good as claimed
text:
Samsung 128 GB USB Flash Drive

This is a great little drive with a few small caveats. The design looks fine but it seems the designer favored function over form. Samsung used good materials while the shape of the drive is bit odd (in my personal opinion) -- of course, design is ultimately subjective.

The micro USB connector was able to connect to my Galaxy s7 without having to remove the case. It was instantly recognized without any hangups.

Transfer Rates:

The device claims to have transfer speeds "up to 130 MB/s" and so I tested this claim with CrystalDiskMark (CDM). I tested this drive and my current 32 GB Silicon Power flash drive (also purchased on Amazon) to see how close CrystalDiskMark and actual file transfers really are. In the image you see that the Silicon Power beats the Samsung every time the drives are read, but the Samsung is the clear winner when you write to the drives...or so it seems. I then tested both drives with 3 different file tests -- all the tests were done on the same USB 3.0 port with the same files, with the same file system format. As you can see, I tested both drives with NTSF and exFAT (I decided to skip FAT32).

The files I transferred were
1) a 10.9 GB .mkv movie file
2) folder with 16 .mkv video files, most of which were about 650 MB totaling 8.0 GB
3) folder containing 604 .mp3 files totaling 2.7 GB.

I formatted the drives between each transfer, ran no other unnecessary programs or processes than the transfer and copied the files from the same drive to ensure the cleanest test possible. After the test I found that the Silicon Power drive often outperformed the Samsung drive even though CrystalDiskMark specified something very different. According to CDM, the Silicon Power was often not even half as fast at writing files as the Samsung. The real world tests show the Samsung to be quite a bit slower when reading and writing files. In fact, when I was transferring the 10.9 GB video file to the Samsung on NTFS, the transfer would hang for nearly 2 minutes before it would complete.

I did three tests on each drive with each file and both file system formats for a total of 36 file transfer tests, averaging the three test results for the conclusion. With the Silicon Power I found the transfer times to be very consistent, often with a few seconds one another. With the Samsung, however, I found there were some tests which showed very different times (I admit, there may have been outside factors).

Conclusion – CrystalDiskMark is either completely useless software or the results you find with it don’t transfer to the real world all that well. Whatever the case, I’ll take real world application over a benchmark tool. It is my opinion, the Samsung 128 GB drive is nice and is still a great deal for $30 – 35. If we were to extrapolate these test results to the 128 GB Silicon Power USB drive, I would think that's the better deal. It just depends on how concerned (obsessed) you are with transfer speed and your need for a micro-USB connector.

My PC Specs:
- Windows 7 Pro 64-bit
- Core i7
- 32 GB RAM
- Samsung 500 GB Solid State Drive

Pros:
- Size is small
- Transfer speeds are OK (see review)
- Dual connectors are useful if you have a phone with a micro-USB connector
- Works well with my Samsung Galaxy s7
- Designed for function

Cons:
- No lanyard included with drive (you need one to avoid losing the cap)
- Other USB drive options which may be faster at reading/writing data

Notes: I copied all the CrystalDiskMark data into the image of the Excel spreadsheet to make comparison easier. I also marked the best times and read/write transfer rates in green and the two Samsung time "anomalies" in read. I posted an image of different USB drives and some other things for size comparison – the drive reviewed here is circled with the comparison drive in the bottom right hand corner.

I will update this review if I find any reliability problems with the Samsung. I have owned my Silicon Power drive for over a year and it's worked fine so far.

title: Finally a headphone which delivers Bluetooth functionality as advertised
text:
At the time of this writing (4/29/2016) MD60 is IMO the best BT headphone I tried with my iPhones 5s-6s+ (Plantronics Back Beat Pro, Bose SoundLink II BT, Sennheiser Momentum 2.0 BT, Sennheiser MM 550-X).
I like and recommend these headphones.

Pros:
- Solid Bluetooth (BT) connection to iPhone 6s plus (ip6s+) for playback
- Solid BT connection to ip6s+ using BT microphone for conversations. Excellent quality of the incoming voice on the other end when using the BT microphone in a quiet environment.
- In 3 weeks of heavy daily use never cut out when ip6s+ in proximity up to 6 feet (when walking streets , at home, jogging, talking over the BT mic)
- Relatively long BT range (and around walls) when connected to my ip6s+. Longer range than ca 30 feet of Sennheiser Momentum 2.0 BT (BT radio class 2) but shorter range than 60 feet of Plantronics Back Beat Pro (BT radio class 1);
- Battery powerful enough to last all day under heavy use (but somewhat less long lasting than Plantronics Back Beat Pro)
Comfortable (but too much heat)
- Quality materials and finish

Cons:
- Insufficient background noise filtering when talking; For example when talking through the BT mic in a windy open space or in a car (BMW X5) on a freeway at 65 mph it was very difficult to understand on the other end. A switch to a standard wired Apple headset made a conversation possible while in the same environment.
- Too much heat around ears after longer use (but all over-the-ear headphones have this problem)
- Statement “BT range 4 times longer than industry” is not precise. IMO better to simply publish the offered BT radio class (1,2,or 3)

Possible improvements:
- Automatic stop of playback when headphone off (as offered by Plantronics Back Beat Pro)
- Implement a firmware update process as offered by Plantronics Back Beat Pro and Bose SoundLink II BT

This is made by Pro-Ject for Musical Fidelity. I will go as far as saying most of what you are paying for here is the name, Musical Fidelity. However, upon taking it out of the box, it's very clear that you have a run-of-the-mill Pro-Ject turntable with a slightly different tonearm and a High-Gloss finish. I also feel that this table is over-priced. There is no way this is a $1k turntable. It seems on par with other Pro-Ject offerings in the $400 + price range, but again, you are paying mostly for the name Musical Fidelity.

My table arrived in true Pro-Ject fashion, the Armrest was loose from the tonearm base where it is mounted (and this is not user adjustable). The arm was flopping around in the rest like a kite in the wind. The platter is also another interesting point. While it seems substantial and thick, as soon as you pick it up, it would seem that it's hollow or maybe not solid all the way through and seems very light for a solid slab of MDF. The cartridge is hap-hazardly mounted at the factory and must be re-adjusted for proper alignment. Even using the Pro-Ject alignment tool, the cart was incorrectly mounted and adjusted.

My level of disappointment was so great that I just packed it all back up and sent it right back to the place which is came from. I have actually auditioned a couple of Pro-Ject tables over the years and have been very disappointed with the quality. Lots of problems with Platter Wobble, Motor induced noise, and just plain poor QC. As I’m not a prestigious reviewer, I cannot get the personal touch in which the table is checked BEFORE they ship it to me…along with a check for a GREAT review, right…

title: Very big. Very expensive. Worth it for me.
text:
UPDATE - November 13 2016 -

So this cooler has been installed in my system since this review was written and I have had zero issues with it. I forget it's even there. It's just peace of mind. And that's exactly what I wanted.

------------

ORIGINAL REVIEW

This unit is installed and working in this system....

Case - NZXT Source 210 (Side panel is REALLY tight. Scrapes heat pipes and maybe bulges a bit)

Motherboard - Gigabyte G1 Sniper A88X (FM2+). Stock backplate works just fine for this cooler.

APU - AMD A10 7860k

RAM - Kingston HyperX Fury 2 X 4 GB 1866. This cooler does clear this RAM but just barely. If you have four sticks you might have to remove the cooler to uninstall.

1 X Noctua 140mm exhaust fan at top. About an inch clearance there.

------------------------------

OK. Right off the bat I have to say my needs were slightly different than probably almost everyone else who buys a cooler like this one. I'm not a gamer and I generally do not use my PC for anything heavy like video editing or anything like that. So it goes without saying I did not buy this with the idea that I was going to overclock my PC. So if you're looking for a full report from someone who bought this for that purpose, you probably won't get much useful info in this review (that's just to save you from reading it unless you want to).

I bought this because the PWM fan speed controls in my BIOS for my motherboard don't work right on the CPU fan header. I cannot trust them to keep the fan RPMs fast enough to keep my CPU temps in check at all times with a run of the mill CPU cooler. I also can't seem to get accurate temperature readings on my AMD APU so that was always a worrying issue in the back of my mind.

So that's why I bought this particular cooler. Since it is just about impossible to use PWM the way my fan header is, I had limited options. I could have bought a smart fan controller but those are not cheap and they add complexity and wires and other things I didn't want to deal with. I wanted a simple solution. The solution I chose was just to buy a huge heatsink with (relatively) quiet, reliable fans that run at the same speed all the time. No PWM nonsense. No guesswork. All that mattered was that my PC couldn't really dish out a thermal situation that this cooler can't easily handle at stock clock speed.

Anyway, installing this Noctua cooler was remarkably painless on my FM2+ socket motherboard with the factory backplate (There is not an AMD backplate included in this kit at all but I guess they assume if you have an AMD motherboard, you already have a backplate. It's far easier than I expected. I don't know why. I expected it to be confusing and troublesome and it just wasn't. I also expected the sheer weight of this thing might be a problem considering it does have to be ultimately supported by a motherboard but that just isn't a problem. The factory backplate for FM2 is VERY solid and it's not going anywhere.

I had one problem with my install. In my NZXT Source 210 case, the tips of some of the heatpipes just barely touched/scraped the side panel when I put it on. After a while I started noticing a faint, low-pitched droning sound. When I investigated, I found that the metal on metal contact between the pipes and the side panel was causing this unpleasant resonance in the case. Long story short is that this cooler is technically supposed to fit in my case but mine is just REALLY tight for some reason. I knew the dimensions were tight when I ordered it so I'm not blaming Noctua for that.

At first I wasn't really sure how I was going to fix this. The noise wasn't really loud but it was just enough to be really annoying after a while. Eventually, I decided to try putting a piece of Gorilla Tape (Which is thick enough to be kind of squishy and provide some noise canceling) on the spot on the inside of the side panel where the pipes were touching. Amazingly, this actually worked. Although the heat pipes are still making contact, they are not vibrating against bare metal and it's much quieter.

So just beware of that. If you happen to have this case, it WILL fit but it can be EXTREMELY tight and the heat pipes MIGHT touch the case. The side panel will fit but in my case, it seems to require some light force. The noise this makes (if it happens) isn't pleasant so you'll have to decide for yourself if rigging it up to silence that is worth it for you. If you have a case that is very close to the same dimensions as mine, obviously you might have the same issue. All I care about is functionality and having a cooler that is quiet and effective and just works.

I am also using a 140mm Noctua exhaust fan at the top of my case.

Long story short, it works and I do not have to worry about overheating at all, as my system and clock speeds are all stock.

Conclusion - I know this is an older cooler and the fans are not PWM and there are probably (slightly) better air coolers but this thing was worth every cent for my needs. PWM wouldn't have been useful for me anyway.

So again, for my needs, I think the price was reasonable. I could have tried to solve my particular problem several different ways but I really wouldn't have saved much money with any other method and this cooler just seemed to be the most straightforward way to make darn sure my system will never have a cooling problem regardless of whether or not I monitor the temps.

title: Save your money and buy the Aquantia AQN-107
text:
The bottom line is that this card does not seem to be significantly better than the Aquantia AQN-107, which offers similar features and is $20 cheaper. Both use Aquantia chipsets.

When it works, the ASUS card is great. 10GBe for $100 is terrific, but... there's always a but.

The ASUS card frequently drops out and stops working. Usually it can be reset by Windows network troubleshooter, but other times it says the cable is disconnected and can require a restart. This is simply not acceptable for networking in 2018; it needs to work all the time, every time.

This being my first experiment with 10Gb/multi-gigabit networking I actually bought both the ASUS card and the Aquantia AQtion 10G Pro NIC AQN-107. I was curious to see if the ASUS outperformed the Aquantia card since it was more expensive. I know they both cards use Aquantia chipsets, but I can't say if they are the same version since ASUS doesn't publish this info in their specs. So far, I have not experienced any problems with the Aquantia card, were as I was very nearly ready to return the ASUS card. So far the extra $20 has only gotten me trouble.

Before returning the card I decided to swap the cards to confirm that there wasn't a problem with the PC housing the card. This process was somewhat enlightening. When exchanged, the ASUS card picked up the Aquantia driver in the other PC seems to be working just fine. I tortured it with a big file transfer, something which would almost certainly have knocked out the ASUS card before. I have also kept a remote window open for 24 hours without dropping out.

The Aquantia card, when switched, would not work with the ASUS driver. I had to install the Aquantia driver, after which it started working working fine.

The ASUS driver was published in April 2017. The Aquantia driver on the other hand is dated 4/23/18 so it is a year newer. It seems that if ASUS had bothered to update the driver, maybe their card would not have these problems.

The card should be a 4 star performer, but I knocked it down to 1 star because it simply would not work with the manufacturer's driver. I gave it an additional star when I found that it seems to work with the Aquantia driver, but this really isn't something I should have to do.

It seems to be right around a year to 18 months until it fails. I can't see paying $249 every year for this. I'll wait until they figure out how to remove the battery from the circuit.

title: Nice trackball, but not for smaller hands.
text:
I have medium sized hands and find this to be a bit too large for me. In order to have both the default left and right mouse buttons within reach meant I had to spread my hand out in an awkward position, and it left my thumb sitting right up against the scroll wheel which got really bothersome after a while. I mitigated most of these problems by remapping the "forward" and "back" buttons above the scroll wheel to be the left and right click buttons instead, then remapping the two long skinny buttons on the right to do back and forward. This works much better.

Other than that, it's a pretty nice trackball. The palm rest is made from a soft rubber and is a very comfortable, non-slip surface. The ball itself is a great size and is very smooth and responsive. The buttons were just a bit stiff at first, sometimes requiring a little extra push to register a click, but I've either gotten used to them, or they have broken in a bit because they seem to work a lot better now. There is a switch for controlling resolution, which is pretty handy for gaming or precise graphics work.

Overall, it still feels too "big" for my hands, but the build quality is reassuring enough that I'm willing to give their smaller trackball a try to see if it's a better fit.

As a side note, finding the driver that works correctly with this trackball took a bit of hunting, as it was not available on their English language site. It turns out that you need version 5.12, but the website only had version 5.0.3. I had to do a bit of Googling to find the actual driver on their non-English site and then had to resort to some guess work to actually figure out which link meant "Download". Hilariously enough, once I did download the driver, the instructions for installation were in English. I assume they will get the correct drivers up on the English language site soon.

title: Pefect to add SSDs to older 3.5" Hot-Swap Servers
text:
These adapters work perfectly to adapt a 2.5" drive to the standard form factor of a 3.5" drive, making them perfect for hot-swap drives bays such as those in servers. The 2.5" mounting holes align with the underside of the drive and are elongated, giving you the ability to shift the drive closer to(or away from) the electric adapter as needed.

The 3.5" portion of the adapter aligns exactly with both the side and bottom mounts of a standard 3.5" drive, so it should work in any situation that a standard 3.5" drive works. It appears to be made out of metal, is strong and does not flex or bend at all.

The electrical adapter appears to be a straight through adapter, meaning there are no electronics on the board itself other than the traces that shift the connector to the position that aligns with a standard 3.5" drive.

title: Short Lived...
text:
UPDATE 12/19/15: I have just returned the XPS 12. I thought maybe there was a chance I could get over the weak battery issue, however, for the second time now, after the device went to "sleep" I could not get the screen to come back on at all, though clearly the device was still on. I just don't think this thing was quite ready for primetime, let alone mass distribution. Oh well...

Well... Where to start?

Let me preface this review by letting you know that I have now had the machine for a full four days. I received it Sunday morning, and have been using it since. Unfortunately, if not regrettably, I feel at this point that I would be remiss if I didn't send it back for a refund. Is it just junk?? The answer is a resounding "NO". On the contrary, it's a beautiful and functional device. Let me start by pointing out the redeeming qualities of the Dell XPS 12.

Screen: Stunning. Gorgeous. Sharp. 4k. Over the years, I have owned too many tablets, smartphones and computers to mention. The screen on the XPS 12 rivals all the best and actually surpasses the vast majority. Resolution (Again, 4k capable), Brightness, Sharpness and overall Clarity are second to none in my opinion. I guess you might say I was pleasantly shocked by the screen on this device. Out of the park, 5 stars, etc. etc.

Keyboard: Wow. I have used minimalist keyboards with various tablets that I've owned. I have also purchased laptops in the past based primarily on the quality and feel of the keyboard. Dell really went to great lengths to deliver this device with an outstanding keyboard. The simple fact that I can type for hours on this device and never feel taxed or fatigued is quite a feat. If not for the amazing screen on the device, I would say the keyboard is the real prize with this machine. Either way, it's 1 or 1A with the screen. Exceptional.

Performance: The machine with the SkyLake processor really hums. I have not had any issues with speed, whether multitasking or not. Bare in mind, I am not a gamer and so can't comment on that aspect of the performance. However, I do believe that for most people's applications, this machine is more than capable. Browsing the web, working in MS Office while listening to music, Netflix, etc., etc... It all feels very snappy and natural on this device. Windows 10 is actually a joy to use, at least for me, but I know that just like politics and religion, I probably shouldn't go there. In a nutshell, the XPS 12 should serve the vast majority with ease and admirable fluidity.

Form Factor: For some, this will be a knock on this device. While the machine is in "laptop mode" (screen docked into keyboard), there is only one angle that the screen can be in. It is NOT adjustable. This doesn't bother me because I feel like the viewing angle is optimal and natural. Again, YMMV... What really appeals to me is the ease of going from laptop to tablet and vice versa. It's a quick and deliberate process, and I like the fact that there isn't much room for error. Pull the tablet slightly forward and up to remove from the keyboard... Set the tablet in the slot on the keyboard and let it lean back to convert to traditional laptop. Very quick, painless and efficient.

By now, you might be thinking... "Ummmm, okay then, why the two stars buddy???"

Here comes the one major caveat (deal breaker) with an otherwise fantastic device...

Battery Life: Ouch. Abysmal. Unacceptable. Atrocious. Laughable. Sad. Disheartening. Ugh.
Is it really that bad? Yep. Now, I believe Dell advertises something like 9 hours of battery life for this thing. Well... to say that's optimistic would be like waking up one morning and handing in your resignation to pursue a career as a professional golfer. Yeah, don't quit your day job! Allow me to shed some light with a couple of examples:

Typical Usage:

-- Browsing the web and watching an episode of Daredevil (in 4k) on Netflix. Time on machine: 1 hour, 45 minutes (drained the battery completely).

-- Shopping on Amazon for Xmas gifts. (Tedious, but I avoid the crowds at least). Time on machine: 2 hours, 20 minutes (actually, this is the most life I've gotten out of the battery).

-- Writing in OneNote. Time on machine: 2 hours. Seriously??

-- Amazon Prime movie. The Gift (Excellent if not unsettling movie.) Time on machine: 2 hours. (Had to plug the machine in with about 10 minutes left in the movie). Ugh (again).

So, maybe battery life doesn't warrant such a hit against an otherwise very respectable machine. For me, it absolutely does. In 2015, if we can't even get through an average flight with our device doing absolutely average work/play on the device, it is inexcusable. This may be the fatal flaw that ultimately dooms the XPS 12. Certainly, I fully intend to return mine and run toward the nearest Surface Pro 4. Sorry, Dell... I even held off on purchasing any iteration of such a device until you released this (fatally flawed) little gem.

Tragic.

title: Excellent service. No vulnerabilities.
text:
I did a lot of research before buying this system from goabode.com and I would like to highlight some of the best features of this device:

1.) Top notch customer support. The times that I have called or emailed they went just going down a script. The read into my problems and fixed them with lightning accuracy.

2.) Battery and cellular backup. My breaker box is in the garage so if I had a system that didn't function without power and a thief turned off the power my home would be vulnerable. With the cellular backup (running on AT&T or T-Mobile whichever is stronger) they can cut the internet to the house and the home will still be protected. Also they have a feature called signal guard which alerts you and the monitoring center if someone opens the door to your house and then destroys your gateway before it alarms.

So even with no power, no internet, and a destroyed gateway your home is still protected.

3.) They offer a wide range of abode branded devices. Some of them like the motion sensors with cameras are just such a good idea so when your motion sensor goes off you know why it went off. Glass break sensors, occupancy sensors, backup siren, keypads, status indicators, water sensors, streaming cameras, key fobs and more. The system is very flexible to fit every home and situation.

4.) The non abode branded devices that are supported (unlike other security systems). As anyone with a few smart things like lights and garage doors if you aren't careful you are going to end up with a separate app for all your smart stuff in your home. Abode has Nest, Alexa, and IFTTT integrations already with more integrations in the works. Abode specifically does not sell a smoke detector but you can buy the First Alert Zwave smoke detector and wham you have an alarm that will alert the monitoring center for a fire (bonus homeowners/renters insurance discount). The list is not exhaustive but it covers just about everything you would need in a smart home. You can find it here:

http://support.goabode.com/customer/en/portal/articles/2267539-compatible-z-wave-zigbee-devices

5.) Fully encrypted communications between all devices. There is a popular DIY system out there that has been hacked and people 150 feet away using a hacked version of the same system can listen for your keypad code because it is sent in the clear. Then they can use your code when you aren't home and disarm your security system. It has already been found they can't fix it without a full hardware refresh. The vulnerability has been known for years now and they have not fixed it yet.

6.) The mobile and web apps are great. The thing you are going to use the most with your security system is something that is not neglected here. It is the forefront of their product and they treat it that way. Smooth reliable interactions, modern design and consistent solid updates for new features. There are some functions that can only be done from the web app but they are few and far between (for example: connecting a non abode device to the gateway). Once they are connected they are fully functional from the mobile apps.

7.) The monitoring plans. They are very flexible and you do not have to pay if you don't want to. There is no contracts and they also offer discounts if you pay up front for a whole year. Let's say you don't have a monthly subscription but you are going out of town for the weekend. You can pay just $8 for professional monitoring, cellular backup and peace of mind while you are away. They also offer a 7 day plan for $15. For full time subscriptions they offer a $10/month or 96/year cellular backup and a $30/month or $240/year for cellular backup with professional monitoring. My homeowner's insurance dropped by 140 each year so I am paying less than $10 a month for professional monitoring (way less than the other guys).

Well if you made it this far you might be wondering what the catch is, get ready:

Like any other smart security system there is an initial investment. Now, before you panic this system isn't going to break the bank but it is a high quality system with great service backing it up. The best BEST part of this system is that you can add more to it as you go very easily. I started out with door and window sensors and as finances allowed I added a couple more motion sensor cameras in other areas. You can start basic and add more as you see a need.

Alright that's it. You made it through the marathon. Now that you have done all the work let me save you some trouble. There is not a more flexible, more compatible, no vulnerabilities and full time professional monitoring system you can buy right now and the other guys aren't even close.

text: I purchased this locally on sale (Fred Meyer) because I have a non-smart 4K TV, am not extremely picky about sound, and the TiVo Bolt doesn't yet stream Amazon Prime in UHD; I am about as close to an ideal buyer for this version of the Fire TV as anyone is likely to be. I separately have a TiVo Roamio that I am extremely happy with, and a 1st gen Fire TV Stick, which I have installed on a secondary TV which works fine whenever I use it. I had no trouble installing the batteries in the remote, nor registering it with Amazon (this step isn't necessary if you buy it direct like a normal person). After running the updates, I streamed just under two minutes of Red Oaks in UHD. It looked great, and I appreciated that it was outputting a 24fps signal, something that TiVos also do, but the Fire Stick, Chromecast, and Roku do not. I then tried to set up Netflix. While entering my password in the Netflix app, the video signal was lost, and the light turned off and didn't respond to the remote. After trying other HDMI ports, I unplugged the power adapter ( much harder than opening the remote, due to smooth sides and a slight taper / draft angle) and plugged it into a Kill A Watt power meter, where it draws zero watts. So, I like the interface, the output quality, the remote, the ease of setup, and the ability to watch Prime Video in UHD on a TV with HDCP 2.2 but no internal HEVC decoder. I dislike the power adapter (RE78VS) and/or the input jack which stopped working after 30 minutes, and that I have to drive back to the store to return it.

title: You probably can use this unless you have or unless you order an additional cable.
text:
The photo shows the problem but the description implies something different.

The DB25 connector studs are not removable and this means that you can't just plug it into the serial port (DB25 female) directly. You must also purchase another cable that is the "go-between" this product's DB25 and whatever you were planning on using this for. Unless you have a non-standard DTE device, a standard device is expecting you to plug in a male DB25 male and to tighten the two side screws to hold it in place. This product, instead, had two female "nuts" and so will not mate directly to the DTE. And, since these female "nuts" on this male DB25 are not removable, you MUST buy another cable with a female DB25 on one end and a male DB25 on the other. In theory, another solution is to use an adapter but there is no reason to manufacture an adapter that doesn't "change" anything except for the "nuts" and screws. The bottom line is to carefully check the DTE (Data Terminal Equipment) you plan on connecting to this DB25. See if those female-threaded "nuts" that extend on either side of this connector shell will not conflict with the existing 1/4"-long hardware on the DTE that you're plugging this into. Removing the "nuts" in the photo would help but I couldn't get them out because you'd have to break open the connector to grip the opposite end for torque.
This whole frustration could be avoided if the Amazon product description would include the same instruction that the installation notes emphasize. Unfortunately, the Amazon description omits the critical need for the additional cable.

"Just connect your computer's or hub's USB port with a digital camera, modem, ISDN-TA modem, barcode reader, Palm III and V, tablet, label writer, fingerprint verification, security system, POS equipment or any of your favorite serial devices."

This IS NOT possible. As the installation instructions mention AFTER you have the product and are wanting to install it, YOU MUST HAVE AN ADDITIONAL CABLE between this device and your serial device. You CANNOT do what it states: "Just connect your computer's or hub's USB... favorite serial devices." Generally, yes, IF you just happen to have a double-ended DB25 cable with a female on one end and a male on the other. Do you? I didn't so I'll have to order one and wait another delivery cycle. This is the reason for the 3-star rating. So, hopefully I have helped you to head-up this issue and have both items when you're ready to use this product as delivered.

title: Putting the "me" in Xtreme.
text:
I was so excited to get this PC. When it arrived I booted it up, and with bated breath, I awaited the unleashing of the Xtreme with no first 'E''s power. Instead I was presented with a distorted screen and a a subsequent boot cycle that said Attempting to Repair PC. So, after 20 minutes and multiple reboots, it was with a heavy heart I put it back in it's package and contemplated a Viking funeral. But as anyone down on their luck will tell you: $700 bucks is $700 bucks. So I sent it back and requested a replacement. When the second PC arrived, I flinched. The truth is I had been hurt before, but the amazon rep promised that, baby, this time will be different.
Upon opening the second PC, I noticed immediately a media card was missing that was on the first. Had I been hoodwinked? Bamboozled? Swindled? Undaunted I tried to ignore it, like you do when you are on a first date and your date is rude to the server but they are SO PRETTY. I held my breath, I fired it up, I got a drink.
When I returned and saw the horror show presented to me on the monitor, my heart sank. "This can't be happening..." I whispered..."not again!" ATTEMPTING TO REPAIR PC. I dropped my drink and it shattered. And that was on carpet.
A sane man would cut their losses. Only a real chucklehead would roll the dice a third time. UNLESS...
Maybe it was bad batch, I told myself. Maybe if I took it back a third time, they will really have changed and won't hurt me like they had before. People can change, why not PCs?
Fast Forward one week:
I am now in the first week of the third PC. I admit, when the doorbell rang I wanted to shut the door in it's face for what it had done to me in the past. But change is a two-way street. If I'm not willing to meet this new PC halfway, what does that say about me?
We are taking it slow, but for now, well, things aren't perfect, but they are good. It's there when I need it, and as long as we take it day by day, I think we just might make it. Together.

title: Meh. Tends to overheat and throttle back. It's neat but the accessories for this device need to be readily available.
text:
Meh.

The CPU runs real hot. 180-190F doing menial tasks.

The major obstacle when first powering this device on for the first time was figuring out how to do it!! No "getting started" instructions included, you must read the online manual to find out the startup procedure. You have to press an unmarked microswitch for 1 second, easy when you know how. Random switch clicking does not turn it on.

Lattepanda website does have a cooling fan to keep the device cool. Guess what, you have to wait for it to come from the far east, not available on Amazon. I ordered the fan which indicated it was "in stock", got an email today saying the status has changed to "back ordered". Who knows when that might come.

The plywood case sounds interesting, but that's the only option here, a plastic case is available if you order from the far east. The lack of readily available accessories is an issue. My first experience with Raspberry Pi was much better, I have 3 of those now doing various dedicated tasks.

By the time you get a case, cooling fan, WIn10 key etc you are looking at $150, which is the price of a budget Chromebook which probably runs better. For a tiny Windows device this is interesting and I look forward to a community building around it. My initial interest in replacing Intel Computer Sticks (which tend to overheat and lockup if left on 24/7) has waned. Looks like the same issues will be present with this device, and its not as polished a product nor does it have the same support. Compute Sticks are cheaper.

The one advantage LattePanda has over a compute stick is the ability to add a MicroSD Card for storage, this should mean major windows updates will actually work. I like that it has multiple USB ports and an Ethernet port. It can be used without having to resort to USB hubs and USB ethernet like a compute stick.

The Lattepanda runs all Windows apps I've thrown at it. Its basically OK, but just not great. Yet.

title: I love the quality feel of the PowerLine+ series cables.
text:
It seems Lightning cables all eventually break after a couple of months of use in my house. We have three kids that test the limits of any charging cable, so when you find a good one, it pays to stick with it. I've been using various Anker cables for the past couple of years and I have had only 2 cables fail and Anker replaced them for me without any hassle! .

The Anker PowerLine+ cables are built better than the cables Apple provided with the device. I have a USB meter that helped me prove that as well. I can only get about 2 Amps when charging my iPad when using an OEM Apple cable. I can get almost 2.4 Amps when using one of these Anker cables. Basically the Anker cables can deliver around 12 Watts and the Apple Cable can only deliver 10 Watts. This would allow your device to charger quicker since more juice is being delivered through the cable.

What I like:
1. The cables are well built and durable.
2. They can charge devices quicker since they are capable of delivering more current than the stock cable or other inferior cables.
3. The PoweLine+ series of cables have a nice quality feel to them over everything else I've tried. They are very flexible.
4. Anker has an 18 month hassle free warranty on these cables, so if one breaks they will replace it for you and it is an easy process!

What could use improvement:

1: I'm mixed on the included cable pouch. It is ice, but I think I prefer just the Velcro cable strap by itself. Just a personal preference though.

Remember, Your charging will only be quick if all of the components being used are quality components, so your weakest link will determine your charging speeds. If you use a cable that is capable of delivering 1 A, then a 2 Amp charger will only deliver 1 Amp and vise versa. Don't skimp on your cables. I've tested many cables that will only deliver 1/2 Amp so your device will charge very slowly, and I promptly dispose these under-performing cables. The Anker cables will help you get optimal charging if used with a quality charger.

title: Simple Setup. Works Wonderfully.
text:
We cut the cable cord, completely, and signed up for the T-Mobile $50 unlimited plan. I use my cellphone as a hotspot to run everything in the house and for streaming Hulu, SlingTV, Netflix and Amazon Video. (We get a very zippy 28 Mb/s speed at our house.)

Everything was great, but my cellphone had a little trouble getting Wi-Fi signal to the far reaches of the house. This little device took care of that.

I took it out of the box, plugged it into an outlet, connected my $49 Kindle Fire to it using the password on the little business card that came in the box. Logged into the admin page using the info that was on the same card. Chose "repeater mode" and entered the password for my cellphone's hotspot, then let it reboot-- and that was it. Done.

So simple that a monkey could almost do it.

I then plugged our Magic Jack into the Ethernet port on the bottom and connected our house phone and fax to it. So now the house phone runs through it and the cellphone hotspot.

In four minutes everything was up and going without even reading the directions.

Now I can sit out on the patio with my Kindle and connect to the internet through my cellphone inside. Video streams fine through it. It works perfectly.

For that price I'm going to buy a few spares to keep on hand.

Five stars!

title: Worthless!
text: Absolute junk! In 2014 I bought 2 systems. First I bought the 21291 system. It was for a hunting club in the middle of nowhere and did not have internet access, so networking was not an issue. However the advertised 450 ft. range of the cameras quickly proved to be a fallacy. It has since had a failed power adapter which is no big deal, and Defender took care of that quickly. All in all that system has done ok, but the second system I bought, (the 21313) has been a real nightmare. It was for my home, and I fully intended to use networking to view remotely. What they don’t tell you is that the wireless system operates on the same 2.4 Ghz frequency that common Wi-Fi systems operate at. So as soon as I turned it on, my internet went down. It took me a while to figure out what was going on, but once I did I called Defender/CWD. Their fix was to separate the camera DVR as far as possible from my AT&T internet modem. So I rewired my house to get them as far apart as I could. The DVR was in the basement and the modem was 2 floors above, and it did nothing to help. After that failed they said all I had to do was buy a new router on the 5 Ghz frequency. Great idea if I intended to spend even more money, but then all the older devices (PS3, iPhone 4, kids tablets, laptops) that only operate at 2.4 Ghz no longer work. So I bought a dual mode 2.4Ghz, and 5 Ghz router. Still didn’t fix the problem. The only solution was to turn off the security system when I wanted to use the internet or even my wireless printer. This system claimed a 750 ft. camera range. Only in someone's dreams. 75 ft. maybe. So having done all that I settled in with my new security system. Some time went by and one night I looked at my security screen and I saw a daytime picture on one of the cameras. I power cycled it and it started working again. After a few days when it was raining, a different camera had a dry sunny picture. It was like a movie when they put a picture in front of the camera. Totally unacceptable. Now I couldn’t trust what I was seeing. After another call to Defender/CWD they suggested I separate the DVR as far as possible from the internet modem! Unless I put equipment in my neighbor’s house, that wasn’t going to help. After several more calls it was obvious they were not going to do anything about it. Amazom.com however agreed to take it back as the manufacturer was not going to help. Then I made the unfortunate decision to give them another chance and bought another 21313 system thinking maybe they had rectified the problems. Straight out of the box one of the cameras was bad. After a phone call they supplied me with an RMA and I sent it back. 2 weeks later my replacement cameras arrived. (they are sold in pairs with a receiver for each pair). One camera worked, and one did not. More phone calls. I asked them to expedite the next replacement. Their idea of expediting was to charge my credit card for the next set and would immediately ship it standard 5-7 business days. A week later after no word from them I called and inquired about the order. They apologized and said the order had been misplaced, but magically just found and would be on the way in 24 hours. Another week goes by before I open my 2nd set of replacement cameras. One worked, and one did not. On my last phone call with them I asked for overnight shipment of known good cameras, and they refused unless I wanted to pay for the shipping. I told them I was done, and would be packing the whole thing up and sending it back. The wireless idea is a good one, but this company hasn’t figured out how to make it work and certainly doesn’t care about their customers. Their idea of quick response is for you to go online and fill out a form and wait 24 hours for a call back when you have a problem. I’ll still try another wireless system at some point in time because it’s the only solution for what I need, but it won’t be from Defender/CWD!

title: Neglected FN keys in many ways...
text:
I bought this nifty mini wireless keyboard recently for use with my Raspberry Pi, since having a nice portable keyboard is easier than hauling around a regular wired or wireless one. Unfortunately, I almost immediately found that this little keyboard doesn't really work.

For this particular keyboard, to press a key like ALT-F1 (to access the first tty terminal on Raspberry Pi or any other Linux computer), you would press and hold the following keys in order: ALT, then FN (to enable auxiliary keyboard functions), and then ESC/F1 (F1 being the FN auxillary function for ESC). It's a bit of a handful to press these keys - you probably will need two hands to do this.

The problem lies in the ability to press some of the other ALT-F* keys. ALT-F1, ALT-F3, and ALT-F5 worked, but for some reason ALT-F2, ALT-F4, and ALT-F6 were not working. This was a major deal breaker for me, considering that you definitely need these keys to access your corresponding terminals on the Raspberry Pi! Keep in mind that these same keys worked for the normal functions - but when you try to access their FN-based functionality, they did not work. (Weirdly enough, these keys do cause the terminal to pause blinking for a bit, just like if you mashed ALT-F1 on the first console...)

Just to make sure, I kept the keyboard near its receiver, and I've tested these particular key combinations on my Linux laptop... again, those particular keys did not work unfortunately. As a result, I immediately returned this keyboard.

Other minor complaints include the backlight and occasional responsiveness issues. The function keys are printed in blue on the wireless mini keyboard, but are not transparent. In the dark, when you turn on the backlight, the regular white keyboard text will shine through, and the blue FN text will not. Even in a brighter setting, the blue text almost becomes non-existent when the backlight is turned on, usually resulting me in turning it off when using FN keys. In terms of responsiveness, it works well for the most part, but very occasionally you may push a key and it takes a bit of time to respond.

This keyboard is not entirely bad though - I purchased this keyboard because unlike the other Rii wireless mini keyboard, it has the mouse buttons as the shoulder buttons on top. The Rii keyboard (at the time of writing) places the mouse buttons on an awkward left position, forcing you to remove your left hand to push those buttons when you are using the mouse. Those mouse buttons worked really well, allowing me to do some easy drag and drop operations without moving too much! The backlight also worked pretty well, with the exception of the FN keys. Finally, this keyboard has a nice removal battery, which allows for future replacement if the battery goes bad. (The newer Rii wireless mini keyboard, at the time of writing, recently changed to an internal hot-glued battery instead.) Alas, it had some serious issues that resulted in a return.

Interesting and useful keyboard - but if you use the FN keys, don't buy this. The FN keys are not visible when backlit, and some of them (ALT-F*) don't work.

title: Wow.  Home Theater that is really the Theater at Home:  Bright, Clear and Colorful.
text:
The brightness, HD clarity and color quality of this projector is just outstanding. Combined with wide connectivity, this is definitely a projector to consider for a home theater, outdoor party theater and even high def presentations (although the size makes it less than ideal as a portable projector to run around to meeting with).

The image quality for high def content, particularly from BluRay, is so high, that I've marked my review as 5 stars in spite of enough issues with the projector to make me consider bumping a star.

A photo of a projection is not the same as being there, but I've posted two photos of projecting from a BD player onto an 8' high wall from about 19' back. One is a shot from Avatar, projected as 16:9 and about 180" diagonal. The other is from a Harry Potter that is a 2:1 ratio and was zoomed in to better fill the wall. The wall itself is painted "Navajo White" - a deeper off white with a yellow/gold tint. In spite of the wall paint, the image colors and clarity are outstanding. I should note that in the daytime, even with the blinds drawn, the image is too washed out to watch when zoomed to this scale. Projecting at about 100" diagonal is fine in the daytime.

Using a Roku 3 (for example) to stream HD content from Amazon and Netflex is amazing.

What's not to like?

There is terrible color shadowing on text from any source, as well as everything projected from an iPhone 6 Plus, iPad Air or MacBook Pro via Lightning to HDMI adapter for the IOS devices and DisplayPort to VGA adapter for the MacBook. Note the two pictures posted of text. In the "Phys" in brown text on a white background (from PowerPoint/KeyNote) you'll see a terrible green shadow on the left and a bad purple fringe on the top of each letter. If you zoom into the "Playback?" text, you'll see the same colored fringe inside the letters. My old Sharp XGA (1024x768) projector has never had any issue like this.

Focus. When you adjust the zoom, you lose the focus and have to focus again. That's just bad engineering, or a manufacturing defect. In contrast, when the optical zoom is adjusted on my old Sharp XGA projector, the image stays clearly in focus through the entire zoom range. The Epson also has a focus assist feature that displays a pattern for you to use to adjust the focus. Part of the process is to move two circles together. They moved only once for me - but generally, just before I could get the focus visually correct, the focus mode exited. Pretty much gave up on it and used part of the projected image for focusing.

Auto key-stoning is both a great thing when it works - and a bad thing when it created a randomly distorted trapezoid on the wall. I had about 50/50 luck with the feature, which is a cool idea - the projector 'reads' the projected image to auto correct the shape. Manual keynoting allows you to adjust all 4 corners of a trapezoid so that the projector can be placed both above/below and left/right of center and still project a rectangular image.

Noise. I'm at 5,400' altitude. The instructions make clear (as with other projectors) that the high altitude setting (challenging to find) must be enabled when over 4,900' altitude. This makes the fan noise go from acceptably low to a distracting roar. I did find that by switching from Normal mode to Automatic Eco mode, the fan speed dropped enough to be acceptable with only a minor drop in brightness. I wish manufacturers would make a projector that uses multiple fans for low velocity high volume air movement to reduce noise.

Sound options. The projector has a small built-in speaker, which is typical and provides basic mono audio output. But, for quality sound output, your options at the projector are limited to basic stereo to feed into an amplified speaker system. If you want 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound, you have to connect your HDMI outputs to a home theater receiver in order to get an optical/digital output for your surround system. (If you're only using a single input, such as a BD player, it may have its own optical output that you can use.) To me, this is a gross oversight for people who want to take the projector and a sound bar, or wireless speakers, into the back yard for a movie party feeding from a device that doesn't have digital audio output, but feeds it via the HDMI connector. Even my 10 year old Sharp LCD TV has an optical out jack that sends any HDMI audio to a digital sound system.

The packaging should be improved. The box was delivered (signature required) and was rattling badly when moved. The batteries, remote control and cord were just tossed into compartments inside the Epson box without any bubble wrap to protect the remote from damage.

In spite of the things that disappoint me (for the price), I'm nonetheless in awe of the image quality and brightness and find it hard not to give this projector 5 stars.

title: Work great so far on 6 GPU rig, If you don't know which ones to get consider these.
text: I fell like I should leave a review for these risers as I knew nothing about risers before researching them. I bought 6 of them for a mining rig, I'm new to mining and don't know much, but from researching I found that pretty much all the risers on the market are pretty bad and that this was the most common part to fail in your rig. After seeing that the risers that have the 6pin to sata adapter cables sometimes melt or catch fire I knew I didn't want a riser with an adapter cable, but instead one that had a sata port on the riser card itself. I found out there are different version of risers. Some have less capacitors that can lead to an unstable riser card, and some do not come with voltage regulators. So in a nutshell I was looking for a card with at least 4 capacitors, a voltage regulator(not sure if this riser has one, not sure how to tell), and the sata port built into the riser card. Of course I also looked for quality. This card is version 008s, they look like they are made well, It has a foam backing which i like. Everything fits snug in the slots, all 6 risers work great, not getting too hot and I've been running the rig for a few days now. These are the first set of risers I've tried and am thrilled that I didn't end up picking bad ones. I would suggest you give them a try.

title: Okay for the money, could be better with more options/features from Garmin
text:
I purchased the Garmin Dash Cam 55 on February 1, 2018. I purchased the 55 specifically for the 1080p at 60 frames per second (FPS). Apparently the 65 model does NOT have the 60 FPS option.

Pros:
-1080p at 60 FPS. A must for me since this is a standard for my personal taste. There's no point in going for 720p at 60 FPS when you want more resolution but shouldn't settle for less than 60 FPS for a dash camera. You're driving for a reason. If you don't have enough frames, I don't see the point in worrying about a clear picture since you're almost always moving when you're commuting.

-Automatic recording on power up* (more on this below; see first con). I don't understand why the majority of dash camera buyers would intentionally buy a forward-facing dash camera that DOESN'T power up automatically the vehicle is started. I've had to live with a makeshift dash camera (smartphone) before I found a good enough dash camera to pull the trigger on and it's not fun have to manually activate and place my smartphone into position to record my driving.

-Small form factor. It fits right behind my rear view mirror and is mostly discreet.

-Discreet (if you black out the obnoxious neon orange). You really shouldn't surprised at the things people do when no one is looking.

-Compatible with 128 GB micro SD cards (officially only compatible with 64 GB per Garmin). My 128 GB Lexar and Samsung micro SD cards work and the camera is able to record up to that capacity too.

-Status light indicator to show it's recording* (more on this below).

-User friendly interface and buttons that aren't flakey or annoying which is a huge plus compared to rival Chinese-based dash camera manufacturers. I had a VicoVation Opia2 before this and I hated the user interface AND the buttons. The VicoVation Opia 2 had buttons that had to be pressed, and you had to wait a half second before pressing the same button or another button. The user interface on the VicoVation Opia 2 just made things even worse with its horrid buttons. Be very happy Garmin understands user interfaces from their GPS products.

-Price. For $200, I'd buy this again if the original lasts at least a year and a half or two. I'd be a bit happier if this was $155 or $175 but it's Garmin so I know I'm mostly getting my money's worth which I can't say with no-name brand dash cameras or non-English based manufacturers.

-Screen size compared to dash camera. It's actually usable. Not a touch but I wouldn't want it to be a touch anyway.

Cons:
-*Every single time it powers up, it displays the disclaimer and DOESN'T record until you either 1.) press the button for "Agree" or 2.) 5-10 seconds pass and it automatically starts recording. If there was a way to defeat this, I'd love for it to be an OEM function.

-The mount is a mix of a magnet that sticks onto your windshield (where ever you want to mount it that will stick) and a pivoting head that inserts into the camera. The give isn't exactly enough to easily twist the camera so it can record who you're talking to from the driver's side window. I'd have to assume this was intended for easy removable and add after setting up the magnet. Definitely not my preference as I leave my dash cameras in my car. The only reason I'd remove it is because of extreme temperatures which aren't common in a year where I live (cold or hot).

-The status light indicator is red when the camera is recording but it's not bright enough in the day to really make a huge difference nor is it fully visible during the day even when you're looking at the screen side of the camera.

-Battery instead of supercapacitor. Unfortunately this is a large draw back if you want to use the parking mode or for long term use. I don't use the parking mode but I do like to keep technology for more than 3 years. Hopefully this dash camera will still power up with an external source once the battery is dead after a year. It's not a very large battery so I can only assume 1.) it was designed for battery use for cheapness or 2.) to generate more sales by making people upgrade/replace their dash cameras from Garmin once the battery is dead.

Etc:
The driver assistance functions (obviously passive) are mostly a gimmick and gives a few false positives. Obviously you can't set up the parameters for these driver assistance functions so there's bound to be a few false positives and oversensitive warnings given each make and model of vehicle has different dimensions. Garmin has taught it somewhat well on how to tell when my car is crossing the lines. The forward collision warning is honestly not functional for 80% of the time it's in operation. Either way, I'm really hoping you're not buying this for the driver assistance features. You're better off getting that OEM from your car's manufacturer

title: Great sound
text:
I am impressed by the sound quality of this little device and how well it can pick up voices and sounds even from 6 feet away. It is the size of a USB flash drive and looks exactly like one as well. It is easily stored anywhere dud to its compact size. There are only 3 buttons on this device and no screen, so using it can be quite a learning curve. Each button pressed on its own or in combination will serve to control the different functions. There is a tiny LED light that blinks red, blue, or purple, to indicate different settings. It will take some time and careful reading of the instructions for you to familiarize yourself around this product, but it is not difficult, just takes time.

It does a good job from arms length and up to halfway across a room. Unfortunately the microphone is so good that it can be quite sensitive to other noises like rustling or paper shuffling in the background.

A few things to note:
*You cannot record sound while the headphones are plugged in.
*To listen to the recording playback, you must connect headphones (or alternately you can hook this up to a speaker using a 3.5mm cable).
*There is no Bluetooth capability.

title: Perfect for my ultraportable 12" Retina Macbook (2015)
text:
When I needed a case for my 2015 12" Retina Macbook, this is what I got. I saw so many reviews for different kinds of cases here, with so much contradictory information, I ended up just going to Fry's with my laptop so I could see what I liked and make sure I had the size right.

Since my Macbook is ultraportable--2 pounds, half an inch thick, and 11"x8", I wanted a very small case to retain as much convenience as I could when working on the road or out of coffee shops, hopefully something I could slip into a normal briefcase or backpack as needed. At the same time, I wanted to be able to carry the power brick, cord, dongles, etc., so the slim neoprene cases were ruled out.

This case is the perfect size for my Macbook (the laptop's corners don't leave any leeway at all for anything bigger; there's a little extra room on top and on the sides, but the case corners are rounded more than the laptop corners). People think I'm carrying a study Bible or something, but I generally have my computer, power cord and power supply, an external HDD and cord, a USB recharger battery and cord, my checkbook, a couple of pens and a small notepad, a USB thumb drive or 2, and 3 USB-C dongles.

title: Excellent "normal" lens for specific purposes
text:
This is a really nice lens for special purposes. A 50mm lens used to be the default lens for 35mm photography, but this isn't that sort of 50mm. I use a EF 24-70mm f/2.8L II USM (and the EF 24-70mm f/2.8L USM before this) as my default lens for general duty and it serves this purpose wonderfully.

The ability to isolate and highlight the subject by using a narrow depth of field is the reason to own and use this lens. It really ought to be used at f 2.0 or lower. I do a great deal of low light candid shooting and the EF 50mm f/1.2 is great for this work. If you want to shoot at f 5.6, use one of Canon's normal zooms. You'll be happier with the results.

I also had videography in mind when buying this lens. As above, the ability to control depth of field is the value that this lens brings to the table. I have not yet had a chance to do much video work with the lens, but I am pretty confident that I will be happy with it for this purpose.

There have been a lot of comments about this lens' autofocusing issues. I've got an EOS 5D Mk III and an EOS 5D. This lens autofocuses quickly and surely on the Mk III; no problems. I find, however, that the lens just does not autofocus reliably on my old 5D. The focusing systems of these two cameras are quite different and the lens' autofocusing performance seems to be sensitive to this difference.

title: Great Introduction to Electronics
text:
I've always been interested in electronics but didn't really know where to start. The Elegoo UNO kit is a great introduction. I knew the items that were included in the kit, what I didn't know was the comprehensive manual on the included CD. It contains an IDE (integrated development environment) which includes a number of sample "sketches" (code that is sent to the board to control it), drivers, and is a useful introduction to electronics. To start it explains how to read the color codes on resistors and how to determine the positive and negative pins of an LED, how to use a breadboard for designing circuits and progressively leads you through more complicated projects.

The breadboard (this is plastic with holes in to allow you to push in components and wires) has double sided tape so you can stick it to your desk or work surface, which is a nice touch, however the enclosed USB cable is a little on the short side, so unless your surface is right next to a USB port, you're going to want a longer cable.

Overall I'm very happy with the product plus the range of accessories that are available as add-ons for future projects.

title: Great microphone!!!
text:
I bought this wireless Uniden CB microphone to complement my 980 SSB radio. I'm usually the trail leader on our offroad ventures and I needed something to help with communications when a trail was questionable. It usually involves me getting out of my Jeep with a hand held CB radio and walking up or down a trail to scout it out before the group can go thru. The hand held CB was fine but it had range limitations. This BC906W microphone from Uniden was the ticket! It has a 300 foot range FROM the 980 SSB radio. It transmits and receives thru the main unit so range is no longer an issue. The volume is more than sufficient. It weighs next to nothing and comes with it's own belt hanger. It has an 8 hour charge but I mounted the charging unit permanently in my Jeep so when I return to the vehicle, I connect it back to the charger so it's always charged. My friends say all my transmission are loud and clear so I know the microphone works well.

I've read some reviewers comments that the wireless microphone takes over the speaker/external speaker. This is only true if you keep the volume settings normal (as you would when you are using it outside the vehicle). If you lower the volume settings on the wireless microphone to it's lowest setting, your CB radios speaker or external speaker will be back in control. Only thing you have to remember is that when you leave the vehicle with the microphone, turn up the volume controls so it takes over again. So far, the Uniden BC906W Wireless CB Microphone has worked flawlessly and I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a microphone you can use outside of your vehicle whether it's a Jeep or an 18 wheeler.

title: Absolutely fantastic sound quality, comfortable to wear, very well-made.
text:
These ear buds are some of the best money can buy. For any basshead that needs a small, easily portable pair of headphones, these are absolutely essential. Withe the different filters, anyone can fine-tune these ear buds to fit exactly what they prefer in terms of sound. Not only do these very effectively block out external noise, but they provide a rich, clear sound and are capable of hitting highs and lows most other headphones could only dream of.

My only real complain is the design of the over-the-ear wire setup. Because it is VERY easy to bend these around, I am constantly having to readjust them and as a result, after about the first year of owning these I did have to send them in for warranty repair because one of the support-wires broke in half. It would be nice if there was some kind of rubber/silicone piece that you could choose to slide the wire into like a cradle so it would keep them shaped properly and take the stress off that support wire.

It's a minor complaint, though. I typically hate over-the-ear designs, but admittedly I have fallen in love with these even on that level - they do not come out or loosen when you are working out, and are overall just very stable, very satisfying headphones. The most important design element, in my opinion, is that the ear buds themselves are encased in a very strong metal shell, so the most critical components are VERY well protected.

title: Great interface and setup, not ideal for multiple children with shared devices
text:
Sooooo close to perfect but not there yet. We will be returning Circle but hope to use it in the future when the feature set more closely meets our needs. Their support was great.

Here's where our primary problem is... We have 4 children and multiple devices and desktops. No child has their own device, they are all shared. Circle absolutely works at tracking online time a child uses on a device. But it requires that the child be assigned to a specific device instead of the child having a centralized account and being able to use their login on any Circle-connected device. So Child A wants to use an iPad. I go to Circle and assign the child to that device. Child A then gets bored of the iPad and wants to use the desktop. I have to go and assign that desktop to him and while I'm there, assign Child B to the iPad since now they want to use it. As you can see, this quickly gets tiresome. Children didn't always tell me when they started using a device so it would track on the wrong account and I was in the app constantly changing assignments.

IF your child has their own device or primarily uses a single device this would work very well. If your devices are shared and you have more than 1 or 2 children, your time is filled up with reassigning devices and making corrections when someone uses another person's time. Side note, Circle doesn't let you make a one time addition of time to accounts. You have to change the daily allowance and then it stays that way until you change it back. So if Child C needs extra time I have to bump his daily limits and then at the end of the day go back and return it to normal settings. Tedious. Please let us give extra time additions without changing the base daily limit!

Also, just FYI, because I didn't find this too clearly outlined... Circle only tracks ONLINE use. Not local games, etc. that do not connect to the internet. It essentially just switches off the internet once the time is up. If your child has a game that is not internet based it will NOT track that time.

I'm really surprised that there is not a solution out there for multiple users on multiple shared devices that tracks all time, not just online. Whoever finally creates this solution will get my money, and probably a lot of other peoples too!

text:
I received the unit today and it was easy to install. There wasn't too much space in the wall, so I connected the house wire directly to the unit opposed to using the enclosed wires and connector. The screws are pretty small but it was certainly doable. I was a bit surprised that my chime didn't work prior to registration. Once the doorbell was registered it chimed just fine. Registration failed the first two times, so I ended up calling support. They picked up within 30 seconds of being in the queue. Took me by surprise. The person I spoke to was awesome, helpful, patient and knowledgeable. It worked the 3rd time of course. For some reason the Android app shows duplicate devices, and the support guy created a ticket and tried to speak to the product manager while I was on the phone. After I had the device working, I mounted it, and while less than ideal position it shows everything I need to see due to the large field of view.

Unfortunately, I have to downgrade my review. The company recently had "maintenance" for about a week during which time the device stopped working, and I was not able to login into the app (from intermittent issues). There was no notice of maintenance. When I explained this was totally unacceptable to break my doorbell for a week and requested a refund, it started working shortly after (on 5/22/2018). They did not address my request for a refund, and when I pointed out they finally responded today (on 6/22/2018) that they will not be able to provide a refund.

Push notifications empty most of the time (80+%), and when you click on them they don't play the video. The work-around is go into the messages tab and find the relevant video there. It then fails to play for me rarely, maybe 5% of the time, and retrying once or twice usually plays those. Push notifications cannot be dismissed (swiped away). La View says this is an Android defect, but this is the only app that has this feature.

The push notification time was wrong, and motion sensor too sensitive for with street in front of house and winter decorations The manual kinda sorta tells you how to change the setting (select device, live view, then top right gear etc). It is a little too early to declare success on the motion sensor change but it seems way better. The motion sensor trigger every night when IR turns on, and whenever a cloud passes over which changes the amount of light it detects. Of the 9 alerts I have received today, 1 has been useful, rest has been light changes.

Some time prior to 1/30/2019 I reported that push notifications intermittently delayed. They asked screenshots which were difficult to obtain but I finally provided irrefutable proof on 3/28/2019 of notification that was delayed by 3-4 minutes. As of 5/10/2019 there has been no resolution.

title: the flash syncs with the shutter just fine. My main usage is in S1 mode
text:
I purchased this approximately 75 days ago and I've used it 3-4 times since then. My experience has mostly been to use this as a slave flash as a back light, so this is how I will be reviewing this product. I use this flash to shoot head shots, mostly.

First of all, I'll start this review by saying it is important for you to read the product description to know exactly what you're buying. If you want a flash with an 'auto' mode or TTL technology, this is not for you. What this flash is, is a basic manual flash which has 8 steps of power, diffuser and bounce card, test/pilot button, rotating head that locks in large intervals (horizontally and vertically), and manual/S1/S2 modes. It also mounts to shoe-mounts, which is tightened by hand.

I've rarely used the flash using the shoe-mount on my camera and in manual mode. When I do, the flash syncs with the shutter just fine. My main usage is in S1 mode, and I normally use an off-camera flash to trigger the Neewer flash, which works well. I've shot this flash in slave mode in normal ambient light, and it picked up the flash of the key light well. It syncs well with the key light and I see no banding at 1/160 or slower shutter speeds.

In very, very few cases (under 5%), the light didn't flash when the key light flashed. I figured out it happened when rapidly clicking the shutter and the flash did not have time to cycle to another charge. Another time, it happened when the Neewer flash was not in a clear line of sight of the key light (flash). So, bear in mind that when using this flash in slave mode, you'll want to have a clear line of sight. When you do, it works flawlessly.

I've used it during shoots that have lasted about 1.5 hours, taken approximately 120 photos, and the flash goes strong with fairly short cycling times. Like all flashes, cycle time to re-charge increases after each burst, so no surprise there. This flash takes 4 AAA batteries, and its charge and cycle time is comparable to modern flashes.

When I attach the flash to a shoe mount, it feels very secure. To me, this is important, because I've had flashes that felt very loose when attaching to an external shoe mount, like on a tripod. This guy feel snug when he's on a tripod adapter or something similar.

The light itself is smooth.. not much else to really say about that.

For a $25 flash, why wouldn't you include this flash in your bag? In my experience, it works great as a slave flash and does the job well. There aren't any real cons that I can think of. I give 5 stars and have recommended this to several photographer friends.

title: Bargain-Priced Linux Netbook, Blemished by Poor Wifi Range
text:
Originally gave five stars for the price, for use as a lightweight Linux machine. I have dropped this to 3 stars because of the extremely limited Wifi range.

I found the Wifi range to be *extremely* limited on this machine. The connection was dropping at 4 to 5 meters from the router. After doing some research and troubleshooting, this appears to be either a design or manufacturing issue, and other people have mentioned similar problems on Windows as well. If you buy this laptop and have similar problems, I solved this with a Wifi range extender (in my case, Netgear N300 - $35).

Runs well with LMDE 2 (Linux Mint Debian Edition 2 - or "Betsy") with Mate desktop. I found the Cinnamon desktop to have choppy performance. It took a bit of futzing with the BIOS settings and partitions, but it is nothing out of the ordinary for Debian users. Wifi hardware worked out of the box, so no need for hard-wired ethernet on the install (which is good, since there is no ethernet jack). I noticed that it only found my "G" Wifi - apparently "N" is not supported. 22GB of space left after the OS install. Performance of this machine is generally peppy running Linux. TouchPad seems to work well under LMDE2, so perhaps the issues reported in other reviews are related more to Windows and not the hardware.

This netbook has been designed to be manufactured at a low cost. You can't upgrade the storage, and the battery isn't exposed. Still, the keyboard has a nice feel, the screen is decently bright, and it looks cool. The design looks nice. Battery life appears to be decent - 6 to 8 1/2 hours under light use (using Linux - Mint LMDE with Mate). No fan in this laptop! It runs quiet and cool.

MineCraft plays reasonably well, with about 20 fps average. A little chunky at times, but quite playable. You *must* drop some of the graphics settings (video) to get consistently good frame rates for Minecraft 1.8 and higher. Good enough for the kids. Note: I don't expect this to be the case if you try to play MineCraft on Windows on this machine, as Windows minimum resource usage is a lot higher, and MineCraft eats a lot of RAM. I tested under Linux only.

title: NOT compatible with Dish DVRs and other devices that reject a fixed IP address *OUT OF THE BOX*
text:
Here's why some people can't get this device to work. The claim that it will work with 'ANY DEVICE WITH AN ETHERNET PORT' is simply untrue. This adapter provides a specific fixed IP address to the device it's connected to. If the device is ok with that, great, it will work, but some devices still require getting their IP address from a DHCP server; with such devices, this adapter will fail.

In particular, it won't work with a current model VIP722 HD Dish satellite receiver/DVR, which requires DHCP. This is unfortunate, as the Dish receiver needs a broadband internet connection in order to enable Sling live TV on mobile devices.

EDIT: Ok, I'm editing this review one hour later, adding one star. The device now functions with the Dish DVR. Big thanks to the Amazon user who noted that the adapter has a HIDDEN web-based configuration page accessible at 192.168.1.252/menu.asp. This page has many useful configuration options which for some ludicrous reason Iogear has seen fit to hide from the average user. (An 'Advanced' link on the default home.asp landing page would have been nice.) Included here is the ability to make this little box into its own DHCP server. I simply toggled this on, and the DVR got its IP address and was able to access the net immediately. Just in time to cancel my order for a more expensive multiport media bridge.

TL,DR: If you can connect your web browser to the device, by cable if necessary, you can use the hidden configuration page at 192.168.1.252/menu.asp to solve my issue and probably many others.

title: Did the job nicely, but take getting used to.
text:
At first, I was afraid to use the solution that came in the package having read some reviews. But the dust specs on my sensor are very stubborn. I ended up using half the swaps because of one very tough spot -- which was a bit of a mistake. I should have stopped after 3rd attempts. Even though I'm afraid it may be too much to repeat the whole process all over again, I did it anyway. And now my sensor is very clean except for that 1 spot which can be healed easily with photoshop.

The paddle fit the full frame sensor of my Canon EOS 5D MK II very well, although like some of the reviewers said, there is a little room on top and bottom of the sensor that the paddle cannot reach -- and annoyingly, that's where some of my dusts were.

Do resist the temptation to go back and forth with the paddle (which unfortunately I did). So, if you have the same problem of sticky dusts like I had; and after maybe your third try and you have 1 dust spot left, STOP. That's better than keep going and risking introducing my dust specs.

The swapping takes a bit of getting used to because all of us are so afraid of damaging the sensor. But I went all out because those blobs of black specs have been ruining too many of my great photos -- especially my perfect sky. So, either that, or taking risks.

I'm happy to report that my risks paid off and now my sensor is CLEAN!!! Hooray. Thank you to you people at UES.

So despite some trials and errors, I still give 5 stars - because it beats paying 60 bucks to have it cleaned professionally.

Hope this helps.
