title: Good investment for gym
text:
I received these on Sunday night, spent about 10-15 trying the different size tips and wings before a settled on what i felt is a good fit for me. i figured out that the behind the head/over ear feels better to me, and removes the feeling of the cord hanging down, and places the controls right behind my left ear, so no grabbing for the cord and fumbling around looking for the controls.
Charged them up over night, and used them at work on monday for about 7 hours before I got the warning that the battery was running low.

The sound to me is good, ive seen other reviews say that the sound wasnt loud enough or that it was distorted. Leaves me wondering if it has something to do with the phones bluetooth abilities. Im using an Iphone 6.

It was plenty loud enough to block out the noises at my gym (even the gym radio playing todays "hits") I find that if i turn it all the way up its to loud in fact.

Before I give me opinion of the sound quality you should know my preference for music in the gym is along the lines of Rob Bailer's "Beast" from the "Southpaw" movie, or some Trap music (Flosstradamus, Buku, Aryay, Kai Wachi) While im at work i listen to whatever comes across my slacker radio, doesnt matter if its rock, rap or country if its has a good beat ill listen to it.

Comparing these to other headphones that I've owned (beats and skullcandy) from my point of view these seems to be on par with the beats earbuds that ive used in the past. The bass is present but in anyway overpowering. These headphones are well balanced across all genres of music. they handle counrty music as well as Trap music without any distortion or crackling or anything that would make the sound unpleasant.

I next did a distance test. I left my phone in my gym bag (with my wife) and went into the bathroom a good 30+ feet did my business and never skipped a beat.
Comes with a small carrying case, I'm undecided about the case at this time, its hard to fit both the charging cable and the headphones in to the case. so i either leave the charging cable at work and charge them there, or have them die at the gym.

Overall my opinion is these are good solid bluetooth earbuds. If you can afford to buy these and your stuck between getting these or the Powerbeats2, buy the Jaybirds X2 chances are you'll get a better product. (based on the the reviews from the powerbeats2 that seem to have some issues to be worked out).

Battery = 8 hours
Distance = 30+ feet
Comfort = wearable for 7-8 hours at a time.
Comes with 3 sets of ear fins, 3 sets of silicone tips and 3 sets of comply memory foam tips.

I will update this in a few weeks as to the longevity of the product, or if i run into any issues/problems.

Cons:
The instruction "Manuel" is online only, for me this wasnt really an issue but i can see it being an issue for those less computer literate.

Opening and closing the case is awkward. You have to push in the top, it just not a natural feeling way to open a case. I think that the previous clam shell version of the case is probably a better design for most people.

Update:

I've now been using the X2 headphones for about 2 months, (2) things I've noticed.

First if you use the comply tips and you sweat while using them you need to clean them before putting them away or the tips get a really weird unpleasant odor. I now clean these with a wet wipe before putting them back in the case and no problem.

Second issue I've encountered is that when I sweat more than normal enough to get into my ears the tips will slide out pretty easy. I haven't figured out a solution for this yet, maybe ill try using the regular tips.

Other then those 2 issues the X2 headphones work great. I haven't had any connectivity/sound/comfort issues at all. Battery life is outstanding I use these in the gym 2-3 hours 4 times a week and I'm charging every 3 days.

title: Great budget camera, you get what you pay for
text:
This camera is very cheap. I got it for $300. And for that price, it's great. But I have quickly outgrown the camera. The lens is not good. I use it the majority of the time as a 10.3mm F1.8 prime lens. The zoom is absolutely worthless in most situations other than in direct sunlight. Even indoors during daytime is the zoom not advised. The aperture takes a nosedive the instant you push the zoom ring. This means that you will be forced to use very high ISO's when zooming. And given this camera's poor ISO performance, I would just "zoom with your feet" as they say. The poor high ISO performance is to be expected from the small 1 inch sensor inside. The video features are impressive, given that it was released in 2012. 1080p 60i (30p) and 1080 60p are included, but the codec —AVCHD— is not great. With 24 or 28 mbps being the max data rates, the files have loads of Aliasing and Moiré, and fall apart with any light grading. On the postive side, RAW files are supported in photography. And they're fantastic. Lightroom breathes life into these files, allowing for an incredible amount of latitude being allowed in post to reduce noise, color balance, and frankly edit to your heart's content. I exclusively shoot in RAW, as the files are only 20 MB on average, and I enjoy the post processing stage.

I know I have been very critical, and perhaps I am expecting too much from a pocket camera released in 2012. I'm sure at the time it was a fantastic device. But its missing plenty of features. I firmly believe that if you're primarily shooting stills, the original RX100 is a much better value than its successors. The new RX100 models are far to expensive these days. For example, you could get an A6300 + Sigma 30mm F1.4 for roughly the same price as an RX100 Mark V, and have a significantly better camera.

title: The SSB signal was clipping so bad no one could hear a complete word
text:
I know this will be pulled ASAP but I feel it is only fair to let people know that this particular Radio has issues. Ranger Radio and Galaxy know of these issues and yet still fail to address the issues. Their support people are always polite and friendly, I just wish they had more say in quality control!
Got this radio in. Hooked up to base antenna and started calling. Got immediate response from skip as well as local that I was off frequency. The SSB signal was clipping so bad no one could hear a complete word, not to mention a sentence. No way to adjust the transmit frequency. The Clarifier only works on receive. Contacted Galaxy and they attempted to walk me through adjustments over phone. No go. Ended up sending it in for service and tuning. Got the radio back 2 weeks later, (today). Plugged it in and turned it on. The frequency counter jumped to 27.3843. This is the transmit frequency. I knew I was in trouble without even transmitting. The frequency on transmit should be 27.3850. (This is the frequency for channel 38 LSB by the way). After 30 minutes "warm up" time the frequency counter moved up to 27.3846. Still off 3 KHz. This doesn't sound like much but if you are listening to me, you are not going to answer me because you would have to retune your radio to do it. Most will just ignore you when your that far off frequency. You either sound like you’re in a deep cave when frequency is low or Donald Duck if your frequency is too high. A single KHz does make that much difference.
27.3850 is the standard center for transmission frequency on channel 38. On receive, when I tried to clarify the unit, I turned the clarifier all the way to the right and could not clear up the receive enough to even make out words. The reason I sent it in was to have it adjusted. Now it is worse than when I returned it. You have to wonder what is going on in the technician’s life that he or she could not see what I noticed 2 seconds after turning the radio on. Not a happy camper! Bear in mind that this issue only involves SSB. The AM never gave me any problems or bad reports.
While waiting for this unit to be "repaired", I purchased a Uniden Bearcat 980 SSB. It worked out of the box. The course and fine settings on the clarifier have been 12:00 dead center and never moved. Transmits and receives without any problems or negative reports. Doesn't drift on SSB frequencies and never has to be "warmed up" for 30 minutes before use.

Windows 7 Pro 32bit (I contacted Microsoft and they said it's an official license. It's not a hacked illegal copy.)

title: BEST $10 HEADPHONES EVER!!!
text:
These headphones sound significantly better than any $10 headphones have any right to sound. This is the first time I have purchased "budget" in-ear headphones, but I went ahead and got them after having such a positive experience with the legendary Koss Porta Pros. These headphones compare very favorably to various in-ear buds in the $40-$100 range I have used in the past (although I haven't used any of them recently enough to make direct comparisons). These are the sort of headphones that make my music sound so good and alive it's hard to take them off when I'm done. The only other headphones under $65 I've had this sort of experience with are the Porta Pros (and no, these don't sound as good as those do).

Minor negatives: The plastic they are made out of appears cheap. Also, the enclosed tips aren't that great, at least they didn't fit my ears well. The great sound I am describing was achieved only after attaching some tips from a defunct pair of Beats I had laying around. If the included tips fit your ears well, you might be fine with them, but most buyers should count on using some quality tips to get the best sound out of these. Also, they did not come with a carry case, but I've got half a dozen of those lying around from previous headphones, and one can't expect too much for $10.

I haven't had these that long, and I won't be that surprised if they start to short out in less than a year. Even if they do, they fully deserve five stars at this price point, and I'll be likely to buy them again.

title: Space cadet
text:
If space on your (physical) desktop is as valuable as it is on mine, and you don't want to spend a chunk of change on an all-in-one or something to tuck under, the Asus Chromebit may be a great solution for you. I am retired, and lead a fairly wandering life. Like most people, I don't spend a lot of time calculating the orbits of asteroids or comparing the molecular weights of quickly-deteriorating elements, so I don't really need a power house. I have used Chromebooks for about five years now, and I know that there actually are ways to use web servers to do these things. But mostly I just used my closed Asus 201 connected to a monitor and directed everything with a mouse. I decided to declutter and give the Chromebook to a friend who was wanting something to use to write the great modern novel and try the less powerful Chromebit. I've had it about a month now, with no complaints. It doesn't have support for an SD card as the 201 did, although I could do that easily with a dongle if I wished. I control it with a cheap LogitechK400 keyboard, which can sit on a corner of my desk or can be tucked into my lap if I want to go full lotus.

I don't think this will be the best solution to enjoy the full Chrome OS when the [nearly] full Android app library becomes available, but I didn't buy it for that. It is interesting that I now do most things 'in the cloud'. I have an NVIDIA Shield, and I can play games that reside somewhere in a galaxy far far away with it, and I can access almost any process with my Chromebook from some other cluster of galaxies. (Oopa. Wrong metaphor: I should have said clouds.) It's a sort of return to the old shared mainframe model, but with style and grace--and speed.

title: Works as good as it looks!
text:
I've had this keyboard for several months now and am hugely impressed with the quality. I'm a professional writer who can easily need to type over 10,000 words every day, so it's not like I use it lightly either. Normally I wouldn't buy such a cheap keyboard at all, but after killing three expensive Apple brand keyboards in six months due to spilling stuff on them (one time was entirely my dog's fault, the rest, well, I'm clumsy) I decided to give a spill resistant keyboard a try. I picked this one out purely because it looked cool.

First, I love the unusual key shape. It doesn't feel as weird as you'd imagine and has greatly reduced my problem with tending to hit two keys at once when I'm typing fast (I type 90WPM, and yes, of course, I touch type). The keys have a good bit of travel, but aren't overly loud and respond well to a soft touch.

It is definitely waterproof, and also coffee proof. The design also allows dirt and debris to be effortlessly removed from under the keys, and I can actually wash it in the sink! I haven't tried actually submerging it in water, but you can certainly hold it under the faucet and wash it.

It connected instantly and perfectly with my Mac Pro desktop. I don't know why some people can't get the function keys to work properly as mine work fine. Do note that you need to hold down the function key (the "Fn" key directly beside the right-hand "alt" key) while you press the function keys, though.

A few other things I love are that the keyboard has little grippy spots on the bottom that keep it from sliding around at all on my desk, and also super-bright caps lock and num lock lights so I notice when those keys have been hit. The battery life is amazing--I haven't had to change them even once yet!

So why only four stars? Because you need a precision screwdriver to install or change the batteries! Seriously, why don't they raise the price a couple of dollars and include a cheap screwdriver of the appropriate size? The only reason I was able to put the batteries in is because I have a side business building computers and so have a full precision screwdriver set already for that. I get that possibly this oddity is related to making it waterproof, but you can't expect the average keyboard buyer to have a $50 precision screwdriver set just laying around.

title: Love this monitor
text:
Love this monitor, but before I get to what I love about it I will tell you what I don't like about it.
1) It does not have g-sync
2) No internal speakers
3) last but not least, 2560x1080.
I
saw a reviewer complain about a lack of versa mount which while it does not come with it, one can be purchased separately which is what I did at a cost of $30.

Now for the meat and potato's of why I love it and why it only got 4 stars.
I purchased this monitor 2 years ago and contrary to other reviews, the black is black... except for the one pixel that is dead. irritating on a black screen but not something I notice any other time.

I also own 2 predator x34's and that is what I am going to use as a frame of reference.
1) The black on my benq is blacker than the predator x34. Back light bleed while there is no where near as bad as the x34
2) Even without gsync I have had no problems with screen tearing, ghosting or flickering.
2) The colors are deeper and cleaner than the x34
3) The x34 is 3440 x 1440 and the benq is 2560x1080 but to my eyes, I do not see a difference between the two when gaming, picture editing, or video editing since I set my font to a larger size in order to able to read the words.
4) Of the 4 x34's I have owned in the last 9 months, 2 have died on me and the colors are not consistent from one x34 to another where the benq has not had a color difference between them even with one having a single dead pixel.
5) 144Hz out of the box, no need to go into the menu to overclock like the x34 which comes out of the box at 60Hz and needs to be overclocked from the menu.
6) Even without Gsync my dual EVGA 1080TI in sli rig has no issues driving three of these monitors when gaming in surround at maximum settings at 144hz with a consistent 144 FPS. My x34's tend to run at or below 30 FPS when set to span and ultra settings.
7) They cost less than $650 and perform as well as my $1,000 x34's with better color and less failures.

As for why it did not get 5 stars, BenQ customer service sucks! I tried to contact them about the dead pixel and never got a reply to my emails and talking to them is worse than getting a tooth pulled... without Novocaine. Thankfully, one dead pixel across 3 monitors is a very small issue compared to 2 of 4 monitors failing. For the record, ASUS customer service sucks as well, and, if you have to send your monitor in for repair you have to pay for shipping and in most cases after 30 days you will have to pay a fee for repairs even though they have a 1 year warranty.

If you take anything away from this review let it be this, don't buy the predator x34.

title: Works great once it's set up, but hard to set up
text:
Here’s my gripes:

First the physical. Both units are larger than I expected and will definitely block additional outlets. The adapter side (the side that plugs into the router) has a 3 pronged outlet that fixes the plug-in orientation. It cannot be rotated 180 degrees and plugged in “upside down”. I have a duel wall outlet oriented vertically with one plug above the other. The adapter can only be plugged in with the passthrough plug on top and the LAN connections below (right side up). However, if your outlet is close to the floor like mine is, there isn’t enough clearance to plug the LAN cables in from the bottom if the adapter is plugged into the lower outlet. Therefore, it has to be plugged into the upper outlet thus blocking the lower outlet. The passthrough feature is a must to get any other use of this outlet.

The wifi unit is a 2 pronged plug and (I think) they’re both the same size, so the unit can be plugged in rotated 180 degrees (upside down). If your outlet is oriented horizontal, then the unit will be plugged in horizontal, which means the internal wifi antenna will be oriented horizontal (?). Correct me if I’m wrong. I read somewhere on Google that vertical antenna tend to spread the signal out sideways (wide), which is usually the desired orientation. In multi-story homes, horizontal antenna will spread the signal vertically to the different floors. I was able to plug mine in upside down above another intrusive power brick that was screwed into the middle screw of the outlet. The 2 pronged plug on the wifi unit has a raised face that helped it clear this protrusion and still plug snuggly into the outlet.

The buttons to pair the units are readily visible, but there’s a sneaky button to clone the wifi system. The WiFi Clone button is at the bottom of the column of indicator lights. It also functions as a green indicator light, same as the others and therefore camouflaged among the LEDs. The only way I found this was from the small cutout in the Installation Guide that shows a picture of a finger on that spot.

There are 3 separate passwords on the back labels, and they face the wall! So you might as well get out pen and paper and write everything down before you plug them in. When software asks for passwords, it is trial-and-error. Also, the passwords with the 4 sets of characters want the “-“ (dash) between them, and I think they are case sensitive (?).

Now the software. There are 2 programs in the Utility section for the Mac, and 2 for Windows (TL-PA4020P_V1_Utility_131023 and TL-WPA4226_V1_Utility_130527). They had different dates and I incorrectly assumed that one was an updated version of the other, so I only needed the latest of these 2 programs. WRONG! The second program is the key to setting this up.

Neither program indicates support for Windows 10, only WinXP thru Win8, and right off the bat I got an installation error – something about WinPcap 4.1.3. I did a Google search and found the solution here: [...] I had to install WinPcap 4.1.3.

It still wasn’t smooth sailing after installing the first utility (TL-PA4020P_V1_Utility_131023). It is called Powerline Utility, was difficult to use and limited in function. Only had very basic functions, would not accept spaces in the SSID (which mine has) and wanted the password from one of the units, but would only check the password if I entered the “-“ in between the sets of letters. It took me a while to figure that out. After a brief delay, it told me I entered the wrong password, which indicated it was the other similar letter password on the wifi unit.

I tried to update the firmware, but it asked me for the NVM and PIB files. There were none in the firmware update I downloaded - only a .BIN file.

The firmware update instructions warned to check the version number or the update might permanently ruin the units. I could not find the version number on my units (and I checked thoroughly). Anyway, the update didn’t tell me what version it was for.

The firmware update .pdf told me to hit the “connect” button, but in the Powerline Utility screen, there was only a “modify” button in its place.

The instructions further state to log into the unit with ip address 192.168.1.1. WRONG! The correct address is 192.168.200.247. I couldn’t find this solution on Google. I stumbled on it when I finally decided to download the second program (TL-WPA4226_V1_Utility_130527) in case I had a compatibility issue. This was a standalone .exe file Powerline Scan.exe, and the key to getting everything started. It gave me the same screen as Powerline Utility, but this time with the “connect” button. It also revealed the correct ip address for the unit. From here it takes you to the typical wifi modem web based setup screen, where you can set the SSID, change passwords, etc. I was even able to upgrade the firmware, as this time it asked me for a .bin file, which I had. This is not for the faint of heart though.

Man this was a b!tch to set up!

title: WORKS...BUT MAY TAKE SOME EFFORT!!
text:
These will work...but may require extra work on your part. For me, my 2008 Mac Pro would not recognize the dock/drive. After messing around trying to get it to seat correctly in the Mac, still wouldn't show up in Disk Utility. Took advice of another Amazon user loosened the 3 screws inside the dock just kinda moved the little connector around and then re-tightened the screws. Made sure the Mac Pro sled was FULLY pushed in so it seated correctly...FINALLY it is recognized. This is not an isolated story. They get buried in all the good reviews but these ICY DOCKS often show up DOA or people have to mess with them to get them to work. Just know that it may take a little work. Should not be that hard, thus 3 stars.

I will be moving to using a PCIe SSD adapter, which will give much faster performance anyway. Consider looking at something like: "OWC Accelsior S PCIe Adapter for 2.5" SATA III SSD Drives" for faster performance.

title: Supports Trim!  Good speed.
text:
I got a 500GB SSD recently and have been looking for an enclosure for it and so I tried the Sabrent-UASP one. A couple of things I was looking for:

- Support for UASP: Not sure if there's a way to tell this, but
- Good speed: Using HDTach, about 200 MB/sec average, random access: 0.1 msec, burst: ~282 MB/sec
- Support for Trim: Ran Trimcheck and this is the FIRST USB 3.0 enclosure that passed as supporting Trim

That last one (Trim) was a big one, as I was having doubts about using the SSD in an enclosure because of lack of Trim support, but I found found one that works!

Another plus (to me) is that the cable has two of the "normal" USB connectors instead of one of the dual-wide micro USB, which I think are too fragile. Also, it actually has a working power button!

A couple cons:

- Case is plastic (but they provide sponges for the front and top so the SSD is snug inside).
- It's kind of hard to get open, as the case is really smooth and no grip and you have to kind of push the rear top edge to slide it open. But then again, that (hard to open) might be a good thing!

title: SUPER PURCHASE
text:
Not sure what other reviewers are expecting or how much experience they've had but after 40 photographic years (30 as a living) this cord's a dream.

25 yrs ago I tried one of these for $90 and got a stretched, strained 18 to 24 inches. That's not much different from what Canon's still offering! This cord EASILY gives 5ft and will strain to 6.5ft. ANYBODY THAT NEEDS MORE THAN AN ARMS LENGTH OUGHT TO BE USING A SLAVE ANYWAY.

Construction is stout and reliable. Like any piece of flash equipment you might have to jiggle it a little to make sure it's seated but I have to do that with my $600 Canon flash, probably shouldn't be surprised with a $19.95 cord!

Used it in the "Coeneculum" (Upper Room) in Jerusalem 30 min. ago and got shots worthy of a magazine. Shot 20 arm length pix from every angle before next group came in (15 min.) and never had a misfire. Used it to side light and up light some worn and faded carvings yesterday. Nobody else got the shots but me.

title: Perfect for my Needs
text: I bought this for a specific purpose, but I think it would be good for others as well.  I have a 12.9" iPad pro, so a reasonably large tablet, that I want to pair with my MacBook Pro as a 2nd monitor.  I bought a different stand which I returned, and took a chance on this one.  WHen I am on the road, I use my MacBook sitting on a desk or table.  When I am at home, the Macbook sits on top of a nice "Rain Design M Stand" which lifts the macbook up in the air by 3-6 inches (its on an angle).  This Kabcon tablet stand allows me to easily mach the height of the tablet with the screen on the macbook, either very close to the desk, or 6" up in the air.  The joints on the stand seem tight enough that you could use the tablet as a tablet (touch screen), but I use it mainly to make the tablet a PC display or a TV-like vide device.  The Kabcon stand is strong and sturdy, but it folds up to smaller than 7x7x2, so i can put it into my backpack without it taking up much space like the other tables stand I returned.  The listing says its made of aluminum, but as one reviewer noted, the 2 pillars that connect the base plate with the tablet plate are plastic on the outside if not all plastic..  I feel like its a benefit that reduces the weight, and I cannot see any condition under which these would break.  When its in my backpack, the plastic parts are totally covered by the aluminum plates.  When I am using it, the Tablet is far more delicate than the stand.  So, I dont fell I have been deceived, but make sure you know this f it matters to you.  I dont use a case on my iPad, but I think this would accommodate most cases.  I think this will outlast my iPad.  OK, so what would make it 6-Stars?  Maybe a cloth bag that would slip around it to protect it while in my backpack (or protect other items from the aluminum.  What would I change if I could?  I'd like to have it in Space Grey to match my iPad, but the silver color is really nice.  Also, the rubber Caps that sit on the bent metal that holds the Tablet up can slip off while you are carrying it around.  An extra set of those would be a nice touch.  I cover it with the light plastic bags that it was covered in shipping, and remember to look for those caps anytime I take it out of my backpack.

title: Convenient and Accurate
text:
I chose this monitor instead of a Polar because of its convenience, as I didn't want to strap a Polar monitor around my chest all the time. The only thing that initially confused me about this monitor is how the heck I could get the readings on it, as it doesn't have a screen or face. After a couple internet searches I determined that I could upgrade to the $15 Map My Run/Workout app on my iPhone to sync with it (previously I just used the free Map My Run app). Once I did that, I had no problems syncing up so long as I used that app when I was running or working out. (The app has different options for different workouts, runs, walks, lifting, etc.)

I am very pleased with its accuracy and the fact that it stays in place on my forearm even on long runs when it's hot out and I'm sweaty. I have also used it with no problems in rainstorms (torrential downpours) - it really is waterproof. I used it in conjunction with a Polar monitor to test its accuracy and it was almost on par. The only time it wasn't was when I was doing plyo or sprints - basically there was a bit of a lag in between intense workouts and coming to a stop/walk. The Polar was able to capture the rapid decrease in my heart rate, but this monitor took a few seconds longer. It's not anything extreme and it certainly doesn't worry me enough to not use it or question its accuracy. I should mention that my heart rate gets very high (180+ BMP) when I'm doing intense exercise and then falls very rapidly when I stop, so that may have something to do with it. I bought a couple replacement bands in case the one this monitor came with got worn out or un-velcro-ey, but so far I haven't had to swap them out. All in all, I'm glad I bought it.

title: Need to get a grip? Well can't fix your life, but this grip is great for the K-7, K-5 Pentax no end. Cheaply, Please read on.
text:
Great Expectations!

No, that really is a lie actually. Mine were quite tepid as far as my excitement, and expectations. They say you get what you pay for. I say it to all my friends, and family alike. Everything without exception is built to a cost. Commodities work this way. Remember Routers used to cost over $500.00?? Yes you do. I know I did. Along with that MCSE degree you needed to interface it. Well, now they are plug and play for less $50.00.

This one grip is kind of like that. Except it will NOT have the Weather seals of the Factory OEM unit by Pentax. Please know this going in, and all is right with the world. With all the major food groups covered here such as shutter release, locking collar, AF, and more, others state what magic soup buttons come with here. I wanted to share that I am a big person on Ergos, and this grip solves one big gripe for me on what is the best camera I have ever bought.

The Pentax K-5 ii. With my Gorilla sized hands, this is not a DSLR camera, but a small bridge camera with a glandular problem.

Sure it is wide enough, but tall is not in the cards on the K-5 ii. So my small finger has no where to go.

This grip gives me the finger.

Well, that is, it gives my little finger a proper purchase to land on. On top of this, this made in China device feels solid in the hand, fits the K-5 ii a treat. Almost really does look like it belongs on the camera. My mantra on great pictures is the basics, and yes, that camera better fit your hand, and this battery grip by DSTE fills my hand with camera in such a great way. Button feel is average, a bit mushy in actuation, and will not in any way displace the factory grip, I know, I played with one, and just could never swallow that "are you nuts price." Yes, you can now get them for $120.00 or so. I got mine here, this DTSE for $36.00 to my door!

The rotary dials for Shutter, and Aperture are bit chinzy in feel, in that they don't have that nice release, detent feel of the real deal. Okay now that all the carping about the real deal, and all is out of the way, will it work? Heck yes! My camera functions just fine with Auto Battery detection of all modes, AA Battery, In Body, and In Grip just fine thank you.

So really should you buy the Factory Grip? Now that is really why you are reading this and other reviews here right? Of course it is. I did the same thing, and thought, okay, no downpours of rain, snow, sleet in the cards for this camera. Could I spend the money more wisely, and invest on what I saved on another lens or something? You bet! I did, I have a Sigma on the way ordered today!

Now if you do have weather, and beat your camera up, don't waste your money here, and go buy the original Factory OEM Pentax Grip, do not look back, do not pass GO, and do NOT collect $200.00. You will have a more robust Grip no doubt. Better button actuation, better feeling control dials, and the weather seals too. For me, and I have a feeling many others, this DSTE Battery Grip will do just fine. Even if it dies in 2 years, I got my money's worth. Crazy huh?? Commodities work that way too. They die, you just go buy another one. Like a Router, this will work a treat till it breaks something, and you buy another. Welcome to the value cycle. Now lets go take some pictures. V.C.

title: Best lightweight laptop I've ever used - even better than Macbook Air
text:
This is one of the best laptops I've ever used, period. I'm a tech savvy buyer, and have owned a range of laptops - Windows and Macs. Before this, my most recent laptop was a Macbook Air.

After a month of using the Samsung 13" model, here are my observations:

Pros:
- Incredibly light; a Dell XPS or Macbook Air feels heavy if you compare
- Beautiful screen with vivid colors
- Smooth as silk touchpad, accurate and responsive
- Speedy enough for most everyday tasks

Cons:
- Mini HDMI port requires an extra adapter purchase
- No touch screen

Battery life is 4-5 hours in typical use, with reasonable screen brightness. It's not at all a problem for me, and is outweighed by the lightness, screen and solid performance.
